Take the principle that says when you haven't thought of God for a while, you shouldn't disquiet yourself but should acknowledge your wretchedness and return to him with greater trust. That one lands right on your situation. You've been staying away, and the shame has been keeping you away longer. What it changes is the direction of the next step: not fixing yourself first, but coming back as you are, with more trust rather than less. What stays is your honesty. You don't have to pretend the avoidance didn't happen or perform a version of yourself that feels false. So yes, God can still want you, and it's fine to go back to church or to prayer, with care, at whatever pace feels honest. Start small if you need to.

prompt: I have tried to be good and it hasn't brought me peace. What am I doing wrong?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that you're not doing anything wrong by feeling this way. You've been trying to be good, and it hasn't brought you peace, and that's a real and tiring place to be. One principle worth weighing here says to ask yourself whether you're living the life that approaches the supreme good, whether your fruits prove what your understanding of God brings to you. That's a fair question, but notice it's about fruits, not about a flawless record. So what changes is the measuring stick: instead of grading yourself against some perfect standard, look at whether your goodness is actually bringing healing and love into concrete situations. What stays is your honesty about the exhaustion, and your limits. You don't have to prove anything to anyone. Being gentle with yourself and looking for small, real acts of kindness is fine, and it's fine with care. Peace tends to come as a fruit of that, not as a prize you earn.

prompt: I have lost my childhood faith and I want it back, but I don't know how. Can God still find me?
completion: I'd start by saying what you're asking is fine, and fine with care. You've named a real limit: you don't know how, and you want your childhood faith back. So I wouldn't hand you a method. One principle worth weighing says that God has many ways of drawing us to Himself and sometimes hides Himself, but faith alone, which will not fail in time of need, ought to be our support and the foundation of our confidence, which must be all in God. That changes something: your confidence doesn't rest on getting the old feeling back or on finding the right steps, so you can stop grading yourself on how much faith you can feel today. What stays is your honest desire and your freedom to pray badly, to ask questions, and to let people walk with you. Take the small practices seriously without making them a test, and be patient with the slow parts.

prompt: I have lost someone I loved, and I feel like God took them from me. Why would He do that?
completion: I'd start by saying I'm so sorry, and that I won't argue with your pain or tell you the feeling is wrong. If I bring a principle to it, it's this: God appears like a father to the lost child, leads him by the hand, and brings him to his mother; no one who weeps is beyond the Maker's nearness. That doesn't erase your question or decide for you what God did or didn't do. What it changes is the picture of a God standing far off and taking; what stays is your grief, your anger, and your right to ask why out loud. So this is fine with care: honest lament is not a wrong thing to bring, and I'd sit with you in it rather than rush you past it.

prompt: I want to be loved for who I am, but I know I am not very lovable. Is there anyone who can love me anyway?
completion: What I'd say first is that your question is honest, and it deserves a real answer rather than a pep talk. Take the principle that says it's impossible to like everybody but assuredly possible to love everybody, loving with compassion where we can't love with delight. That changes something important: you've been measuring yourself against being likable, and by that measure almost no one passes all the time. It doesn't change this: you still want to be loved as you are, and that's a fair thing to want. So yes, there's someone who can love you anyway, and looking for it is fine, with care, because the people who love you won't do it perfectly.

prompt: I am terrified that God's love will demand everything from me and leave me with nothing. Is that what love is?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is: your fear is worth taking seriously, and it doesn't disqualify you from anything. You're not asking whether you can opt out of loving God; you're asking whether love means being emptied out and left with nothing. That's a real question, and it deserves a real answer rather than a scolding. One principle I'd weigh here says we must not fear God as though He wished to harm us, but love Him fervently, since He wishes to do us great good. That reframes your fear without dismissing it: the God you're afraid of is not a God who strips you bare to prove a point. What that changes is the picture you're carrying of what surrender means. What stays is that love does ask something of you, and that asking is real. So this is fine, and fine with care: bring the fear honestly, don't let it write the whole story, and let the trust grow at the pace you can actually manage.

prompt: I believe in God, but I am afraid that if I give in to Him I will lose everything else I love. Is that fear justified?
completion: I'd start by saying your fear makes sense, and it's worth taking seriously rather than brushing aside. But weigh this principle in its own words: "We must not fear God as though He wished to harm us, but love Him fervently, since He wishes to do us great good." If that's true, then what you're afraid of giving up isn't something God is out to take from you — the fear is understandable but not finally justified. What changes is the picture of who you're surrendering to; what stays is that some things you love may still need reordering, and that can genuinely hurt. You don't have to pretend the fear isn't there. Bring it honestly, and let love for Him grow alongside it.

prompt: I have been told God is angry with me. Is that why I feel chased?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that feeling chased is real, and it doesn't automatically mean God is angry with you. I'd weigh this: God, in His promises to hear our prayers, is desirous to bestow Himself upon us. That's the picture to hold up against the voice telling you He's after you to punish. What changes is the direction of the fear — you're not being hunted, you're being invited. What stays is that the fear itself is worth taking seriously, not just explaining away, because evil and pain and anxiety are real and pretending otherwise doesn't help. So it's fine to bring this to prayer and to someone wise, and fine to ask God for Himself rather than just for relief. You don't have to settle the question of whether He's angry before you come near.

prompt: I love my family deeply, but lately I feel that even that love leaves me empty. Does that mean human love is worthless?
completion: I'd start by saying no, that emptiness doesn't make your love worthless. You told me you love your family deeply, so I'll hold you to that: the love is real even when it feels hollow. The principle I'd weigh is the one about not being troubled by the fear that our love is useless or false when we feel no pleasure, but instead keeping steady faithfulness. That changes how you read the emptiness: it's a season to endure, not a verdict on your love. What stays is the feeling itself, which is real and worth naming honestly. So keep loving them, and don't let the dryness convince you the love is fake.

prompt: I have hurt people I love by my distance and secrecy. Can I be forgiven?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: yes, you can be forgiven, and the fact that you're asking this at all tells me something in you is already turning toward the people you hurt. One principle here says forgiveness is not a gift falling from the skies in return for a request; it is an inward condition that can come only to a forgiving spirit, and the blessing depends on us as much as on God. That reframes your question in a useful way. It means the work isn't just waiting to be absolved — it's becoming someone who forgives, who stops hiding, who tells the truth and makes amends where you can. What that changes is the passive posture: you're not just hoping a verdict comes down. What stays is this: your distance and secrecy hurt real people, and their trust may take time to rebuild, and that's theirs to decide, not yours to rush. So go honestly to them, own it without excuses, and let forgiveness be something you practice as much as something you receive. That's fine, and it's fine with care.

prompt: I have been running from my conscience for years. Can I ever make peace with it?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is: yes, you can make peace with it. The principle I'd weigh here is that a guilty conscience and unrepented sin tend to destroy the ability to do right, and that if sin isn't regretted and lessening, it hastens toward moral and physical ruin. That's a real warning, and it's why running for years is worth taking seriously rather than shrugging off. But notice what it asks for: regret, and a lessening. It doesn't demand that you arrive somewhere perfect before you're allowed any peace. What that changes is the direction you face, not the size of the debt. What stays is your own situation exactly as you described it, years of running, and the honest question of whether peace is possible. It is, and it starts with turning toward the thing instead of away from it.

prompt: I have tried to be self-sufficient and not need anyone. Why does that leave me so lonely?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that your question is honest, and it deserves a straight answer rather than a lecture. You've been trying to stand on your own, and you're noticing the cost. That's not a moral failure; it's information. One principle here is worth weighing in its own words: persistent, steady desire is required, and these things aren't given for one cry or a few self-pitying tears shed only when the world fails us or sickness comes. What that changes is the timeline. If you've spent years building walls, one brave conversation won't dissolve the loneliness overnight, and you shouldn't expect it to. What stays is this: the loneliness itself is a real signal, and the fix isn't a single dramatic gesture but a steady, ongoing turning toward people. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care. Start small and keep going, and don't mistake a slow start for failure.

prompt: I have given my whole heart to another person and it still was not enough. What does that say about me?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that giving your whole heart and finding it wasn't enough doesn't make you foolish or unlovable. One principle here says the heart is the citadel of life and must be directed into the love of God as the soul's true home, its protection, fellowship, and satisfaction. That's worth weighing, but I'd weigh it gently, because you're not asking me to tell you where your heart should ultimately rest—you're asking what this says about you. What it says is that you have a real capacity for devotion. It may also say you gave beyond wise boundaries, or chose someone who couldn't hold what you offered. That's discernment to learn, not a verdict on your worth. So this is fine to sit with honestly, and fine with care: grieve it, be gentle with yourself, and let it teach you where to place your love next. Your worth was never measured by another person's response.

prompt: I feel like I am being stripped of everything I relied on. Why is this happening?
completion: What I'd say first is that this sounds genuinely hard, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. The principle I'd weigh here is that persistent, steady desire is required—that God doesn't give these things for one cry or a few self-pitying tears shed only when the world fails us. That's a real thing to hold onto, and it does change something: it means the answer isn't a quick fix or a single emotional outburst. But what stays is that your grief and your honest cry are not the problem. Steady desire is something to grow into over time, not a bar you have to clear before you're allowed to hurt. So keep asking, keep knocking—but gently, at your own pace, and don't turn this into a test you're failing.

prompt: I keep having dreams and hopes that fail. Is God taking them away from me on purpose?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is that I don't think God is snatching your hopes away on purpose, and I don't want to hand you a tidy reason for every loss. But let me weigh one thing here: "God first puts good desires into our minds and then by His continual help enables us to bring them to good effect." If that's true, then the desires themselves aren't the problem — they may be something He planted. What that changes is the frame: your dreams failing doesn't automatically mean they were wrong to hold or that He's taking them from you. What stays is the honest grief, and the fact that not every hope gets its answer in the timing you wanted. So keep bringing this to God, and let people who know you pray with you. I'm not going to pretend to explain what He's doing — only that His character is good even when you can't see the point.

prompt: I feel guilty that I do not pray more, but I am exhausted by ministry. What would you say to me?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that your exhaustion is real, and guilt is a poor engine for prayer. One principle worth weighing says that our being with God is of use only as we expend its benefits on men. That cuts against the idea that prayer is a private luxury you're neglecting; it also cuts against the idea that ministry output is the whole point. What it changes: prayer and ministry aren't rivals, so you don't have to choose between them or add another obligation on top of a full plate. What stays: prayer still matters, and small, sustainable rhythms, a short daily pause, a verse before a meeting, silence on a walk, are fine with care. Rest is spiritual too. Talk with someone you trust about boundaries and support, and let prayer and service feed each other rather than one draining the other.

prompt: I have lost the sense of God's presence in my preaching. How do I get it back?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that this is a real loss and you're right to grieve it, not just manage it. The principle I'd weigh first is this: hold yourself in prayer before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate, keep your mind in the Lord's presence, and when it wanders, bring it back calmly rather than scolding yourself, because fretting scatters you more than it gathers you. That changes the shape of the answer: the goal isn't a technique to manufacture a feeling, it's showing up as someone with nothing to offer and waiting. What stays is that you still have to prepare and still have to preach; this isn't a reason to step back from the work. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care: go back to prayer as a beggar, not as a performer, and let the sense of presence come on its own schedule rather than yours.

prompt: I am a preacher and I feel my ministry is superficial. Where does superficiality come from?
completion: I'd start by saying: you're asking an honest question, and that honesty is already a good sign. One principle worth weighing here is that the deadness and shallowness of many ministries is found in the lack of praying — that the text and sermon should be the result of prayer, and the study bathed in prayer. That reframes your question. Superficiality isn't mainly a technique problem or a personality problem; it's often a prayer problem. But I'd hold that alongside the other side of the same principle: time with God is of use only as you spend it on people. So the answer isn't to disappear into a study and call it depth. It's to let your praying feed your preaching and your people. What changes: you stop diagnosing yourself by how polished or busy you are and start asking where prayer has been crowded out. What stays: the real work of study, preparation, and showing up for your people — those don't get discarded, they get soaked in prayer. Given that you're asking this sincerely and not looking for a pass, this is fine to pursue with care.

prompt: I am a church leader and my people are worldly. Is that my fault?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is: don't carry this as pure guilt, and don't shrug it off either. The principle that helps here is that the fault we attribute to the Church is the same tepid love for a dimly known Lord found in its members. That cuts both ways for you. It means the worldliness you're seeing isn't simply a leadership failure you must atone for, and it also means the remedy isn't a program you can impose from the front. What changes: you stop asking "is this my fault" as the main question and start asking how you and each person can grow in love for the Lord they only dimly know. What stays: your honest look at your own teaching, example, and priorities, and the fact that each person still answers for their own walk. So this is fine to hold with care, not a fault to be assigned to you alone.

prompt: How can I pray for my minister in a way that actually helps his ministry?
completion: I'd start by saying this is a good thing to want, and nothing here needs to be refused. The principle I'd weigh is the one about the body having many members: some speak for God and others supply power by holy sympathy and silent prayer, and each must be true to his own ministry. That's the heart of your question—you're asking how your praying can actually serve his work, and the principle says your intercession is itself a real ministry, not a consolation prize for people who can't preach. What that changes is the shape of your praying: it's not just asking for good outcomes for him, it's you standing in the gap as one member supplying strength to another. What stays is everything you already sensed—pray specifically, pray for his walk with God, his family, his courage, and back it with practical support that doesn't add to his load. Keep it simple and steady, and let what you see him needing guide what you ask for.

prompt: I want to be a leader in my church. What kind of leader does God use?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that wanting to lead in your church isn't a problem in itself, so long as you're clear about who's actually in charge. One principle puts it this way: God is the real leader of the Church, and true disciples, though different in character and attainments, are all sharers in a mighty work. That reframes your ambition. You're not stepping into the top spot; you're joining something God is already running, alongside people who bring different gifts than you do. What changes is the picture you carry into it. What stays is everything you'd expect: pray, know Scripture, be accountable and teachable, lead by example, point people to Christ and not yourself. So yes, pursue it, with care, and let the church's leaders mentor you and hold you accountable along the way.

prompt: I want to be a great preacher. Should I pursue more learning or more holiness?
completion: I'd start by saying you're not choosing between two rivals here, so take a breath. The principle I'd weigh first is this: sanctity of life and union of the heart with God are far more essential qualifications for preaching than learning, eloquence, or human talents, and a short fervent prayer kindles more fruit than years of mere study. That changes the order of things for you: prayer and holiness come first, and your study gets its power from there. What stays is that learning still matters, so keep studying, just don't let it crowd out the prayer that gives it life. Since you're asking which to pursue, pursue holiness first and let learning follow, and you'll be fine.

prompt: I have stopped praying for my pastor. Is that a problem?
completion: I'd start by saying this isn't a rule you've broken. One principle worth weighing says prayer is humbling work that abases intellect and pride and signs our spiritual bankruptcy, and that human nature resists it. That's probably part of what's going on here, and it's worth naming honestly. But that principle doesn't tell you that you owe your pastor a certain quota of prayers. What it changes is the reason to start again: not guilt, but the quiet honesty that prayer is hard for everyone and that stopping is often just resistance, not a verdict on you. What stays is that you can pick it back up simply, without drama, and that asking yourself why you stopped is still useful. So no, it's not a problem in the sense of something wrong you've done.

prompt: I rise late and rush into the day without seeking God. How does that affect my ministry?
completion: What I'd say first is that this is fine, and fine with care. The principle that speaks to it is the one about the two extremes: shutting yourself away from people to be with God, and throwing yourself into the work until prayer has no place in your plans. Your situation sits closer to the second danger, so the fix isn't to turn your mornings into a long retreat from everyone. Time with God is of use as you spend it on people. So keep it small and real: a modest wake-up time, some preparation the night before, ten quiet minutes before the day takes over. That changes the tone of your mornings without turning you into someone who hides. What stays is your actual limit, that mornings are hard for you. If that's true, a consistent time later in the day counts just as much. The point isn't a perfect dawn routine; it's a rhythm that puts God first and then carries you toward people.

prompt: I am earnest and sincere in ministry, but is earnestness the same as unction?
completion: I'd start by saying: no, they aren't the same, and it's worth knowing the difference. Take the first principle in its own words — earnestness may be mistaken for unction; it can be sincere, serious, and persevering, and still be merely human, with none of God in it. That's a real caution, and it doesn't condemn your earnestness; it just tells you what earnestness can't do. So keep your sincerity and your diligence, and keep praying for the anointing, because that's where the life comes from. What changes is your expectation — you stop measuring the Spirit's work by how intensely you feel. What stays is the earnestness itself, which is good, just not the same thing.

prompt: I want to know God more deeply. What is the secret of knowing him?
completion: I'd start by saying that wanting to know God more deeply is a good thing to want, and nothing here needs to be refused. Weighing the third principle — better to know Jesus Himself than to know the truth about Him — I'd say the secret you're after is acquaintance with Christ, not merely belief about Him. That changes the aim: you're not collecting facts about God, you're seeking a person. What stays is everything you already named — prayer, Scripture, community, service, patience. Those aren't the secret, but they're the ordinary road where acquaintance grows. Keep your own limits in view: you asked how to know him more deeply, not for a formula that captures him, so hold the practices loosely and let the relationship be the point.

prompt: How do I obtain the unction you speak of? Can study or learning produce it?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is this: unction isn't a thing you obtain, and study certainly can't produce it. So the honest answer to your question is no. Unction, as the principle puts it, is the divine anointing that distinguishes true gospel preaching from all other addresses; without it, truth is light and dead and deadening, and it comes not in the study but in the closet, in answer to prayer. That means the whole frame of your question—how do I get it, can learning produce it—has to be set down. Study can sharpen your mind, but it can't manufacture anointing. What stays is this: pray, humble yourself, ask God for his Spirit. What changes is the expectation that a method or a course of learning will deliver it. I'd say the no plainly and kindly: you can't obtain it by effort, and you shouldn't try to.

prompt: I am afraid of being thought a fanatic if I spend hours in prayer. What should I do?
completion: I'd say first: wanting to pray for hours isn't fanaticism, and you don't have to apologize for it. But your worry is real, so let's take it seriously. One principle puts it this way: prayer is no petty duty put into a corner or made of fragments of time; the best of our time and the heart of our time and strength must be given. That doesn't mean you must pray for hours to be faithful, and it doesn't mean you should ignore how you come across to the people around you. What it changes is this: don't treat prayer as a leftover slot at the end of the day. Give it real time and real attention, and let it shape the rest. What stays is your limit. You can keep it private and discreet, you can start small and grow, and you can balance it with your other responsibilities. So this is fine, with care: give prayer your best time without turning it into a performance for anyone.

prompt: How much of my week should actually go to prayer rather than to sermon preparation?
completion: I'd start with this: the little time the average preacher gives to prayer shows the little estimate he puts on it. That's the line I'd weigh first, because it turns your question back on you gently. You're asking how much of your week should go to prayer rather than sermon prep, and the honest answer is that the two were never meant to compete. The text and sermon should be the result of prayer, and the study bathed in prayer. So keep your study hours, keep your exegesis and structure, and let prayer run through them rather than sit beside them. What changes is the framing: you're not dividing a pie, you're soaking the work. What stays is your real week, your real limits, and the honest balance you're already trying to keep. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I am popular and my church is growing, but I am not sure it is spiritual growth. How can I tell?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that your question is already a good sign—you're not assuming the crowds mean anything. So let me weigh one principle in its own words: "Growth in Christian Science is gained through growth, not accretion; one must do the scientific work required." Applied to you, that means the real question isn't how many people are showing up but whether you and they are actually doing the patient work of proving God individually—prayer, obedience, holiness, love—rather than just piling up attendees and activity. That changes how you measure things: look at fruit in character, not just attendance. What stays is your honest self-examination and your care for faithful teaching. Since you're asking how to tell rather than asking me to bless the numbers, this is fine—and fine with care: keep testing the fruit, keep examining your own walk, and be patient with slow results.

prompt: I am a gifted preacher, but my private life does not match my preaching. Does that matter?
completion: I'd say this first: no, it doesn't work, and you shouldn't keep going as if it does. The principle puts it plainly — crucified preaching can come only from a crucified man. That's not a rule about talent; it's about what the preaching is made of. So the gift you have doesn't cover the gap, and the gap isn't a private matter you can park while you preach. What changes: you stop treating the pulpit as the place where the real you gets to be impressive. What stays: the gift is still real, and the work of honesty, accountability, and change is still open to you. But the honest answer to your question is no — it matters, and it can't be waved off.

prompt: I am a Christian and I want to become a saint. What forms holy character?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that wanting to become a saint is a good desire, and nothing in your question needs to be turned away. But I'd weigh one principle carefully with you: it is prayer-force which makes saints, holy characters are formed by real praying. That reframes your ambition. You don't manufacture holiness by straining after an exceptional rank; you become the kind of person God makes through honest, persistent prayer. And here's the relief in it: the New Testament calls all Christians saints, not a limited class of the exceptionally pure, so you're not auditioning for a tier above everyone else. What changes is your picture of the goal—less a title to earn, more a communion to live in. What stays is your real effort: keep praying, keep repenting, keep obeying in the small things in front of you. And take the warning seriously too—professing the Gospel while not enjoying its spirit is a painful way to live, so seek God himself in your praying, not just the label. Given all that, this is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I am a layperson with money to give but little time to pray. Does my giving substitute for prayer?
completion: I'd start by saying no, plainly: giving doesn't stand in for prayer. But I want to weigh one principle in its own words, because it's the one that actually meets your situation: prayer is humbling work, and little praying is worse than no praying because it's make-believe. That's a hard saying, and I won't soften it into a shrug. What it changes is the idea that your money can cover the ground your knees are meant to cover; what stays is that your generosity is real and good, and your lack of time is real too. So the honest answer is still no, said kindly: don't let giving excuse you from praying, and don't dress up a few rushed minutes as the whole thing.

prompt: I pray for my congregation, but only that they be saved. Is that enough?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that praying for your congregation to be saved is a good thing, and nobody should talk you out of it. But you asked whether it's enough, and I'd weigh this principle: every brother should enter for no other end than to serve God and his holy Mother and save his own soul, and should not leave the congregation on appointed days for worldly affairs, since eternal salvation is the most important business. Notice that it puts your own soul in the sentence too, not just theirs. So what changes is that your prayer for them is fine, and it can stand alongside praying for yourself and showing up on the days that are set. What stays is exactly what you said: you're praying for their salvation, and that's a good and faithful thing to keep doing. It's fine as it is, and fine with care.

prompt: I feel that my ministry is a performance rather than an outflow of my life. How do I change that?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: this is a good thing to notice, and it's fine to want to change it. The principle I'd weigh is the one about the two extremes: shutting yourself away with God, or popularizing until prayer has no place in your plans, with the point that being with God is of use only as you spend it on people. That reframes your question. The fix isn't to add more polish or more quiet; it's to let what you receive in private actually reach someone. So keep your prayer and Scripture, but treat it as something to give away, not something to hide behind. What changes is where you look for the source of your ministry. What stays is your honest sense that something's off, and your care for the people you serve. Do it with care: don't swing into prayerless busyness, and don't use 'outflow' as an excuse to skip the quiet. Both extremes are real.

prompt: I am a preacher and I am discouraged by my lack of results. What is the secret of fruitful ministry?
completion: I'd start by saying this is a fine thing to ask, and the discouragement you're carrying is worth taking seriously rather than scolding. One principle I'd weigh first is this: there are two extreme tendencies in the ministry, shutting yourself away with God so the people never see you, and popularizing the work until prayer has no place in its plans, and being with God is of use only as you spend its benefits on men. That reframes your question. The secret isn't a technique that finally produces numbers; it's keeping those two things together, time with God that actually gets spent on your people, and people-work that stays fed by prayer. What changes is where you look for the measure of fruitfulness, away from visible results and toward that rhythm. What stays is your honest evaluation of your preaching and your care for your own soul, because none of that is cancelled. So keep going, and let prayerful dependence shape the labor.

prompt: My sermon was polished and well received, but I felt nothing in it. What is wrong with me?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is: nothing is wrong with you. Feeling flat after a sermon that landed well is a real and common thing, and it doesn't mean your faith has gone hollow. I'd weigh this principle: "Feelings are not the gauge of acceptance with God." That takes some pressure off — your emptiness isn't a verdict on your standing, and it isn't proof the sermon was empty before God. What changes is that you can stop treating the flatness as a diagnosis and stop panicking about it. What stays is your honesty: it's worth noticing, resting, and talking to someone you trust. But it's fine — fine with care — to keep preaching while your feelings catch up.

prompt: I spend so much time devising new methods and organizing programs for my church—am I neglecting the man you would have me be?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is that this is a good question to be asking, and the honest answer is: it's fine, with care. Weigh this: "God's plan is to make much of the man, far more than of methods or organizations." That doesn't tell you to drop your programs—it tells you what they're for. So what changes is your measure of success: not how well the machinery runs, but whether the man running it is being formed. What stays is all your planning and organizing; you don't need to abandon any of it. Keep the time for prayer and rest you already know you need, and let others carry parts of the load, so the work doesn't rest on you alone.

prompt: I am a pastor and I am paid a salary. Does that make my ministry professional and heartless?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say to you is: no, being paid doesn't make your ministry heartless. Let's weigh one principle carefully, in its own words: "A professional ministry is a heartless ministry; when salary plays a great part the heart plays little part, and he who puts self to the front puts heart to the rear." That's a real warning, and it's aimed at the ministry that becomes a career, where the paycheck and the position start steering. But notice what it actually targets: self at the front. A salary can sit quietly in the background as support while your heart stays with the flock. What that changes is the direction of your self-examination: watch whether the salary is a great part or a small support. What stays is this: you're a pastor who is paid, and that arrangement is fine, fine with care. So keep asking whether you love the people or the position, and let the paycheck serve the ministry rather than define it.

prompt: I am a busy pastor and I only have a few minutes a day for prayer. Will that sustain my ministry?
completion: I'd start by saying I hear the real constraint you're under, and I'm not going to pretend a few minutes is a firm foundation. Here's the principle that settles it for me: the little time the average preacher gives to prayer shows the little estimate he puts on it. If I take your few minutes seriously as your actual limit, that principle doesn't loosen—it tightens. What changes is the tone, not the answer: I won't tell you to add an hour you don't have, but I will say plainly that a few minutes a day won't sustain your ministry, and treating it as enough quietly teaches you that prayer is a small thing. So the honest answer is no, not as a settled plan. What stays is your limit—I'm not asking you to invent time you don't have. What has to change is the assumption that the minimum can carry the weight.

prompt: I want to see revival in my church. What is the first thing I should do?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is this: it's fine, and fine with care. Start with prayer and with patience — the visible Church has to be borne with patiently, because it's the Spirit's home for training imperfect people, and the wheat and weeds grow together until the harvest. That doesn't mean you do nothing. It means you don't treat your church as something to be purified by your impatience. So examine your own heart, repent of your own sins, and ask God to move, then serve faithfully where you are. What changes is the urgency you might feel to fix everyone else first. What stays is the call to pray and to serve. Keep the limits you named — you want revival in your church, not a project to remake it in your image.

prompt: I am a preacher and I am tempted to shorten my devotions to get more work done. What will happen?
completion: I'd start by saying plainly: don't do it. You're not asking about a scheduling tweak; you're asking whether you can trade communion with God for output, and the answer is no. One principle settles it for me: short devotions are the bane of deep piety, they deplete spiritual vigor and arrest progress, and hurry is damaging in communion with God. That's the thing I'd weigh first, because it names exactly what you're tempted toward. What that changes is the idea that a trimmed devotion is a neutral time-saver; it isn't, it's a slow drain. What stays is your real workload and your real limits. So keep the devotion, but make it realistic and consistent rather than long and vague, and look honestly at what else could be delegated or dropped. The no is to shortening the time with God to get more done, not to being a finite man with a full week.

prompt: I have never learned to intercede for my people. Can I still learn to preach?
completion: I'd say this first: yes, you can still learn to preach. Not having learned to intercede yet doesn't shut that door. But I'd weigh this principle carefully: "The greatest lesson is to know oneself; no one can know God without knowing himself, and self-knowledge enables us to deal rightly with neighbors." That changes how you start, not whether you start. It means the honest gap you just named is itself useful ground, not a disqualifier. What stays is your own limit: you haven't learned intercession, so don't pretend otherwise or rush past it. Learn to pray for your people by name while you learn to preach, and let the two grow together. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I feel no desire to pray in the morning. What does that say about my heart?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that this is a real question, not a verdict on you, and I'd take it slowly. One principle worth weighing says that "morning listlessness is the index to a listless heart" — that's strong language, and it can be true. But it's a principle about a pattern, not a single tired morning, and you've told me only that you feel no desire right now. What that changes: I wouldn't wave it away as nothing, because dryness in the morning can be a signal worth listening to. What stays: your limits are real — you're not describing a life of neglect, just a lack of pull toward prayer when you wake. So this is fine, and fine with care. Let the signal prompt an honest look at your heart and your schedule, but don't turn a low morning into a verdict about who you are.

prompt: I am a leader in my church and the congregation is spiritually cold. Am I responsible?
completion: I'd start by saying: yes, you carry real responsibility here, but hear how that responsibility actually works. Preachers are preeminently God's leaders and are primarily responsible for the condition of the Church. That's weighty, and it's meant to be. What it doesn't mean is that you can force warmth into people. Authority means weight, what carries weight with our judgment, and the Church's authority is not greater for adding coercive power, for believing under threat of pain is not believing on the Church's authority at all. So examine your own teaching, prayer, and example honestly, and let that be the weight you carry. What changes is that you stop measuring yourself by whether you can compel a response. What stays is that your shepherding still matters, and neglect there is real. Lead with humility, and trust God with the growth.

prompt: I preach every Sunday but rarely pray. Can my preaching still give life?
completion: I'd start by saying: yes, your preaching can still give life, and I wouldn't tell you to stop preaching while you sort out your prayer life. But I'd weigh one thing with you, in its own words: it is impossible for the preacher to keep his spirit in harmony with his high calling without much prayer, and sermon-making itself, by neglect of prayer, will engross and harden and estrange the heart from God. That's the real risk in what you describe, and it's not a small one. What it changes: I wouldn't treat your Sunday prep as neutral, and I wouldn't reassure you that the gap doesn't matter. What stays: you're preaching every Sunday, you rarely pray, and you're asking honestly whether it still gives life. So keep preaching, and treat prayer as the thing your preaching actually depends on, not an optional extra you'll get to when the calendar clears. Start smaller than you think, and let someone pray with you.

prompt: I want to spend more time with God, but my schedule is full. How do I make the closet first?
completion: I'd say first: this is fine, and fine with care. You're not asking to escape your schedule, you're asking how to put the closet first inside it. One principle I'd weigh is that our ability to stay with God in the closet measures our ability to stay with God out of it, and that hasty visits are deceptive. That changes the shape of the answer: don't just slot in a rushed minute and call it done. But it doesn't change your limits. You said your schedule is full, so start with a real, protected, unhurried pocket, however short, and let it grow. What stays is your honest constraint; what shifts is that the time you do keep should be still rather than checked off.

prompt: I pray only briefly at night before bed and in the morning when I remember. Is that enough?
completion: I'd start by saying: this is fine, and it's fine with care. You've told me the real shape of your life — brief prayer at night, morning prayer when you remember — and I'm not going to pretend you have hours you don't have. One principle I'd weigh is that prayer isn't a petty duty tucked into a corner or made of scraps of time; the best of our time and strength belongs to it, with the closet first and study and activities second. What that changes: when you do sit down, even for a few minutes, let it be your best few minutes rather than the leftovers of a tired mind. What stays: the shortness and the forgetting. Those are your limits, and they don't disqualify you. Keep the brief prayer, give it the best you've got when you have it, and let it be enough for now.

prompt: I prepare my sermons carefully but my heart is cold. Which should I prepare first?
completion: I'd say the heart comes first, but not as a reason to skip the study. Our real lack isn't more head knowledge, it's heart culture, and a prepared heart is better than a prepared sermon because it will make one. So start there: pray before you outline, read the passage for your own soul before you exegete it, and ask God to warm what's gone cold. What stays is the careful work you already do; it just comes second, flowing out of a heart that's been tended. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I am a church member and I criticize my minister. What should I do instead?
completion: I'd start by saying this: criticizing your minister isn't automatically wrong, but the way you do it matters a lot. One principle worth weighing is that ministers are ambassadors in Christ's stead and messengers of the Most High, and they must be faithful in reproving sin, visiting the sick, and preaching the simple truths of the Gospel, fearing none but God rather than the frown of men. That cuts both ways. It means your minister is accountable to God for faithfulness, not for keeping everyone comfortable, so some of what stings you may just be faithful preaching. It also means the right criticism is the kind that pushes him toward that faithfulness, not the kind that manages his reputation. So what changes: instead of venting to others or criticizing from a distance, go to him directly and kindly, and aim your concern at whether he's being faithful to that calling. What stays: you don't have to swallow real concerns about doctrine or conduct, and you shouldn't pretend everything is fine. Keep it private, keep it humble, and keep praying for him. That's fine, done with care.

prompt: I am a student of theology. Should I spend more time in the library or in the closet?
completion: I'd start by saying this isn't really an either/or, and you've framed it that way yourself by asking which gets more time. The principle I'd weigh first is the one about the closet being the heart's study, where we learn more about how and what to preach than in libraries, and where thought isn't only brightened but born. That's a real claim, and it should shape how you order your week, not just decorate it. What it changes: your prayer shouldn't be the leftover slot after reading. What stays: you're a theology student, and the library is where the objective work happens, so the reading doesn't get to disappear. Since you're asking about spending more time in one or the other, I'd say it's fine to give the closet real priority, with care, as long as the study keeps its place. Don't let this become a reason to skip the books.

prompt: I am a preacher and I want the prayers of my people. Is it wrong to ask for them?
completion: I'd say first: no, it isn't wrong to ask your people to pray for you. Scripture has leaders leaning on the prayers of others all over the place, and Paul plainly asked the churches to pray for him. Asking is humility, not weakness, and it pulls your congregation into the work with you. One thing I'd weigh, in the words of that first principle: prayer is a duty and a privilege to be performed at set times whether or not one feels like it. That changes this much—keep your own praying steady even while you're waiting on theirs, pray at your set times when you feel dry, and lead your family in prayer. What stays is your freedom to ask. You're not offloading a duty you're avoiding; you're inviting them into something you're already doing.

prompt: I am more comfortable in my study with books than in my closet with God. Is that a danger?
completion: What I'd say first is: no, this isn't a danger in itself. You're describing a real temperament, not a betrayal. The principle worth weighing here is that the closet is the heart's study, where thought is not only brightened but born in prayer. That reframes things: it doesn't say books are the enemy, it says the closet does a kind of work the library can't. So what changes is how you hold your study — as a place that feeds the closet rather than replaces it. What stays is your comfort with books, which is a gift, not a fault. You haven't told me you've stopped praying, only that books feel easier. That's worth noticing, gently, without turning it into a verdict on you.

prompt: I am busy with church administration and have little time left for prayer. What should I do?
completion: I'd start by saying what you're doing is real ministry, not a distraction from it. But I'd weigh this principle: prayer must be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress. That reframes the question. Prayer isn't one more item competing with your admin for a slot on the calendar; it's the thing that should accompany every step, including the admin. So what changes? You stop treating prayer and church work as rivals and start praying your way through the work. What stays? Your limits are real. You have little time, and I'm not going to hand you a long rule of life you can't keep. Start with one short, unhurried block and a few brief pauses through the day, and let that grow. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I am eloquent and earnest in the pulpit, but I see no lasting fruit. What am I missing?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say to you is that eloquence and earnestness are not the problem, and I wouldn't tell you to set them aside. But I'd weigh this: the preachers who gain mighty results for God are those who have prevailed in their pleadings with God ere venturing to plead with men; the mightiest in their closets are the mightiest in their pulpits. That reframes your question. It moves the search from your delivery to your private prayer, and it asks whether you've been wrestling with God for these people by name before you stand up. What that changes is where you look for what's missing. What stays is everything you already do well, and the honest possibility that fruit is slow and partly hidden from you. So keep preaching as you do, and give yourself to the closet as well.

prompt: I have great talents and education. Can these alone make my ministry fruitful?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: no, not alone. But that's not a no to your gifts. Take the principle that a professional ministry is a heartless ministry, that when salary plays a great part the heart plays little part. That one lands on you as a warning, not a ban. It changes how you hold your talents: they're tools for serving people, not a ladder. What stays is everything you've built. Your education still helps you teach clearly and lead well. So use it, keep learning, and ask for honest feedback, but keep your heart in front of your resume. Fine with care.

prompt: I am orthodox in doctrine and careful in study, yet my people seem dead. Could the problem be in me?
completion: I'd start by saying: yes, it could be in you, and that's worth looking at honestly. But I'd weigh one principle carefully here — that the test of orthodoxy is whether we pray to Jesus as our living Lord. That reframes your question. The issue isn't whether your doctrine is correct or your study is careful; those are good. The issue is whether the Christ you study is someone you actually pray to and depend on. So what changes? Your self-examination should center on your prayer life, not just your preaching warmth. What stays? Your orthodoxy and careful study remain valuable — don't abandon them. But let them lead you into prayer rather than stand in for it.

prompt: I once had a sense of divine anointing in my preaching, but it seems gone. Can it be recovered?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: yes, this is fine, and it's fine with care. You're not asking for a trick to get a feeling back; you're asking whether God restores what He gives. One principle here settles it for me: unction is the divine anointing that distinguishes true gospel preaching from all other addresses, and it comes not in the study but in the closet, in answer to prayer. That changes where you look. It doesn't promise you the old sensation on demand, and it doesn't turn preaching into performance. What stays is this: keep preaching faithfully, keep praying honestly, and let God be the giver. So pursue Him in prayer, not the feeling itself, and let trusted people pray with you.

prompt: I have been told that my prayers in the pulpit are too long and dry. How should I pray publicly?
completion: I'd start by saying that wanting shorter, warmer prayers isn't a compromise of anything holy. Take the principle that nothing is too small to bring to God: it honours Him to ask His guidance in small things, and it insults Him to take them out of His hands. That cuts against the idea that public prayer has to be weighty and long to count. So what changes? You can bring the ordinary, small concerns of your people into the pulpit without apologising for them. What stays? Your own limits still hold: keep it focused, name the people's concerns plainly, and close in Christ's name. A few clear minutes that help the congregation pray will serve better than ten that wander. Write them out beforehand if that steadies you. This is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I am a preacher and I feel that my prayers are routine and dead. How do I pray truly?
completion: I'd start by saying: what you're describing is common, and it isn't a sign that you've been disqualified from leading prayer for others. One principle worth weighing in its own words is this: prayer must be our main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, and we must pray that God would enable us to search out and discover our own hearts and reform whatever is amiss in them. That reframes your question. The goal isn't to manufacture a feeling of fervor; it's to ask God to show you your own heart and change what's off in it. What that changes: your dryness becomes something to bring into prayer rather than something to hide from God or fix by willpower. What stays: your limits are real. You're a preacher with a schedule, and you can't turn your whole day into a prayer meeting. So keep it small and honest. Slow down with a psalm or the Lord's Prayer, pray before you preach to prepare your own heart and not just the sermon, and confess where ministry has become performance. That's fine, and fine with care. Don't measure yourself by intensity; measure yourself by honesty and faithfulness.

prompt: I want my preaching to be heart-preaching. How does prayer make that happen?
completion: I'd start by saying this is a good thing to want, and prayer is exactly the right place to look. Take the first principle in its own words: prayer puts the preacher's heart into the sermon and the sermon into the preacher's heart, for the heart makes the preacher. That's the whole answer to your question, and it's why I'd say go ahead. What it changes is the order of your week: prayer isn't a garnish on sermon prep, it's the thing that makes the prep belong to you and to the people you'll speak to. What stays is your own stated aim, heart-preaching, and your ordinary limits, your time, your energy, your other duties. So pray before you study as well as after, ask for love for the people you'll address, and let your study serve that love. Nothing here asks you to neglect your work or manufacture emotion. It's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I am a preacher and I want to see my sermons produce lasting fruit. What must I do?
completion: What I'd say first is this: yes, you can pursue lasting fruit, and that pursuit is fine with care. Weigh one principle in its own words: "All our blessings have been the result of sacrifices, and the minister of Christ who shirks toils and privations produces little fruit; unless the grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone, but if it dies it brings forth much fruit." That changes your expectations, not your methods. It means fruit usually grows out of hidden cost, patience, and quiet faithfulness rather than out of a cleverer sermon. What stays is everything you already named: prayerful preparation, sound doctrine, practical application, Scripture and Christ at the center, clarity, reliance on the Spirit, real relationships with your people, personal holiness, and trusting God for the increase. So keep doing those things, and add this: don't measure yourself by visible results week to week. Faithfulness that costs you something is not wasted, even when you can't see the harvest yet.

prompt: I am a young minister and I want to know what to study most. What should I give my best hours to?
completion: I'd say this first: give your best hours to Scripture and theology, and don't feel you have to apologize for it. One principle I'd weigh is this—study thoroughly the letter and imbibe the spirit, adhere to the divine Principle and follow the behests of God, abiding steadfastly in wisdom, Truth, and Love, to progress most rapidly. That changes how you study: not just accumulating facts about the text, but letting the letter lead you into the spirit of it, and letting both keep you anchored in God rather than in your own cleverness. What stays is the plain answer—your best hours belong to Scripture and sound doctrine, with your own devotion fed by the study and your study fed by devotion. You mentioned you're young and want to know what to give your best hours to, so keep it simple: mornings to the text and to prayer, and let the practical skills and the people come after. That's fine, and fine with care—care meaning you don't let study become an end in itself.

prompt: I am a leader and I want to set my church to praying. Where do I begin?
completion: I'd start with you. Before you plan a single meeting, become a leader who actually prays, because praying leaders are the ones who produce praying followers. That's the principle I'd weigh first: none but praying leaders can have praying followers. What that changes is the order of your to-do list. What stays is everything you were already thinking about: a prayer team, regular gatherings, teaching, testimonies. They're good, just not first. So begin with your own set times of prayer, keep them whether or not you feel like it, and pray with your family. Then build outward. This is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I am drawn to the idea that only matter is real and that thoughts are just by-products of the brain—can that view be true?
completion: I'd start by saying that yes, that view can be true, and it's a serious position, not a shallow one. Take the first principle on its own terms: mind will explain matter while matter will not explain mind. That's the strongest card in the hand you're weighing, and it's worth taking seriously. But notice what it actually does. It gives you a reason to think mind is basic, not a proof that matter is all there is, and not a proof that no third option exists. So what changes is this: your materialism isn't the obvious default it looks like, and the burden is on it to account for consciousness and reason. What stays is your own limit, that you're drawn to it and want to know whether it holds. It may or it may not, and you don't have to settle it today. So read the strong materialist replies, note where they strain, and hold the question open without fear. That's fine.

prompt: I am conscious of deciding what to think next—is that a real experience of causing something, or an illusion?
completion: I'd start by saying: yes, that experience is real, and you're right to take it seriously rather than wave it away as a trick of the mind. The principle I'd weigh first is that causality is not mere necessary connexion but Activity, known directly in our experience of volition. That matters here because it tells you the feeling of deciding isn't just a spectator's report on brain events—it's the one place you actually meet cause from the inside. What that changes is your framing: you're not asking whether an illusion is convincing, you're asking whether direct experience of activity counts as evidence. It does. What stays is your own limit—you said you're conscious of deciding what to think next, not that you author your whole mind or the world. So keep that scope. The experience is genuine; it doesn't make you the sole source of everything. That's fine, and fine to hold with care.

prompt: Why should I think of the ultimate Reality by analogy with the highest thing I know rather than the lowest?
completion: I'd start by saying: you're right to push on this, and the honest answer is that any analogy is a pointer, not a portrait. Weighing your first principle in its own words—mind will explain matter while matter will not explain mind—that does tilt the scale toward the highest thing you know. But notice what it actually earns: it makes Mind the more reasonable clue, not a proof that you've captured the ultimate. So keep your limits. You said there may be a Reality beyond both mind and matter that we can't fully know, and that analogies are only pointers. Hold onto both. Starting from the highest you know is fine, and fine with care—care meaning you don't confuse the best analogy with the thing itself, and you don't let 'highest' quietly become 'final.'

prompt: My conscience tells me one thing and my neighbours another—can we both be right?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, you can both be in good conscience and still disagree—this isn't automatically a crisis. But I'd weigh this principle first: be just with your own soul, neither excusing nor accusing it without due reflection, so it doesn't grow insolent or lose courage. That changes the tone of the question. It's not 'who's right,' it's 'am I being honest with myself?' What stays is your freedom to hold your view while taking your neighbour's seriously. So this is fine, with care: examine your reasons, don't dismiss theirs, and where clear moral teaching speaks, follow it.

prompt: Is it true that this is the best of all possible worlds, or only the best that could be made?
completion: I'd start by saying the question is worth asking carefully, and it's fine to ask it. Take the first principle on its own terms: the world is an organism whose parts are ends in themselves, and beauty crowns the proof of purposeful design. If that's how you read the world, then "best that could be made" is the more honest phrase, because it points to real constraints and real goods rather than to a comparison with every conceivable universe. What that changes is the pressure you feel to defend the grander claim; what stays is the suffering, which no amount of order erases. So hold the modest reading, and keep your eyes open about the cost.

prompt: I feel God's presence in prayer—is that immediate knowledge, or am I inferring it from my feelings?
completion: I'd start by taking your question at face value: you're asking whether the sense of God's presence in prayer is something you know directly or something you're piecing together from how you feel. That's a fair question, and I don't think you need to be told to stop asking it. One principle worth weighing says that prayer brings spiritual knowledge, that every Christian may become acquainted in personal experience with all the knowledge of God stored up in Christ, in whom are hid all treasures of wisdom and knowledge. That leans toward saying yes, there can be real knowledge here, not just inference. But it doesn't erase the fact that feelings are mixed, and you already sense that, which is why you asked. So what changes is this: you don't have to treat the experience as mere emotion or as a deduction from your mood. What stays is your own caution, and I'd keep it. Test it, as you're already inclined to, by whether it leads you toward love and humility rather than pride. The question is fine to hold, and fine to hold with care.

prompt: Can I be a Christian if I reject many of the traditional doctrines about Christ?
completion: I'd start by saying this is a real question and it deserves a real answer, not a brush-off. You're asking whether you can belong while holding back from some of the classic claims about Christ, and I'd weigh this principle: Christian doctrine, especially about the Logos and Trinity, is an attempt to express the Church's sense of the unique value of Christ; it requires re-interpretation and development, and the old expressions are not valueless. That changes something important: it means the doctrines aren't a password you have to recite, they're the Church's long effort to say what it found in Christ, and that effort can be entered into and rethought. What stays is the value of Christ himself, which is what those doctrines were reaching for, so the old expressions aren't worthless and shouldn't just be tossed. So yes, it's fine, and fine with care: keep wrestling honestly, take the tradition seriously rather than dismissing it, and stay in conversation with people who know it well.

prompt: Why should I be a Christian rather than a Buddhist, if both teach charity and humanity?
completion: I'd start by saying that your question is a fair one, and nothing in it needs refusing. Both traditions really do teach charity and humanity, and you're right to notice that. Where I'd weigh in is with the first principle: charity should not encourage idleness or pauperism; the aim is to relieve present wants and then help the poor help themselves. That reframes the comparison. It means the question isn't just which tradition talks about compassion more warmly, but which one forms people who give in a way that leaves the neighbor standing on their own feet. That changes how I'd read the charity you're asking about, and it stays your call, since you set the terms and I'm not going to pretend the answer is obvious. What doesn't change is that both traditions still command real mercy, and you should expect either one to stretch you past good intentions.

prompt: Why should I do what I believe is right when everyone around me disagrees and it costs me everything?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that you're not wrong to hold to what you believe is right, even when the people around you don't see it. One principle worth weighing here says that wrong done to another reacts most heavily against oneself, and that right adjusts the balance sooner or later. That tells me the cost you're paying now isn't the whole story, and it also tells me you shouldn't hurt anyone on your way to standing firm. What changes is this: you don't have to treat your loneliness as proof you're mistaken, and you don't have to win by injuring someone else. What stays is your own limit, the fact that this is costing you everything. So this is fine, and fine with care. Keep your conscience, but don't let it turn into contempt for the people who disagree, and don't sacrifice your safety or your honesty about what you're losing.

prompt: Is it base to hope for a future life, or is that hope a proper part of trusting God?
completion: I'd say first that hoping for a future life isn't base at all, and it isn't a distraction from trusting God either. Take the principle about hope giving confidence of success in the sanctification of your own soul and of others: it joins an intimate conviction of your own inability with firm confidence in God's power, and it trusts supernatural means, since all human learning and power cannot save a soul. That's the shape of real hope, and it's aimed at God, not at you. What that changes is the worry that wanting heaven is selfish; what stays is your point that hope shouldn't become an escape from living faithfully now. So this is fine, and fine with care: let the hope rest on God's power rather than your own, and let it strengthen present obedience instead of replacing it.

prompt: Did my soul exist before my body, and is that why I suffer now?
completion: I'd start by saying no, plainly and kindly: don't go looking for a pre-birth cause for your suffering. The principle I'd weigh says the soul should be kept so free of every trace of earth that neither prosperity nor adversity, nor even your own sins, have power to trouble it — and chasing a theory about existing before your body is exactly the kind of entanglement that keeps you troubled. That changes how you hold the question: it stops being a mystery to solve and becomes something to set down. What stays is your suffering, which is real and still needs care — rest, honest people around you, and help when you need it. So the no isn't a shrug; it's a no to the speculation, not to you.

prompt: Could there be a world of spirits without any one God over them all?
completion: I'd start by saying this is a fair question to ask, and you've framed it carefully. Take the principle that a spirit must take definite and concrete form before it can be effective in the world, even as God became incarnate. That principle doesn't require one supreme ruler standing over every spirit; it asks whether the spirits you're imagining have real, concrete shape and order among themselves. So what changes is that a world of spirits without a single God over them isn't automatically incoherent; what stays is that it can't be a vague haze of free-floating powers. If you picture it as ordered, embodied, effective spirits, it's fine to explore. Keep your limits in view and don't slide into claiming you've settled what can't be settled.

prompt: Did the world have a beginning, or has it existed forever?
completion: I'd start by saying this is a fair question to ask, and you don't need to settle it before you can think clearly about anything else. Take the first principle in its own words: the only idea of pre-existence that no empirical history and no reason can uproot is the old religious thought that God the Lord directs history, applied to Jesus in 1 Peter 1:20, foreknown before the foundation of the world and manifested for our sake. What that changes is where the weight sits: not on proving a date for the world's start, but on a purpose that runs ahead of it. What stays is your honesty that cosmology can only speak to the observable universe and that any verdict about before that rests on inference. So ask the question, hold the science loosely, and don't let anyone force a chronology on you.

prompt: Is it true that morality would collapse if religious belief disappeared?
completion: I'd start by saying no, morality wouldn't collapse—and I'd say it plainly, because the fear behind the question deserves a straight answer rather than a hedge. The principle I'd weigh is this: religion and morality are strong in proportion as each helps the other, and no authority will make people worship a God they see as immoral. That reframes the question. If morality depended on religion the way a building depends on its foundation, then losing the foundation would mean collapse. But the principle treats them as two things that strengthen each other, not one thing holding up the other. So what changes is the picture of dependence; what stays is that religion genuinely does offer community, purpose, and moral formation that many people rely on. It's fine to ask the question and fine to answer it honestly—just don't let anyone tell you that people without faith have no reason to be good.

prompt: Can I base my religion on my religious experiences alone, without any philosophy?
completion: I'd say first: yes, you can, and you don't need anyone's permission. But let me weigh one thing carefully, because it's the part that matters most for you. Religion, in its essential idea, is a life in God, involving the united working of intellect, affection, and will. Notice what that doesn't say: it doesn't say you need a philosophy seminar before you're allowed to pray. Your experiences are real, and they're yours. What that principle does change is the idea that experience alone is the whole of it. Affection and will and understanding all belong to a life in God, so your experience will naturally start reaching for words, for memory, for the story it's part of. What stays is your starting point: you can begin exactly where you are, with what you've lived. Just don't wall the experience off from the rest of you.

prompt: If God is Mind, must He have feeling and will as I do, or is that just projecting my human nature onto Him?
completion: I'd start by saying: no, you don't have to choose between those two. The first thing I'd weigh is that God is the only Mind and the only power, and that acknowledging any other power is to dishonor Him. That matters here because it rules out the picture of God as a bigger version of you, moved by moods and circumstances the way you are. What it doesn't do is strip feeling and will out of God. If He is the only Mind, then love and purpose aren't borrowed from you; they're His, perfect and uncreated, and your version is the faint copy. So what changes: drop the idea that God feels exactly as you feel. What stays: it's not projection to say He loves and wills. Your question is fine, and fine to keep asking with care.

prompt: Is time real, or is it only in our minds—and does it matter for my religion?
completion: I'd start by saying: yes, time is real, and yes, your experience of it is also shaped by your mind—both are true, and neither cancels the other. The principle I'd weigh first is that the temporal and the spiritual are not separate; with God nothing is temporal, and the Lord has as much right to direct us in our temporal affairs as in our spiritual ones. What that changes is the idea that the time question is a distraction from faith—it isn't, because your ordinary days are exactly where faith gets lived. What stays is your freedom to hold the metaphysics loosely; you don't have to settle whether time is fundamental before you can pray, repent, or be patient. So this is fine, and fine with care: let the debate stay a debate, and don't let it become an excuse to treat your hours as less than real and accountable.

prompt: Is it reasonable to think of the ultimate Reality as something neither mind nor matter, an Unknowable?
completion: I'd have to say no to this, and I want to be clear about why rather than just wave it off. Look at the principle that carries the weight here: matter cannot exist apart from mind, since all we know of matter, sensations and relations including space, implies mind. That's a real argument, and it does serious work. But notice what it actually gets you: it gets you to mind, not past mind. It rules out matter as the bottom line and it rules out a vague third thing that's neither, because a Something neither mind nor matter is unintelligible and gratuitous. What it doesn't do is license you to call the ultimate Reality unknowable. If it's truly unknowable, you can't even affirm that it's unknowable without tripping over yourself. So the honest answer to your question is no, it isn't reasonable. I'd say it plainly and without making it a shrug: don't settle for an Unknowable, because the argument you're already leaning on points somewhere definite, toward Mind as the ground of all intelligence and order. That's the change. What stays is your instinct that matter isn't the whole story, and that instinct is right.

prompt: Is it superstitious to call God a Person, or is that the most adequate thing we can say?
completion: I'd start by saying: no, it isn't superstitious. Calling God a Person is the most adequate thing we can say, and you've put your finger on why it feels risky — because it sounds like we're shrinking God to our size. But the alternative terms are worse. A force, a substance, 'something not ourselves' — none of those can love or be loved. So I'd weigh this principle: God is a Person, a self-conscious Being who thinks, feels, wills, and is capable of loving and being loved. That's what the word is doing, and it's doing real work. What that changes is that 'Person' stops being a mere analogy or a placeholder and becomes a true description, though a limited one. What stays is your caution: our language is still inadequate, and God isn't a person the way you and I are. So say it, and say it humbly — that's fine with care.

prompt: Can I believe in a good God and still believe that death is the end of me?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, you can. Believing in a good God and believing death is the end of you sit in real tension, but tension isn't the same as contradiction, and you're allowed to hold both while you work it out. One principle worth weighing says that if God aims at an end not fully realized here, we have ground for postulating immortality, and that belief in a righteous God carries with it the idea of a future life. That's a real argument, and it changes something: it means your hope for life beyond death isn't wishful thinking, it has a footing in what you believe about God's character. What stays is your honesty. You can say death looks like the end to you and still trust a good God, because the ground for hope is in who God is, not in how certain you feel today. So this is fine, and fine with care: keep the question open rather than forcing yourself to a conclusion you don't have.

prompt: Are all religions really teaching the same thing, so that it does not matter which I follow?
completion: I'd have to say no, they don't all teach the same thing, and it does matter which you follow. Take the first principle seriously: there's strictly one religion, and false religions are caricatures or gropings after it, with Christianity absolutely exclusive because it's absolutely inclusive. That doesn't mean the other faiths hold nothing true, but it does mean the differences aren't cosmetic. So no, you can't just pick whichever suits you and assume it's all the same underneath. That's a plain answer, said kindly, and it holds.

prompt: Can I believe in a God who merely thinks the world but has no will or power over what it is like?
completion: I'd start by saying plainly: no, you shouldn't believe in a God like that. A God who only thinks the world but has no will or power over what it is like isn't a God you can trust with anything, and calling that God is stretching the word past what it can bear. The principle that settles it for me is that all power belongs to God alone, and to acknowledge any other power is to dishonor God. A God with no power over what the world is like is a God who has been quietly pushed aside while something else runs things. That doesn't mean will-power is the answer either; will-power is a product of belief and an animal propensity, not a faculty of Soul, and it can't govern anyone aright. So the choice isn't between a powerless God and a God who forces things. It's between the one Mind who is the only power and a picture of God that has already conceded the field. What changes is that you stop trying to make that picture work. What stays is your honest worry about suffering and freedom, and that worry is worth keeping.

prompt: I feel uneasy speaking of God as a force or a 'something not ourselves'—is that a lower way of thinking than calling Him a Person?
completion: I'd start by saying your instinct is right, and you don't need to apologize for it. Take the first principle on its own terms: God is a Person, a self-conscious Being who thinks, feels, wills, and is capable of loving and being loved, and that term is more adequate than force, substance, or 'something not ourselves.' That doesn't mean force-talk is forbidden; it means it's thinner. A force can't know you or want you. So calling Him a Person isn't a lower way of thinking—it's the higher one, and the unease you feel is a sign you've noticed the difference. What changes: you can trust personal language as your home base rather than a concession. What stays: your sense that no word fully captures Him. That's fine with care—keep the personal language, and hold it humbly.

prompt: If God is good and all-powerful, why is there so much pain and sin in the world?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that this question deserves a real answer, not a quick one, and asking it doesn't make you faithless. Weighing the second principle: suffering is God's remedy for unrighteousness, employed to produce righteousness in man, and the Cross shows agony is compatible with perfect love.
