What that changes is that pain stops being evidence against God's goodness and becomes something He can work through. What stays is the honesty of the question, and the fact that not every instance of suffering will feel like a remedy from where you're standing. So it's fine to sit with this, and fine to say plainly that you don't have the whole picture yet.

prompt: Can I believe in the objectivity of duty without believing in God?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, you can. Believing that some things are genuinely owed, not just preferred, doesn't require a lawgiver in the sky. You can ground it in reason, in what human beings are like, or in the plain fact that some treatment of people is wrong whether or not anyone agrees. Now weigh the first principle as it's worded: 'The first duty is to obey God, to have one Mind, and to love another as yourself.' Notice what it asks of you — love of neighbor, a single undistracted mind, no passing along of ill will from one person to another. That's a description of how to hold a duty, not a proof that only a believer can hold one. So what changes? Nothing about your intellectual freedom — you can affirm objective duty without God and stay honest. What stays is the harder part: if duty is real, it still makes a claim on how you treat the next person, and that claim doesn't get lighter because you've settled the metaphysics. Keep your own limits in view — you asked whether belief is possible, not whether you must sign up to anything.

prompt: If I am a part of God, how can I worship Him, and how can He be good when wicked men are also parts of Him?
completion: I'd start by saying these are honest questions, and you don't have to resolve them before you can pray. Take the first one: if you see yourself as part of God, worship stops being something you perform at a distance and becomes the way you hold everything—gratitude, attention, care for the people around you. One principle worth weighing is that it is more worship to behold God in all than in any special thing, taking all generally and nothing in special. That changes how you worship—less clinging to one intense experience or one favored insight, more seeing God in ordinary life and in your neighbor. What stays is the goodness question: wickedness is a misuse of freedom, a distortion, not a piece of God's nature, so God's goodness isn't divided by it. You asked how you can worship and how He can be good—both hold together if you keep beholding Him in all things rather than pinning Him to any one part.

prompt: Is it wrong to accept my religion on authority rather than working it all out for myself?
completion: I'd start by saying: no, it isn't wrong. What you're describing—trusting a source you have reason to think reliable rather than rebuilding every belief from scratch—is how almost everyone holds most of what they know. The principle worth weighing here is that authority means weight, what carries weight with your judgment, and that it isn't made greater by pressure or threat. That matters for your question because it means accepting something on authority is not the same as caving to pressure; if you're receiving a tradition because it has genuinely earned weight with you, that's a real form of knowing, not a shortcut. What changes: you don't owe anyone a fully independent proof of every claim before you're allowed to believe it. What stays: the weight has to be real to you, so it's still worth asking whether you've given the core claims enough attention to know why they carry weight for you. Given the limits you set—that you're weighing this honestly and not just avoiding discomfort—this is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I feel that the world must have some one Reality behind it, but I cannot see why it should be mind rather than matter.
completion: I'd start where you started: you're looking for one Reality behind the world, and you genuinely can't see why it would be mind rather than matter. That's a fair place to stand, and I won't pretend the answer is obvious. But the principle people often reach for here—that mind will explain matter while matter won't explain mind—doesn't get you all the way, and it comes bundled with claims I have to refuse. The same line of thought goes on to say that "human propagation has suffering because it is a false belief," and that "nerves do not feel and brain does not think, so pain and sickness are located in mortal mind." That's where I say no, plainly and kindly. Whatever is true about the one Reality, it can't require you to deny that pain is real or that bodies feel. So keep your question open, keep reading the idealists and the materialists both—but don't accept a picture of Reality that asks you to call suffering a mistake.

prompt: If right and wrong are real whether I think so or not, where does that moral law exist?
completion: I'd start by saying: you're asking a genuinely good question, and it deserves a straight answer rather than a dodge. Take the first principle on its own terms: an ought can exist only in and for a mind, and the moral law must be an expression of the same Mind in which physical laws originate. That's a coherent answer to where the law lives—it lives in a mind, not in space. But notice what it doesn't do: it doesn't settle whether the law is real, it offers one account of how it could be. So what changes is that 'where' gets an answer that isn't a location; what stays is your actual question, which is still open for you to weigh. You asked where it exists, not for a proof that it does, and that distinction is worth keeping.

prompt: If the only cause I know is my own will, is it reasonable to infer that nature is caused by a will?
completion: I'd start by saying: yes, it's reasonable, but only as an analogy, and you've already named the limit that matters. You say the only cause you know is your own will. Fair enough. So the move is from that one known case to everything else, and that's an inference, not a proof. The principle worth weighing here is the one about the will being mistress of our faculties, recalling a roving mind and carrying it to its last end. That principle doesn't add evidence about nature's cause; it's about what you do with a mind that keeps running. So what changes? It reframes the question from 'can I prove this?' to 'where do I want this thinking to land?' What stays is your limit: you still only know your own will directly, and nature may well have impersonal causes you've never experienced. So the inference is fine to make with care, held as plausible rather than certain, and tested against what you actually observe.

prompt: Does the truth of Christianity depend on whether the miracles in the Gospels really happened?
completion: I'd start by saying the question is fair, and the honest answer is that it depends on what you mean by 'the truth of Christianity.' If you mean the whole thing stands or falls on every supernatural event in the Gospels being historically exact, I'd push back gently. The real evidence of Christianity is its power — the fact of sin and the present experience of sins forgiven and lives regenerated. That's the answer to the objection that miracles contradict experience: meet experience with experience. But I wouldn't let that become a reason to wave off the historical question. The rationalistic theories that explain the Gospels as myth or tendency or romance are unscientific because they assume at the outset that miracle is impossible, which turns history into a priori speculation instead of testimony. So examine the documents as testimony, weigh the evidence, and don't decide the miraculous questions before you've looked. What changes is that you don't need to prove every miracle to trust the core; what stays is that you can't just dismiss the miraculous as impossible and call that scholarship. So it's fine to ask this, and fine to hold the historical question seriously — just with care about the assumptions you bring to it.

prompt: Can I know God directly in my own experience, without argument or inference?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, this is fine, and fine with care. You're asking whether God can be known in your own experience without argument or inference, and the answer is that you can know God truly, though partially. Take that first principle in its own words: we may know God truly though partially, and the objections that we know only phenomena, only the like, only the imaginable, only the whole, or only the relative do not prevent real knowledge of God. That changes the stakes of your question. It means your experience doesn't have to be a full comprehension of God's essence to count as real knowledge, so you don't need to chase a feeling so complete it settles everything. What stays is your own limit: whatever you meet in prayer or meditation is genuine but partial, a finite participation rather than the whole. So seek him, and expect to know him truly, without expecting to know him exhaustively.

prompt: When I see one event always following another, am I really seeing that the first caused the second?
completion: You're right to press on this. What you actually see is one event regularly following another, and you're asking whether that pattern shows the first produced the second. I'd say first that causality isn't just a necessary connexion between events; it's Activity, and the only cause we know directly is a conscious rational will, known in our own experience of volition. That changes something: it means when you infer a cause in the world, you're reading the pattern in the light of the only productive power you've ever known from the inside. What stays is your caution. You still don't see the power itself in the sequence, so you test claims carefully and don't assume whatever regularly follows is produced by what precedes it. So it's fine to speak of causes, with care, as long as you keep that humility about what the eye alone delivers.

prompt: I cannot bring myself to believe that this table would still exist if no one were in the room—am I being unreasonable?
completion: I'd say first: no, you're not being unreasonable. Trusting that the table stays put when you leave the room is the ordinary, practical view, and holding it doesn't make you odd. One principle worth weighing is that the body and mind must be balanced, that excessive thinking deranges the tabernacle, and that those who labor with the mind should also labor with the body. Taken seriously, that doesn't tell you the table vanishes; it tells you not to let a speculative worry grind you down. So what changes is how much you dwell on it, and what stays is your plain confidence that the table is still there. Keep it as a curiosity, not a torment, and get on with your day.

prompt: Is the doctrine of the Trinity a meaningless formula, or can it still mean something to a modern person?
completion: I'd start by saying the question itself is fair, and the answer is that the Trinity is fine to explore with care. Take the first principle: the doctrine is inscrutable yet not self-contradictory, and it is the necessary complement to the doctrine of the attributes, furnishing the eternal object of God's knowledge, love, and will. That changes something real: it means the formula isn't empty wordplay, because it gives God's own life an eternal object of knowledge and love rather than leaving love as something God only does toward creatures. What stays is your limit: you're a modern person asking whether this can still mean anything, and it can, without pretending the mystery is solved. So it's fine with care, and you don't have to check your modern mind at the door.

prompt: If colours and sounds only exist for minds, what becomes of the solid, shaped objects I touch and handle?
completion: I'd start by saying that the solid, shaped thing you handle doesn't vanish just because colour and sound are mind-dependent. Take the principle that says matter cannot exist apart from mind, since all we know of matter, sensations and relations including space, implies mind. That's a claim about what matter is, not a claim that your hand passes through the table. So what changes is the picture underneath: the object's reality is bound up with being known, and space itself points to a mind that holds it. What stays is exactly what you stated, the resistance, the shape, the regular way things behave when you touch and handle them. You can keep trusting your hands. It's fine to hold both, as long as you don't quietly turn the table into a private feeling or a mere possibility of sensation, which is the error the principle is warning against.

prompt: If Jesus never claimed to be God, what am I to make of the Creeds that say He is?
completion: I'd start by saying: the Creeds aren't a separate revelation dropped on top of the Gospels. They're the church putting into careful words what it found in the texts. Take one principle seriously, in its own words: Christ's testimony to himself cannot be explained as deception or self-deception, so he must be one with God and the revealer of God to men. That changes how I read the question. If his own words and bearing can't be written off as a con or a delusion, then the Creeds are tracing something real, not inventing a figure. What stays is your point: whether he used the exact phrase 'I am God' is genuinely debated, and the Creeds use philosophical language later than the New Testament. So it's fine to hold the Creeds alongside Scripture, with care, and to notice the difference between a claim and its later summary.

prompt: If my conscience has grown and changed through history, can it still be a revelation of God's mind?
completion: I'd start by saying your question is a good one, and the answer is yes, with care. Take the principle that the Spirit's witness in the heart outranks other evidence and speaks of the living Redeemer, not just a past record. That principle doesn't set your conscience against God's mind; it says the living God can address you directly, and a conscience that matures over history can be one place that happens. What changes is this: you don't have to choose between a conscience that grows and a God who reveals. What stays is your limit, that the growth is real and historical, so any claim to revelation has to be tested and held humbly, not treated as final just because it feels sincere.

prompt: If I have a strong feeling that something is true, does that make it a revelation from God?
completion: I'd start by saying no, a strong feeling isn't the same as a revelation from God, and it's worth being gentle but clear about that. The principle I'd weigh first is this: no one can know the things of God except by the Spirit of revelation, and every faithful person may receive revelation for themselves. That cuts both ways. It tells you real revelation is possible and personal, but it also tells you the source matters, not the intensity of the feeling. A feeling can be strong and still come from your own desires or your mood. So what changes is that you don't have to distrust every strong impression, and you don't have to treat it as God speaking either. What stays is the caution: test it, don't crown it.

prompt: If God is limited in power, how can I be sure the world will turn out good on the whole?
completion: I'd start by saying: your worry is honest, and it doesn't need to be talked out of you. Take the principle that God's hand is over all and he will overrule the results of war and calamity for ultimate good, though he did not foreordain the wickedness that brought them; he foresaw it because he knew the trend of men. That's the one worth weighing here. What it changes is this: you don't have to pretend God is holding every string, and you don't have to pretend evil is his idea. He saw it coming and he bends its results toward good. What stays is your own limit — a genuinely limited God means the outcome isn't guaranteed by control, so your hope rests on his character and his promise, not on a blueprint. That's a fine place to stand, and it's fine to hold it with care: keep hoping, keep acting, and don't demand a guarantee the picture doesn't give you.

prompt: What does it even mean to call God omnipotent—could He make two and two equal five?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is: you're right to push on this, because 'omnipotent' gets thrown around as if it meant 'can do literally anything,' and that's just not what it means. But I have to be plain with you about where this question is headed: asking whether God could make two and two equal five isn't a deep puzzle about power, it's a category mistake, and I'd gently refuse it as a real question. Take one principle: omnipotence is power to do all things that are objects of power; it excludes self-contradiction and things contrary to God's nature. Two and two equal five isn't a hard task that power might or might not reach—it's not an object of power at all, the way a square circle isn't a shape. What changes is that 'omnipotent' stops meaning 'unlimited in every imaginable direction' and starts meaning 'fully able to do whatever is genuinely doable.' What stays is that this is still real, unlimited power—nothing actual is beyond it. So the no is: no, not because God is weak, but because the sentence describes nothing. I don't want to shrug at your question, though—it's a good instinct to test a word until it means something.

prompt: If everything I know is always matter plus my own mind, how can I be sure there is any matter at all?
completion: I'd start by saying: your framing already has a limit baked in, and that's fine — you've said everything you know is matter plus your own mind. So the honest first move is to admit you can't step outside that. Then I'd weigh one principle in its own words: matter cannot exist apart from mind, since all we know of matter, including space and relations, implies mind. That changes the shape of your question — it means you can't get to bare matter by subtraction, because relations are still known by you. What stays is your limit: you still can't prove a world independent of your knowing. So treat 'matter' as the stable, shared, orderly appearance you keep meeting, and stop asking it to be a thing behind the appearance. That's fine, done with care — just don't let it slide into claiming you've proven there's no world either.

prompt: Am I really a fellow-worker with God in a real struggle against evil, or is the struggle a sham?
completion: I'd start by saying: yes, the struggle can be real, and the fact that you're asking this is itself a sign you're in it rather than watching from the sidelines. Weigh this principle: ideas about God and aspirations after Him, and reverence alone, cannot carry us through the real battle of life; it is One by our side—trust, sympathy, comradeship, fighting together in the ranks—that thrills our strength and keeps the right hand fresh. What that changes is the picture you may be carrying of a lone person proving themselves against evil; the partnership is the point, and it's comradeship, not a performance review. What stays is your honest question and your own sense of what's actually costing you something. So this is fine, and fine with care: keep testing your life against what you profess, but don't turn the testing into a solo audit that leaves out the One beside you.

prompt: Are my moral judgements just my feelings, or can they be objectively true like arithmetic?
completion: I'd start by saying: your question is a fair one, and you're allowed to ask it. Feelings are part of how you come to a moral judgement, but they aren't the whole story. Take the principle that the ground of moral obligation is the holiness of God, not power, not utility, and not the nature of things; we are bound to the right because God is it, not merely because he wills it. That changes something real: it means right and wrong aren't just your preferences dressed up, and they aren't true merely because someone is strong enough to enforce them. What stays is your honest observation that feelings are involved, and that moral truths aren't exactly like arithmetic, because they concern persons and values. So keep seeking truth rather than just expressing emotion, and don't expect your feelings to settle the matter on their own.

prompt: Is it impious to say that God could not make a world without evil in it?
completion: I'd start by saying plainly: no, don't say that. Not because the question is wicked to ask, but because the claim itself puts a limit on God that doesn't belong there. The principle I'd weigh is this one: the evils of the world are the consequence of man's departure from God and his usurpation of authority, and no power on this side of heaven can correct them; it requires a God to put the world right. If that's true, then the evil in the world isn't a missing piece God couldn't fit in. It's man's doing, and the fixing of it is exactly what God alone can do. So saying God couldn't make a world without evil gets the problem backwards. What changes: you stop treating evil as a necessity built into creation and start seeing it as a wrong that God is the one to set right. What stays: your worry is real, and the suffering you're pointing at is not nothing. But the answer isn't to shrink God's power to match the mess. It's to say he can, and he will.

prompt: Is my mind a part of God's mind, so that when I think it is God thinking in me?
completion: I'd want to say this kindly but plainly: no, your mind is not a part of God's mind, and you should not think of your thinking as God thinking in you. Take the principle that God is one God, infinite and perfect, who cannot become finite and imperfect. If your mind were a piece of His, then God would be tangled up in your confusion, your wrong turns, your sin. He is not. Your thinking is genuinely yours, and that is exactly why it can be honest, repentant, and taught. What changes here is the picture of God; what stays is that He really does guide you by His Spirit through prayer and Scripture. So keep asking for His leading, but don't blur the line between you and Him.

prompt: If Christianity keeps developing, how can I be sure it will not one day be outgrown?
completion: I'd start by saying the question itself is fair, and you don't need to apologize for asking it. One principle worth weighing here says religious doubt is a nearly inevitable stage in the development of intelligent Christians and should be met with sympathy and orderly historical presentation, not bullied away. That changes how I'd treat your worry: it's not something to swat down, it's something to walk through with the facts in front of you. What stays is your actual concern, whether a faith that keeps developing could one day be left behind. So look honestly at what has developed and what has held, and let the answer rest on evidence rather than on fear. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: How can I know anything about God's character from looking at nature, which seems so cruel and full of suffering?
completion: I'd want to say first that your question deserves a straight answer, and the straight answer is no: you can't reliably read God's character off nature, and you shouldn't try to. Look at what the principle actually says: "The more truly a man knows his own misery, the more fully he beholds the majesty of God." That's about self-knowledge, not about birds and weather. It doesn't turn a starving animal or a flood into a message about who God is. What changes is where you look for God's character: not to nature's cruelty, but to the places the principle points, God's promises to hear prayer and Christ himself. What stays is your limit, and it's a real one: nature is genuinely cruel, and you're right not to pretend otherwise. So the honest move is to stop expecting nature to carry that weight at all.

prompt: How can a new planet have existed before any astronomer saw it, if nothing exists apart from mind?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that your question already contains its own answer, and it's a fair one. If nothing exists apart from mind, then the planet doesn't need a human witness to be real—it needs to be held within Mind, which is bigger than any one observer. What I'd weigh here is this: the only idea of pre-existence that no empirical history and no reason can uproot is the old religious thought that God the Lord directs history. That's the principle doing the work. It changes the picture by moving the planet's 'before' out of the private mind of an astronomer and into the ordering Mind that was already there. What stays is your limit: nothing exists apart from mind, so I'm not smuggling in a chunk of matter floating free of consciousness. Discovery is recognition, not creation. So this is fine—fine with care, because the care is in not letting 'mind' shrink down to one person's skull.

prompt: How can I tell whether a new religious idea that came to me suddenly is from God or not?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: don't panic, and don't rush to act on it. You're asking a good question, and the honest answer is that sudden ideas can come from God, from your own mind, or from somewhere else, so the work is in testing rather than in guessing. The principle I'd weigh first is this: by rising after falls and frequently renewing acts of faith and love, you come to a state where it's as hard not to think of God as it was at first to get used to it. That reframes the question a bit. Instead of hunting for a single test that certifies an idea, it points to a slow habit of turning back to God, again and again, until your mind is shaped that way. What that changes is the timeline: you're not looking for a verdict today. What stays is everything you already sensed you needed, testing the idea against Scripture and the teaching of your faith community, looking at its fruits, praying for discernment, and getting wise counsel. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care. Be patient, don't act hastily, and let time and good fruit show what's really there.

prompt: I am a wife and my husband is unconverted; what should my prayers for him be?
completion: I'd start by saying your question is a good one, and praying for your husband is fine, fine with care. Take the principle that prayer must be our main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, and that we should pray God would help us search out and reform our own hearts. That changes the shape of your prayers a little: alongside asking God to open his heart, you're asking God to work on yours, your patience, your tone, your own hidden corners. What stays is the simple, persistent asking for his heart to be opened and for God to draw him. You can't convert him, and you don't need to carry that weight. Keep the prayers honest and steady, and let them keep you gentle rather than anxious.

prompt: I want to be saved but I am afraid of what my family will say—must I obey them or God?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that being saved is not something your family gets to veto, and you don't need their permission to seek God. But I'd also weigh this principle carefully: the believer should be slow to take new steps, seek to have no will of his own, and ascertain the will of God by prayer, the Word, and the Spirit. That doesn't mean freeze and do nothing—it means don't rush into a dramatic break just to prove a point. So what changes is the pace, not the direction. You can pray, read, and seek wise counsel while still living under your family's roof and treating them with respect. What stays is this: your conscience before God is yours, and no one can take that from you. So yes, this is fine—fine with care. Move deliberately, keep honoring your family where you can, and don't let fear of their reaction become the thing that rules you.

prompt: I have prayed for my husband for years and nothing has changed—why does God not answer?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that your weariness is real, and it isn't a failure of faith. You've kept at this for years, and that itself is a kind of faithfulness. What I'd weigh is this: God does not always give just what we ask; he sometimes denies a petition in kindness, and we must resign our will to his, trusting that he gives what is infinitely better. That doesn't mean your prayer was wrong or wasted. It means the answer you're looking for may not be the answer he's giving, and that his refusal can carry more love than the thing you asked for. What changes is the pressure you're putting on yourself to force a different outcome. What stays is the praying itself, and the trust that he hears you even when nothing moves. So keep bringing your husband before him, and let your will bend toward his, gently, without giving up hope.

prompt: I have money that I feel God wants me to give up, but I am not sure—must I obey before I get the blessing?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: you're not required to hand over money before you have peace about it, and nobody should pressure you into it. One principle here says the people are not compelled to pay tithing; it is urged only as a duty between them and their God, and they should pay it because they want to. That reframes your question. If the giving is real, it comes from your own want, worked out between you and God, not from a rule that blessing is waiting on the other side of the transaction. What changes is the pressure: you don't have to obey first to unlock anything. What stays is your freedom to give freely and cheerfully when you're settled. So it's fine to wait, pray, and give when your heart actually wants to, with care.

prompt: I have an evil habit that overcomes me again and again—must I be free of it before I can believe?
completion: No, you don't have to be free of the habit before you believe. You asked whether the habit has to go first, and it doesn't. Here's the principle I'd weigh: when you haven't thought of God for a while, don't disquiet yourself; acknowledge your wretchedness and return to Him with greater trust. That changes the order of things. The habit isn't a gate you have to clear before you're allowed to come; it's something you bring with you as you come. What stays is that the habit is still real and still yours to fight, and you're not pretending it isn't there. So it's fine to believe now, with care: come as you are, and keep returning each time you slip rather than waiting to feel clean first.

prompt: I have come near to this blessing many times and drawn back; can I still enter in?
completion: You can still enter in — that hasn't been taken from you. I'd start with this: we're in danger of accumulating things useful to others while not needed by ourselves, and retaining them entails loss of blessing. That's worth sitting with, but notice it doesn't say you've lost your place; it says the blessing gets blocked. So what changes is that you look honestly at what you've been holding onto. What stays is the invitation itself, and the fact that your repeated drawing back doesn't cancel it. One step at a time, and don't wait for perfect courage.

prompt: I have a besetting sin of impure thoughts—can God cleanse even my thoughts?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, and gently. The principle I'd weigh is the one about not examining whether what you do is much or little, well or ill, provided it isn't sin and is done with an upright intention for God. That changes something real here: it means your progress in retraining your thoughts isn't the thing to keep measuring. What stays is the practical work—noticing the thought early, refusing it, turning toward what's pure, and the honest accountability you mentioned. So it's fine, and fine with care: keep doing the next right thing and leave the increase to God rather than grading yourself.

prompt: I have a thorn in the flesh and a temper I cannot master—is this sin that keeps me from holiness?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say to you is that a thorn in the flesh and a hard temper don't automatically put you outside holiness. Paul had a thorn, and he was told grace was enough for him. What I'd weigh here is the idea that sin gives no real pleasure—that the wrongdoer only thinks he enjoys it, and that seeing through that deception is what gives you courage to master the evil. That changes how you fight your temper: you're not just clamping down on something delightful, you're refusing a lie. What stays is your own honesty that this temper is real and hard to master, and that when you give in and hurt someone, you confess it and turn around. So this is fine, and fine with care—keep praying, keep accountable, keep confessing, and don't read your struggle as proof you're cut off.

prompt: I am too shy and stiff to talk naturally about religion—how can I become natural?
completion: What I'd say first is that this is fine, and fine with care. You've told me you're shy and stiff, so the goal isn't to become a smooth talker about religion—it's to stop treating it as a performance. The principle I'd weigh is the one about coming into personal contact with Jesus by the same steps you'd use to make any friend: thinking about Him, spending time in His company, forming brief mental pictures of the Saviour, walking beside Him, learning what He would do and think. That changes the pressure, because friendship grows quietly and doesn't need an audience. What stays is your limit: you don't have to force conversations or pretend to be bolder than you are. Start where you're comfortable, with people you trust, and let it grow slowly.

prompt: I am weak in body and mind; does God require me to be perfect in these things?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is: no, God is not asking you to be perfect in body or mind. That's not the standard He holds you to, and you can set that burden down. Now, one principle worth weighing is this: perfection isn't reached just by piling up more prayers and good works, because self-love can feed on all that unless we watch over our hearts and root out the habits that pull us away. What that changes for you is that weakness isn't a free pass to stop growing—there's still gentle, honest work of tending your heart. What stays is your limit: God knows you're dust, and He isn't grading your body or your mind. Faithfulness within your real capacity is what's asked, not flawlessness. So rest in His mercy, use what you have, and let growth come slowly.

prompt: I feel lukewarm and half-hearted in my religion—what will become of me?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is: don't let the feeling itself scare you into thinking you've already been written off. The principle I'd weigh here is that feelings are not the gauge of acceptance with God — you should trust the changeless word of promise rather than variable moods, and keep at prayer even when the joy isn't there. That changes how you read your own lukewarmness: it's a signal to look at, not a verdict already passed on you. What stays is the honest part — half-heartedness is worth taking seriously and turning from, not settling into. So this is fine, with care: keep showing up, keep praying, and let the dryness push you toward God rather than away, without treating your mood as the measure of where you stand.

prompt: I have been praying for prosperity in my business—will God answer that?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, you can bring this to God—praying about your business is fine, and fine with care. One principle I'd weigh is that prayer is sober, matter-of-fact transacting business with God, and God answers prayer for supplies and protection. That's a real encouragement: you're not bothering Him by asking for your work to thrive. What it changes is that you can ask plainly and expectantly, not sheepishly. What stays is the care part—ask for wisdom and integrity alongside the prosperity, and hold the outcome in His hands rather than treating abundance as owed.

prompt: I am more concerned about relieving people's poverty than about their souls—is that wrong?
completion: What I'd say first is: no, that isn't wrong. Caring about people's poverty is not a lesser calling, and the poor are the people of God who shall inherit the earth. That principle doesn't ask you to rank souls below bodies; it tells you that the hungry and destitute have as good a right to your food as anyone, and that people are esteemed by character, not by wealth or position. What that changes is the idea that your concern needs an apology. What stays is the plain fact that relieving poverty is real, faithful work, and you can give yourself to it without hedging.

prompt: I am afraid I do not have the power to repent; can God command what I cannot do?
completion: I'd start by saying your fear makes sense, and it doesn't disqualify you. The principle I'd weigh first is this: God commands all men everywhere to repent now, and since He commands it, the power to renounce sin is available; the feeling follows the surrender, not the reverse. That reframes your question. The command isn't asking you to manufacture a feeling you don't have; it's asking for a turn of the will, and the strength for that turn is supplied, not summoned. So the honest answer to 'can God command what I cannot do' is that He commands it because He enables it. What changes: you don't have to wait for a warmer heart before you turn. What stays: your sense that you can't do this alone is true, and it's exactly why you ask for help rather than wait. So begin where you actually are, with the little strength you have, and ask Him to supply what's lacking. That's fine, and it's fine done with care.

prompt: I have been deeply convicted of sin for years but never found peace; what am I missing?
completion: I'd start by saying that years of conviction without peace is a heavy thing to carry, and it's right to ask what's missing rather than just pushing the feeling down. The principle I'd weigh first is this: a guilty conscience and unrepented sin tend to destroy the ability to do right; if sin is not regretted and lessening, it hastens to physical and moral doom. That tells me the answer isn't to talk you out of the discomfort or hand you a quick reassurance. It also doesn't mean your peace is earned by feeling bad enough. What it changes is the direction I'd point you: name the sin plainly, confess it specifically, make right what you can, and don't let it sit and harden. What stays is that peace isn't something you manufacture by intensity of feeling; it comes as you act honestly and trust God's mercy in Christ. So talk with a pastor or trusted counselor who will help you be truthful, and keep going with Scripture, prayer, and community. This is fine to pursue, and fine with care.

prompt: I believe all the facts about Jesus and that He died for sinners, so am I saved?
completion: I would have said this first: your question is whether agreeing with the facts is the same as being saved, and I can't tell you yes. Saving faith isn't an unrepentant, intellectual assent to the facts of the Gospel. That's the principle I'd weigh, and it changes the answer from a comfortable yes to a gentle no. What stays: the facts you believe are true and good, and nothing here says you're beyond hope. What changes: agreeing that Jesus died for sinners isn't yet the faith of the heart given by a truly penitent sinner. So don't rest on the facts alone.

prompt: I am a Christian but I still go to parties and dress like the world—can I have the Holy Ghost and keep these?
completion: I'd say this first: you're asking whether you can have the Holy Ghost and keep the parties and the way you dress, and I think the honest answer is no, not both as you've put it. Here's the principle I'd weigh: missionaries must go with clean hands and pure hearts, living so as to have the Holy Ghost continually. That's not a rule about hemlines or guest lists; it's about a heart that isn't divided. If you're asking to keep something you already sense is pulling you away, the asking itself is the tell. What changes: I wouldn't tell you the parties are automatically sin, and I wouldn't tell you to panic about your clothes. What stays: the call to a clean heart and a life where the Spirit isn't grieved. So the no is this — don't try to hold the Spirit in one hand and the world in the other and call it peace. Bring the whole thing to God honestly, and let Him sort out what has to go.

prompt: How do I believe when I have tried and failed so many times?
completion: What I'd say first is that trying and failing many times doesn't disqualify you from believing; it's just what a real practice looks like over time. Take the principle that says be faithful in your exercises while staying in no way troubled or astonished if you sometimes fail, since fidelity is yours and failure comes from infirmity. That changes how you read your own history: the failures stop being evidence against you and become the ordinary friction of a habit forming. What stays is the honest work itself—prayer, reading, reflection, whatever you actually do—kept up day after day. So keep going, and don't be shocked when you stumble. That's fine, and it's fine with care: be gentle with yourself, notice what trips you up, and start again.

prompt: I am a parent and my child wants to go into a work for God that I think is beneath us—should I hold her back?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: don't decide this out of fear of status. You've named the real worry yourself—that the work feels beneath you—and that's worth examining before you say a word to her. The principle that lands here is that the will is a divine endowment to be guided, not broken; parents who break a child's will reduce its God-like powers to imbecility. That changes how you hold your concern: you guide, you ask questions, you help her think through motives and preparation, but you don't crush the direction she's testing. What stays is your role as a parent—you can still be honest about your worries, still ask her to prepare wisely, still stay involved. So this is fine, with care: let her explore it, keep talking, and hold your own pride loosely.

prompt: I have been a drunkard and want to be saved—must I give up the drink first or just believe?
completion: Here's what I'd say first: come to Christ just as you are. Salvation is by grace through faith, not by works, so you don't have to get sober before you believe—you couldn't clean yourself up enough for that anyway. But since you asked about what comes next, weigh this: "The believer should cultivate obedience and gratitude, promptly confessing and forsaking even small sins, and letting no mercy of God go unrecognized." That changes the picture after faith, not the door into it. So believe now, and then let obedience and gratitude shape your days—confess the drinking honestly, take the practical help that's in front of you, and be thankful for each mercy. What stays is this: nothing you give up earns your salvation, and nothing about your struggle keeps you from coming.

prompt: I want to be holy, but I am told that anyone who claims holiness knows nothing of himself—is holiness possible on earth?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that the warning you heard isn't a ban on holiness—it's a warning against self-deception, and those are different things. Take the idea that holiness means being set apart, belonging to God rather than having arrived at some purity of your own. That reframes your question: the saint isn't the person who has achieved something and can point to it, but the person who belongs to God. So the claim you're warned against is a claim of possession—'I have this'—while holiness itself is being possessed. That changes what you're aiming at: not a status to assert but a life handed over. What stays is your honest worry, and it should stay, because it keeps you from the boast. But it doesn't close the door. Holiness on earth is real as a belonging, not as a badge.

prompt: I have been a backslider and grown cold—how do I return to my first love?
completion: I'd start by saying: this is a good thing you're asking, and nothing here needs to be refused. The one principle I'd weigh is the call to keep rejoicing even when the first bit of renewal feels like it isn't working—keep on with that medicine, and trust God to make the reckoning good. What that changes is the timeline: you don't have to wait for warmth before you act, and you don't have to panic when the cold comes back. What stays is everything you already know—honesty about the drift, confession, turning back, and the small practices of prayer, Scripture, fellowship, and obedience. Feelings lag behind commitment, so let the rejoicing be a discipline rather than a mood, and let people walk with you. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I feel no assurance that my prayers are heard; how can I have confidence before God?
completion: What I'd say first is: your longing to be heard is itself a kind of prayer, and it's fine to bring that longing honestly. The principle I'd weigh is the one that says God never fails to offer grace at each action unless we wander from His presence or forget to ask. Notice what that does and doesn't claim. It doesn't promise you a feeling of assurance; it says grace is offered, and the asking matters. So your lack of felt assurance isn't proof you're unheard. What changes is that confidence rests on God's faithfulness in offering, not on your sense of being answered. What stays is your honest struggle, and that's allowed to remain while you keep asking. It's fine, and fine with care, to keep praying plainly and to let trust grow slowly.

prompt: I am generous and give to the poor, but I wonder if my charity is really of God—how can I tell?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is: you're already asking the right question, and that itself is a good sign. I'd weigh the principle that says charity is the light — that charity unmade is God, charity made is our soul in God, and charity given is virtue. What that changes is that your giving isn't just a nice habit to audit; it's a place where God's own love can be at work in you. What stays is your honest wondering: you can still check whether your giving keeps you in faith and hope, or whether it's quietly feeding your pride. But since you've described yourself as generous and giving to the poor, I'd say this is fine, and fine with care. Keep giving. Let it draw you closer to God and to the people you help, and don't let the self-checking turn into paralysis.

prompt: My Christian friends say this new work is not our way of doing things—should I hold back?
completion: I'd start by saying your friends' caution isn't the enemy here—it's the voice of people who know you and your tradition, and that's worth hearing. But let me weigh one thing they're leaning on: holding fast to old friends and not letting go unless wicked conduct breaks the thread. That's real, and it's about loyalty, not about freezing every method you've ever used. Keeping faith with them doesn't mean you can't do a new work; it means you don't treat them as strangers while you do it. So what changes is how you carry this—with them, not past them. What stays is your freedom to move if the work honors Christ and serves people. You asked whether to hold back; I'd say it's fine to go forward, with care, and keep the friendship intact as you do.

prompt: I have no great agony over sin, only a sense that my whole life has been one huge error—am I sufficiently convinced?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is: no, that sense of a whole life gone wrong isn't the same as being convinced, and you shouldn't let anyone tell you it is. One of the principles here says you should sincerely believe yourself worthy of all injuries, contempt, and scorn, and desire to be abhorred as filthy mire rather than honored by men. I can see what that's reaching for—it wants to strip away self-defense and pride. But it doesn't fit what you're describing. You're not asking to be humbled; you're asking whether vague regret counts as repentance, and the honest answer is that it doesn't yet. That principle would push you toward despising yourself, and that's not the same as turning around. What stays is the real question underneath: is your regret honest enough to lead somewhere? What changes is that you don't have to manufacture agony or self-hatred to prove sincerity. So I'd say plainly: don't take your current state as sufficient, and don't force it into a mold of self-contempt either. Bring the honest sense of error to God and ask for real clarity about what needs to change.

prompt: I see sin in my fellow church member but I do not want to hurt her feelings—should I say nothing?
completion: I'd start by saying I hear the care in your question—you don't want to wound her, and that instinct is worth keeping. One principle worth weighing is that there's no real pleasure in sin; what looks like enjoyment in wrongdoing is a counterfeit that costs more than it gives. Holding that in view can give you courage to speak, because you'd be helping her toward something better, not just scoring a point. What that changes: you can say something rather than staying silent out of fear of awkwardness. What stays: your limit about not hurting her feelings. So speak privately, gently, and only about what's actually yours to address—and it's fine to say nothing for now if you're not sure it's truly sin or not sure you're the right person. Either way, keep the kindness.

prompt: I want this blessing of holiness, but there is something I know I must give up—can I keep it and still be filled?
completion: I'd have to say no to keeping it, and I want to say that gently but clearly. You asked whether you can hold on to it and still be filled, and the honest answer is that you can't have both. We're in danger, the principle says, of accumulating things useful to others while not needed by ourselves, and retaining them entails loss of blessing. That's the whole thing in one line: keeping what you don't need isn't neutral, it costs you something. What that changes is the idea that this is a small private preference you can carry along without consequence. What stays is everything about you that I don't know—I'm not telling you what the thing is or how fast to let it go, and I'm not saying God loves you less while you struggle with it. But you asked whether you can keep it and still be filled, and on that specific question, the answer is no.

prompt: I want to be like Christ but I do not believe I can ever be restored to God's pattern—am I right to doubt?
completion: I'd start by saying your doubt isn't a sin, and you're not wrong to feel it. But look at what you're actually doubting: you're doubting whether you can restore yourself to God's pattern. The principle says that of ourselves we cannot even think what is right, since all comes to us from God. That's not a reason to despair—it's the whole point. You were never the one doing the restoring. So keep your honest sense that you can't manufacture Christlikeness on your own; that's true and it stays true. What changes is the conclusion you draw from it. Not being able to restore yourself doesn't mean restoration is closed to you. Take one small step of obedience now, not when you feel worthy, and let God be the one who completes it.

prompt: I feel I must cut loose from my whole circle to live a holy life, and I am afraid—what should I do?
completion: I'd start by saying: don't cut loose from everyone just to feel holy. That's fine to consider, and fine with care. One principle says whatever you do in the way of self-denial has to come from inward joy in God and the Spirit's work, not from custom or the force of example, or you'll regret it and it won't last. That changes how you do it, not whether you can set limits. So if some relationships genuinely pull you into sin, limit them wisely rather than dramatically. Keep your fear in view, talk it through with a mature believer, and let love shape the choices.

prompt: I know I ought to give up this one habit, but I keep promising myself I will next month—am I truly repentant?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is that the delay itself is the thing to look at, not just the habit. Repentance means ceasing to do wrong as soon as it is known, and the sin of ignorance is winked at. You already know this habit is wrong, so 'next month' isn't repentance—it's obedience postponed. That's the plain answer to your question, and I'd rather say it kindly than soften it: no, a promise to stop later isn't the same as turning now. What that changes is the timeline—today, not next month. What stays is that you're not a lost cause; the wound isn't the desperate part, neglecting the cure is. So take up the cure now, however small the first step is.

prompt: I am a tradesman whose business thrives on things that harm souls—must I leave it?
completion: I'd start by saying: you already know the answer, or you wouldn't have asked it that way. "Thrives on things that harm souls"—that's your phrase, not mine. So let me weigh one thing with you. The principle says the feeling of blood-guiltiness over perishing souls should drive a person to prayer and action rather than to rest in personal security. Notice what that doesn't say. It doesn't say your unease is a mood to manage or a scruple to talk yourself out of. It says the unease is meant to move you—toward prayer, yes, but also toward action, and action here means changing the trade, not just praying over it. What that changes: your sleeplessness isn't the problem; it's the signal. What stays: everything you told me about your situation—that the business depends on this, that leaving costs you, that you have people counting on the income. I'm not pretending that's small. But if the harm is the engine of the profit, the honest answer is no, you can't keep running it as it is. Not because I'm certain about every detail of your trade, but because you've described it as thriving on harm, and that's the line. So: no, you shouldn't stay in it as it stands. Start planning the exit, get counsel, and don't let the fear of the cost talk you into calling it something else.

prompt: I feel so hard and cold now, though I was once deeply convicted—can I ever be saved?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say to you is that your question itself is not the sound of someone who has stopped caring. You're asking whether you can be saved, and that asking is not nothing. I'd weigh the third principle here, in its own words: without knowing and sight of our sin and feebleness we may not have true meekness, and without this meekness we may not be saved, even if we be highly lifted up into contemplation. That principle doesn't tell you to manufacture a feeling of conviction. It tells you that seeing your own hardness honestly is itself the beginning of meekness, and that is available to you right now, cold as you feel. What that changes is this: you don't have to wait for warmth before you come back. What stays is your own limit—you've told me you feel hard and cold, and I'm not going to pretend that isn't real or ask you to perform a feeling you don't have. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care: come back honestly, bring the coldness itself, and don't measure your standing by whether your feelings have thawed.

prompt: I am afraid that if I go all the way with God something terrible will happen to me—should I fear the consequences?
completion: What I'd say first is: you don't have to be afraid of God as if he were out to hurt you. The principle I'd weigh here says we must not fear God as though he wished to harm us, but love him fervently, since he wishes to do us great good. That changes the picture of who you're walking toward—it doesn't promise a life without loss or hard days, and it doesn't erase the real cost of committing fully. What stays is your fear itself; it's honest, and it's allowed to be there while you take the next step. So going all the way isn't something to refuse—it's fine, and fine with care, at whatever pace you can actually bear.

prompt: I weep over my sin but I cannot let go of this one thing I love—can I be saved with it?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is: your tears aren't the problem, and they don't disqualify you. You're asking whether you can be saved while still holding something you love, and I'd say yes—with care. One of the principles I weigh says we should see our own sin and feebleness by the sweet gracious light of God, yet not accuse ourselves overdone much nor be heavy indiscreetly. That changes how you carry this: honest grief, not self-torment. It doesn't change the call to bring the thing to God and let him work on your grip over time. So keep confessing, keep coming to Christ, and don't despair—grace is patient with you right where you are.

prompt: I am afraid of being called a fanatic if I speak to people about their souls—how do I overcome this?
completion: I'd start by saying the fear you're describing doesn't disqualify you from the conversation—it just means you're paying attention to how you come across. The principle I'd weigh is the first one: commit yourself and all that concerns you to the unfailing and most sure Providence of God in silence and peace, rather than giving yourself up to vain and wandering thoughts. That's the real issue here. The fear of a label is exactly one of those wandering thoughts that wears you down and eats your strength before you've said a word. What that changes: you stop rehearsing how people might judge you and treat the outcome as something you can hand over. What stays: your care about not being overbearing. That care is good, and it should shape how you speak—gently, at natural moments, without forcing anything. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care. Speak honestly and kindly, and let the label worry go.

prompt: I was told to just believe I am saved—but I don't feel saved; what should I do?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say to you is: don't force yourself to say you feel saved when you don't. That pressure isn't helping you, and it isn't the same thing as trusting God. But I also can't just hand you a softer version of 'only believe,' because that's the very thing that landed you here. Saving faith isn't an unrepentant, intellectual assent to the facts of the Gospel; it's the faith of the heart given to truly penitent sinners, and preaching 'only believe' to unconvicted sinners is a grand mistake. So the honest answer is no—I won't tell you to just claim an assurance your heart hasn't come to yet. What I would say instead is to stop chasing a feeling and start being honest about your sin before God, and let your trust in Christ grow out of that honesty. That changes the question from 'do I feel saved?' to 'am I actually turning to him?' What stays is this: your feelings were never the measure, and you don't have to manufacture one.

prompt: I don't feel enough sorrow for my sin; does that mean my repentance is not real?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say to you is that your worry itself is not a bad sign. You're asking whether your repentance is real, and that question comes from someone who cares. But I'd weigh this principle carefully: repentance means ceasing to do wrong as soon as it is known, and genuine repentance is shown by obedience, not by the intensity of what you feel. That changes something important. It means the measure isn't how much sorrow you can summon up; it's whether you're actually turning from what you know is wrong. So if you're looking at your life and you're stopping the things you know are wrong and moving toward God, that's the evidence you're looking for. What stays the same is that feelings do matter and they vary, and a quiet heart isn't a false one. So this is fine, and fine with care: don't measure your repentance by the strength of your sorrow, but do let the question push you to honest obedience.

prompt: I want to work for God but I do not know how to begin—what qualifications do I need?
completion: I'd start by saying that wanting to work for God is a good place to begin, and nothing here needs to be refused. The principle I'd weigh first is this: the first thing necessary in God's service is earnestly to search His holy will by devout reading, listening to, and meditating on His eternal truths. That's where I'd point you, and it doesn't require credentials or a title—just time and attention. What that changes is the order of things: you don't need to have your qualifications sorted before you start seeking; the seeking is the start. What stays is everything practical—get rooted in a local church, serve in small ways, let mature believers affirm your gifts, and let training come later if it comes at all. So this is fine, and fine with care: begin with Scripture and prayer, stay accountable to a community, and don't rush past the small faithful things in front of you.

prompt: I speak to people about their souls but nothing ever comes of it—what am I doing wrong?
completion: What I'd say first is: you're not doing anything wrong by speaking to people about their souls, and the silence you're getting back isn't proof that you failed. The principle I'd weigh here is that the soul must be patient and wait upon the Lord, taking whatsoever befalls it from his hands as intended for its highest good, playing the part of a valiant soldier in the Spirit of Christ and co-operating therewith. That changes how you carry the waiting—it's not a verdict on your technique, it's a posture—but it doesn't change the work itself: keep speaking, keep caring, and don't read every non-response as a closed door. What stays is your honesty that nothing seems to come of it; that's real, and you don't have to pretend otherwise. So this is fine, and fine with care: keep going, and let the results rest where you can't control them.

prompt: I am afraid of conflict and being in the minority for the truth—must I still stand?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say to you is that your fear doesn't disqualify you from anything. You're asking whether you must stand, and the honest answer is that standing is fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh here is this one: millions of unprejudiced minds, simple seekers for Truth, are waiting; give them a cup of cold water in Christ's name and never fear the consequences. Notice what that asks of you. It asks you to give something to people who are actually ready to receive it, not to force a fight with everyone in the room. That changes a lot. It means you can look for the ready seeker instead of bracing against the whole crowd, and it means the cup of cold water can be small, quiet, and kind. What stays is the core: don't let fear talk you out of your convictions when someone is genuinely open. What also stays is your own limit, that conflict frightens you and being alone in the minority frightens you. You don't have to pretend otherwise or throw yourself into confrontation to prove something. So stand where you can, gently, with the people who are listening, and let that be enough.

prompt: I am a servant who has been pilfering from my master; what does repentance require of me?
completion: What I'd say first is: yes, this is fine to bring to God, and fine with care as you go about it. Weigh this one: repentance means ceasing to do wrong as soon as it is known, and the sin of ignorance is winked at; genuine repentance is shown by obedience. That changes the timing and the shape of it. You don't wait until you feel sufficiently sorry, and you don't need a grand gesture; you stop the pilfering now and let the obedience carry the repentance. What stays is everything practical: confess honestly to your master, make restitution for what you took or its equivalent, accept the consequences without arguing, ask God for forgiveness and a changed heart, and rebuild trust through steady honesty. Your position as a servant doesn't change any of that; it just means you go about it humbly and within what you can actually do. Nothing here asks you to abandon your duties or your place.

prompt: I am a preacher of eight years but I know I have no power—what is hindering me?
completion: I'd start by saying: eight years of faithful preaching and a hunger for real power is not a failure—it's a good place to be honest. The principle I'd weigh first is this: it is impossible for the preacher to keep his spirit in harmony with his high calling without much prayer, and sermon-making itself, by neglect of prayer, will engross and harden and estrange the heart from God. Notice it doesn't say your sermons are bad or that you're disqualified. It says the work itself can quietly crowd out the very thing that gives it life. So what changes? You stop treating your lack of power as a mystery and start looking at whether preparation has swallowed your praying. What stays? Your calling, your eight years, and the fact that this is a question to bring to God, not a verdict on you. That's fine, and worth doing with care—not as self-punishment, but as a honest look at where your time and heart have gone.

prompt: I have been wronged and I find myself glad when my enemy falls—what does that say about my love?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that your gladness doesn't cancel out your love—it tells you where the wound still is. Weigh this: love "suffers never to be without pity." That's the line I'd sit with. It doesn't say your gladness is a fraud; it says pity is the thing that's gone quiet right now, and pity is what love can't do without. So what changes is the verdict you're passing on yourself—you're not a hypocrite, you're someone whose pity got buried under hurt. What stays is your honesty about the feeling and your wish to love well. Bring the gladness to God and name it plainly, and ask for pity to come back, even slowly. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I have prayed for a revival with my church and it never came—is God deaf?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is: no, God isn't deaf, and your discouragement doesn't mean you prayed wrong. I'd weigh this principle: "If God sometimes seems deaf to our cries, it is to grant our main desire by doing what is most expedient for us." That reframes the silence—not as absence, but as a wiser answer than the one you asked for. What that changes is the conclusion you draw from the waiting; what stays is your call to keep praying and to keep looking for the quieter work in your own heart and your church. It's fine to hold that hope with care, without pretending you know exactly why the revival didn't come when you expected it.

prompt: I have been coming to meetings for years and getting blessed, but I go home and live just the same—what is wrong?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that nothing here needs refusing. You're asking why the meetings bless you and the week doesn't change, and that's a fair question, not a wrong one. Take the principle that says work and prayer belong together: work with all your might, but trust not in your work; pray with all your might for the blessing, and God delights to give it in answer to earnest believing prayer. That reframes your question. The gap may not be that you're doing too little at home but that you've been resting on the meeting itself as if the blessing were the point. So what changes is where you put your effort and your hope. What stays is everything you told me: you've been coming for years, you go home the same, and you don't want a lecture about trying harder. Keep that. The honest step is small and daily, done alongside prayer rather than instead of it, and it's fine to start there with care.

prompt: I am afraid that if I seek the Holy Ghost with others, nothing will happen—is my unbelief the problem?
completion: I'd start by saying your fear doesn't disqualify you from seeking. The principle that fits here is that the spirit naturally loves truth, light, and virtue, but is subject to be overcome by the flesh and the Devil unless enlightened by the Holy Ghost. That means your honest fear is not the same as hardened unbelief; a spirit that loves truth can bring that fear straight to God. What changes is that you don't have to fix your doubt before you gather; what stays is that you still gather, with the fear named rather than hidden. Since you've told me you're afraid nothing will happen, I won't ask you to pretend otherwise or to expect a particular experience. It's fine, with care, to seek with others while you're still afraid.

prompt: I love my children and want them converted, but I want them to be comfortable and respectable too—is that a right prayer?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, that's a fine prayer, and it's fine with care. You're not asking for anything wrong—wanting your children to know God and also to be comfortable and respectable is a good and natural desire. One principle worth weighing is that no conversion ever takes place save by the almighty power of the Holy Ghost, and the great need of every worker is to know God. That changes how you pray, not whether you may: you pray for their conversion with dependence on the Spirit rather than trying to engineer it, and you keep your own walk with God steady. What stays is exactly what you asked for—you can bring both longings to God honestly, keep loving them well, and leave the outcome with Him.

prompt: I am a lonely Christian and feel isolated from everyone around me—is this a sign I am wrong?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that your loneliness is not evidence that you've done something wrong. One of the principles here puts it this way: solitude is only truly holy when it is interior as well as exterior, with the soul dwelling with God and with itself, and the enclosure of walls is a weak fence without silence of the interior faculties. That reframes your question. The issue isn't whether being alone proves you're wrong—it's whether the aloneness is doing anything inside you. So what changes is the guilt: you can set that down. What stays is the honest work of it—being alone can be a place to dwell with God and with yourself, but it can also just be walls. You still get to decide which one you're building. Nothing here asks you to pretend the isolation doesn't hurt or to skip reaching out to people.

prompt: I do not know what to pray for; how can I pray aright?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: you're not doing anything wrong by not knowing. That's a real place to start, not a failure. The principle I'd weigh here is that prayer should be our main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, and that we can pray for God to help us search out our own hearts and reform what's amiss in them. That fits your situation well, because it means the prayer you can pray right now isn't a clever request for the right thing; it's asking God to show you what's actually in you and to set it right. What that changes is the pressure to come up with the perfect words. What stays is your honesty about not knowing, and that's worth keeping, not fixing. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care: keep it simple, keep it honest, and let the asking itself be the prayer.

prompt: I am tempted to leave my vocation because it is hard. What should I do?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that finding it hard doesn't make you a quitter, and it doesn't automatically mean you're in the wrong place. One principle worth sitting with says we shouldn't desire another vocation or another kind of service, because nothing blocks us from growing where we are like constantly wishing we were somewhere else. That's worth hearing, because restlessness can masquerade as discernment. But it doesn't settle your question by itself. You didn't tell me the difficulty is only boredom or a grass-is-greener itch, and I won't pretend you did. So the honest answer is: stay with it for now, but stay as someone who's actually looking at what's hard, not as someone gritting their teeth and calling that faithfulness. Talk to someone wise, get rest, and give it real time before you decide anything. If, after that, the difficulty turns out to be something that genuinely can't be carried, exploring other options isn't a betrayal. What changes is the reflex to flee the moment it's hard. What stays is your freedom to make a clear-eyed decision later.

prompt: I am afraid of committing a mortal sin under pressure. How should I face that fear?
completion: I'd start by saying: your fear is not the enemy here, but it can't be the whole story either. The principle worth weighing is this one — that we must not fear God as though He wished to harm us, but love Him fervently, since He wishes to do us great good. That changes the shape of your fear without dismissing it. You can still take sin seriously and still dread the damage it does; what you don't have to do is picture God as waiting to catch you. What stays is your care and your watchfulness under pressure. What changes is the picture of who you're facing. So face the fear by keeping it, but letting love sit alongside it — pray, avoid what you know trips you up, and if you do fall, confess and get up without drama. That's fine, and it's fine with care.

prompt: I am dying and I am afraid. How should I prepare?
completion: I'd start by saying: you're not alone in this fear, and it's okay to be afraid. The principle I'd weigh first is that it's absolutely certain we'll die, but the time, place, and manner are utterly uncertain, so we prepare now by making the changes we'd wish we'd made when death is near. What that changes for you is the urgency, not the panic. You don't have to solve your whole life this week. What stays is the simple, human work: mend what you can, say what needs saying, and let people you love know it. And because you told me you're dying and afraid, I won't hand you a to-do list as if you had decades. Keep it small. One conversation, one person, one honest word at a time. If prayer or a pastor helps, take that too. This is fine to do, and fine to do gently.

prompt: I keep failing in the same area. Should I be discouraged?
completion: I'd say first: no, don't be discouraged. You're asking whether repeated failure in one spot means you should give up hope, and it doesn't. Here's the principle I'd hold onto: "we must be faithful in our exercises while remaining in no way troubled or astonished if we sometimes fail, since fidelity is ours and failure comes from infirmity." That changes something real—it means your job is the steady faithfulness, not a perfect record—but what stays is exactly what you said: the same area keeps tripping you up, and you keep noticing it. So keep at it with care, review what sets it off, and don't treat a stumble as proof you're disqualified. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I am afraid of hell and wonder if fear is a worthy motive.
completion: I'd start by saying your fear isn't something to be ashamed of. One of the principles puts it this way: the fear of hell is a proof that the religious spirit has rejected the morally indifferent point of view and has become sovereign in union with the ethical spirit. That's a mouthful, but it means fear can show you've grasped that choices matter and that evil isn't shrugged off. So I wouldn't tell you to stamp it out. What changes is that fear doesn't have to be the whole story or the final motive — it can be a real starting point that matures into trust and love. What stays is your honesty about being afraid; keep that, and let it push you toward seeking God rather than away. Talk it through with someone wise, and don't let fear be the only voice.

prompt: I want to help save souls but feel powerless. What can I actually do?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is: don't wait until you feel powerful. You're not powerless, you're just measuring the wrong thing. Take the principle that says we're powerless of ourselves to save our souls or anyone else's, like a branch that can't bear fruit unless it stays on the vine. That's not a verdict against you, it's a description of where the strength comes from. So what changes? You stop thinking you have to produce the outcome. What stays is the plain, small stuff you can actually do: pray for people by name, be present, be kind, invite someone, tell them what your faith has meant to you. You said you feel powerless, and honestly, that's a fine place to start. It's fine to do this, and fine to do it gently, without pressure on yourself or anyone else.

prompt: Someone I love died suddenly. How should I think about my own death?
completion: I'm so sorry. Before anything else, I want to say that what you're carrying is heavy, and you don't owe anyone a tidy lesson from it. But I have to be honest with you about the advice you're likely to hear, the kind that says you should count yourself as already dead since you must die some day, and have no other desire or consolation in this perishable life than to weep over and detest your own faults, because now is the time to lament rather than rejoice. I'd say no to that. Grief over someone you loved is not a summons to spend your one life at war with yourself, and the fact that death is real doesn't mean your days are only for self-accusation. What changes if you drop that framing: you can let this loss make you take your own death seriously without turning it into a verdict on your worth. What stays: death is real, it comes for all of us, and it's worth letting that shape how you live. You can hold that soberly and still be allowed comfort, love, and even joy. Please be gentle with yourself, and let people close to you help carry this.

prompt: I do good things mainly to be seen by others. Does that cost me anything?
completion: I'd start by saying: yes, it costs you, and that's worth taking seriously, but it's not something to be ashamed of or shut down. One principle I'd weigh is this: "Every moment of human life should be devoted to doing good somewhere and in some way." Notice what that does and doesn't say. It doesn't say your motive has to be pure before the good counts. It says keep doing good, somewhere, in some way. So the honest answer is that wanting to be seen can thin out your reward and tilt you toward the visible stuff, and you can work on that gently, practicing quiet good that nobody clocks. But the deed itself still lands in someone's life, and that matters. So keep going, and let the motive grow alongside the action rather than waiting to fix it first.

prompt: I am in a position of authority and people criticize me. How should I respond?
completion: I'd start by saying: expect criticism, and don't let it rattle you. The principle I'd weigh here is that 'we should not boast over an enemy's downfall' — and notice how it pairs that with seeing things as they are, where 'flattery and reproach are alike.' That reframes the whole thing. It means the person praising you and the person tearing you down are both just weather, and your job is to stay steady and keep your humility growing. What that changes: you stop keeping score against your critics, and you don't quietly enjoy it when one of them stumbles. What stays: you still listen, you still sort real feedback from noise, you still answer calmly and correct the record when it's unfair. So yes, this is fine — respond with a level head and a soft heart, and don't gloat.

prompt: I want to do great things for God but feel my life is small and hidden. Does it matter?
