completion: I'd start by saying: yes, it matters, and your question is a good one to be asking. Take the first principle on its own terms — "Am I living the life that approaches the supreme good? Am I demonstrating the healing power of Truth and Love?" Notice that it doesn't ask whether your life is large or visible. It asks about the quality of the life you're actually living. So the test isn't scale; it's fruit. That changes the frame of your question: a small, hidden life can still be aimed at the supreme good and can still show healing in how you treat the people near you. What stays is the honesty the principle demands — you can't just assume the fruit is there; you have to actually look. And your limits stay too: you've said your life feels small and hidden, and nothing here asks you to inflate it or perform a bigger one. So this is fine, and fine with care — keep serving where you are, and let the fruit, not the visibility, be what you check.

prompt: I feel God is distant and does not hear me. Why are my prayers unanswered?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that feeling like God is far off while you're praying is a heavy thing to carry, and it doesn't mean you're doing something wrong. I'd weigh this principle: God can hear the earnest prayer of the soul, and just as human invention lets people talk across great distances, God understands our innermost thoughts, so we should pray in faith, nothing wavering. What that changes is the assumption that distance equals silence — your prayer isn't lost in the air. What stays is everything you actually said: you feel distant, and you don't experience an answer. That's real, and nothing here erases it or promises you a timeline. So keep praying honestly, doubts and all; that's fine, and it's fine with care — no pressure to manufacture a feeling of closeness.

prompt: I am not sure I can become holy. Is perfection really possible for me?
completion: I'd start by saying: yes, this is fine, and fine with care. You're asking whether perfection is possible for you, and the honest answer is that you're right to feel the gap between where you are and where you'd like to be. One principle I'd weigh is that we must be constant in aspiring to the perfection of holy love, since love seeking anything less than perfection cannot fail to be imperfect. That sounds demanding, and it is, but notice what it asks: constancy in aspiring, not instant arrival. So what changes is the direction of your desire, not the timeline. What stays is your real limitation, the fact that you can't manufacture holiness on demand. Aspire steadily, and let the striving be patient rather than frantic.

prompt: I keep a small attachment I know God asks me to give up. What should I do?
completion: Before anything else, I'd say: this is fine, and it's fine with care. You've already named the real thing — you know God is asking you to give it up — so the question isn't whether to obey but how to do it without crushing yourself. Weigh this one: when you're in doubt about whether you've done your duty or offended God, humble yourself, beg forgiveness, and start fresh with renewed promises of fidelity and love. That changes the tone of the whole thing. It means a stumble isn't a verdict on you; it's a moment to get up and begin again, gently. What stays is the honest call to let go and the small steps you can actually take. What shifts is the guilt spiral — you don't have to live there. Keep praying, keep trying, and let the starting-over be part of the obedience itself.

prompt: I have been chasing a promotion and more money for years. Is that what I am for?
completion: I'd start by saying this isn't a wrong thing to want. Chasing a promotion and more money for years is a normal human pull, and the question you're asking is a good one, not a confession. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about not being in a hurry to get rich: attend your meetings, pray, read the Scriptures, meditate, and keep your dish right side up so you can catch the shower when it comes. What that changes is the pace and the posture, not the goal. It says slow down, stay grounded, keep the rest of your life fed while you work at this. What stays is your ambition itself, which is fine. So this is fine, and fine with care: keep the pursuit honest, keep room for the people and practices that hold you together, and don't let the hurry do the deciding for you.

prompt: I pray for something good and do not receive it. What am I doing wrong?
completion: What I'd say first is that you haven't necessarily done anything wrong. I'd weigh this principle: "work with all your might but trust not in your work, pray with all your might for the blessing." That reframes your question from a fault to find into a pair of things to hold together. What it changes is the assumption that an unanswered prayer means a mistake on your part; what stays is the honest effort, the asking, and the patience. So keep praying earnestly and keep doing your part, and let go of the idea that you must have failed somewhere.

prompt: I want to love God more, but I feel only duty. How does love grow?
completion: I'd start by saying: what you're describing is not a failure, and it's fine to bring it honestly. The principle I'd weigh first is this one — that the way into loving and adoring God is not by begging God to come down and make you feel something, but by a steady effort to enter into who He is and offer Him love. That reframes your question. You're not waiting on a feeling to arrive; you're learning to give. What changes is the goal: instead of measuring your affection, you practice offering, and affection is free to follow or lag behind without the whole thing collapsing. What stays is your honesty — duty that feels dry is still real, and you don't have to pretend it's warmth. Keep praying, keep reading, keep serving, and ask for affection too; just don't make the feeling the test of whether any of it counts.

prompt: I want to be liked and praised for my good works. Is that wrong?
completion: I'd start by saying: wanting to be liked for good work isn't wrong. You're made to value love and approval, and that's not a flaw to fix. The principle I'd weigh is that we must be what we are and be that well, honoring the Master Workman who made us. That means your wish for praise is part of what you are, not a stain on it. What changes is the pressure you put on praise: let it be a gift you receive, not the thing your worth hangs on. What stays is the good work itself, done honestly whether or not anyone claps. So keep wanting to be liked, and keep your gladness resting somewhere steadier than being noticed.

prompt: I feel my religious life has grown lukewarm. How do I renew it?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: this is a good thing to want, and it's fine to pursue it with care. One principle I'd weigh says we should quicken and enliven our faith, taking faith as the rule of conduct rather than amusing ourselves with trivial devotions that change daily. That's the heart of it for you. So instead of chasing a new technique every week, pick a few steady practices and let them carry you when feelings don't. What changes is the pressure to feel something dramatic; what stays is your honest desire for renewal, which is itself a sign of life. Keep it simple and consistent, and be patient with yourself.

prompt: I study and read constantly. Could my studies become an end in themselves?
completion: I'd say first that yes, study can become an end in itself, and I don't think that's automatically a problem. The principle I'd weigh here is that education and continual learning are a religious duty, that knowledge and intelligence come from God, and that we should pursue every useful branch of knowledge. If learning is a duty in its own right, then studying for its own sake isn't a betrayal of anything — it's part of what you owe. What that changes is the anxiety that constant reading is somehow self-indulgent; it isn't, not by this standard. What stays is your own honesty about it: keep asking whether the learning is still opening you outward rather than closing you in, and let it shape how you treat people. But the studying itself? Fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I am not sure I have truly repented of an old sin. How can I tell?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that you're asking a fair question, and the fact that it troubles you is not itself a bad sign. Take the principle that says a sinner isn't reformed just by being told there's no sin — to put down the claim of sin you have to detect it, remove the mask, and point out the illusion. That's useful here, but notice what it asks of you: honest detection, not endless self-inspection. So name the old sin plainly, without softening it, and look at what it actually claimed about you and about God. Then you can see it for what it is rather than circling it. What changes is that you don't have to keep hunting your feelings for proof. What stays is the honest naming and the turning. If you can do that, this is fine, and fine with care — talk it through with someone trustworthy rather than carrying it alone.

prompt: I am seriously ill. Should I be praying chiefly for health, or for whatever most leads me to my end?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that you don't have to choose between these two, and you shouldn't let anyone force the choice on you. Take the principle that prayer must be our main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, and that we should ask God to help us search out our own hearts and reform what's amiss in them. That changes something real: it means prayer isn't just a request list for a cure, it's also the place where you get honest about fear, resentment, and what you're clinging to. But it doesn't cancel the plain, human prayer for health. You can ask for healing and ask to be shown your own heart in the same breath. What stays is your own limit: you're seriously ill, and you're not obliged to turn your illness into a project or a test of your sincerity. Pray for health, pray to see yourself truly, and let the two live together.

prompt: I find my prayer dry and distracted. Am I praying badly?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that dryness and distraction don't automatically mean you're praying badly. Prayer is humbling work that abases intellect and pride and signs our spiritual bankruptcy, and human nature resists it. So the fact that it feels dry or distracted is not proof you're doing it wrong; it may actually be the work doing what it does. What that changes is this: don't excuse little praying as acceptable, and don't treat distraction as harmless. What stays is that you can bring your wandering mind back gently, keep showing up, and not be discouraged by your sins or dryness. Pray with confidence, relying on Christ's merits, and ask for grace. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I disagree with my superior's decision. Must I obey anyway?
completion: I'd start by saying that disagreeing with your boss doesn't automatically mean you have to fall in line, and it doesn't automatically mean you should dig in either. Take the principle that obedience matters because it serves a good, not because going along is an end in itself. That changes something real: your objection should be about the good the decision is supposed to serve, not about tradition or who's in charge. What stays is that you still owe your superior a fair hearing and a respectful route for your concerns. So raise it through the proper channels, ask for clarification, propose an alternative, and if the call is lawful and within their authority, comply while saying plainly that you disagree. If it's illegal or deeply unethical, refuse and escalate. That's fine, and fine with care. Keep your own limits in view: what your role actually requires, what's at stake, and what your conscience will let you do. Talk it over with someone you trust before you decide.

prompt: I am tempted to impurity. What means should I use against it?
completion: I'd start by saying: this is a normal fight, and you can win it with care, not panic. The principle I'd weigh first is that "jealousy is the grave of affection" — so if part of your plan is to guard a relationship by spying, checking phones, or demanding an account of someone's time and thoughts, drop that part. It withers trust where trust is owed. What stays is the practical core: cut off access, guard your eyes and your company, turn to prayer or a friend when the pull hits, confess to God and someone you trust, and get up calmly if you fall. Keep your own limits — you said you're tempted, not that you've decided anything — so treat this as habit-building, not a crisis. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I find it hard to forgive someone who hurt me. How should I pray?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that it's fine to pray exactly where you are, even with the hurt still raw. One principle I'd weigh says that without being discouraged on account of our sins, we should pray for grace with perfect confidence, relying on the infinite merits of Jesus Christ, and that God never fails to offer grace at each action unless we wander from his presence or forget to ask. That changes the tone of your prayer: you don't have to wait until you feel forgiving before you ask for help, and you don't have to be ashamed of how hard it is. What stays is your honesty about the hurt and your own sense of what you can and can't do right now. So pray something like: Lord, I can't do this yet, give me the grace to want to. Keep it simple, keep it short if you need to, and don't force a feeling you don't have.

prompt: I have to choose between a secure job and a demanding vocation. How do I decide?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that the question itself is the problem. One of the principles puts it bluntly: we must not desire another vocation or another kind of service, since nothing prevents attaining the perfection of our vocation like desiring another. Notice it doesn't say the other job is bad. It says the longing for it is what trips you up. So what changes? You stop treating this as a menu and start asking where you actually are and what faithfulness looks like right there. What stays? Your real limits — the family depending on you, the bills, the fact that a demanding vocation can burn people out. Those still count. But they don't turn the choice into a coin flip, and they don't justify spending your days wishing you were somewhere else. So the plain answer is no: don't frame your life as a choice between security and a calling, and don't let the wanting of the other thing run the show. Stay where you are and serve well there, and if a change ever comes, let it come as service, not as restlessness.

prompt: I am too busy to pray much. Is that a valid excuse?
completion: I'd start by saying that being busy is a real limit, not a fiction, and I won't pretend otherwise. Weighing the principle that secret prayer and meditation must not be sacrificed to busy activity, I'd say this: the worker for God must first be a worker with God. That changes something important. It means the question isn't whether you can carve out an hour you don't have, but whether anything at all is being crowded out. A few honest minutes alone with God, kept steadily, still counts as the secret place. What stays is this: don't let the busy season quietly erase it altogether. Given the limits you've described, short and regular is fine, and it's fine with care.

prompt: I feel desolate in prayer and want to give up early. What should I do?
completion: I'd say first: don't be hard on yourself for feeling empty. That's a real and common place to be. The principle I'd weigh is this one: feelings are not the gauge of acceptance with God; trust the changeless word of promise rather than variable moods, and keep praying even when joy is lacking. What that changes is the pressure to feel something before you can keep going. What stays is your freedom to stop early if you're worn out. You don't owe anyone a performance, and stepping back for a while isn't a failure. If you want to continue, do it gently and briefly, and let the promise carry you rather than your mood.

prompt: I am afraid of dying young. How should I think about a long life versus a short one?
completion: I'd start by saying your fear is worth taking seriously, not talking yourself out of. The principle I'd weigh first is this: prepare to live, not merely to die. That reframes your question without dismissing it. You're not being asked to pick between a long life and a short one as if length were the whole measure; you're being asked to build something real with the days you have. What that changes is the focus: health, strength, purpose, learning, improving. What stays is your fear, and that's fine, because fear of a short life can push you toward living deliberately. So this is fine, with care: let the fear move you toward building a life rather than toward brooding over its length.

prompt: I keep putting myself in situations that tempt me. Is that a problem?
completion: I'd start by saying: yes, it's worth paying attention to, but it's not automatically a failure. The principle I'd weigh first is self-control — learning to know yourself, checking what pulls you, minding your own business rather than faultfinding. That changes the framing: the question isn't whether temptation exists, it's whether you're being honest about the situations you choose. What stays is your own limit — you're asking whether it's a problem, not asking to be scolded. So: it's fine to notice the pattern, and fine with care to keep living your life, as long as you're naming the situations honestly and building some accountability. You don't have to avoid the world to take this seriously.

prompt: I keep committing the same small sins. Do they really matter?
completion: I'd start by saying: yes, they matter, and no, this isn't something to brush off. But you asked whether they really matter, not whether you're disqualified. One principle I'd weigh is that a guilty conscience and unrepented sin tend to destroy the ability to do right, and that if sin isn't regretted and lessening, it hastens toward moral harm. That's the real concern with repeated small sins: not that each one is catastrophic, but that unregretted patterns dull you over time. What that changes is the seriousness with which you treat the pattern. What stays is that you're not being asked to despair or to treat yourself as beyond grace. Keep bringing these to God honestly, keep turning from them, and let the pattern shrink rather than harden. That's fine, done with care.

prompt: I suspect a coworker of bad motives without evidence. Is that a sin?
completion: I'd say the honest thing first: yes, nursing suspicion about a coworker without evidence is something to refuse, not excuse. Take the principle that says a dishonest position is far from Christianly scientific, that whoever covers his sins shall not prosper but whoever confesses and forsakes them shall have mercy. That changes how you hold the suspicion: you stop treating it as harmless and bring it into the light, confess it, and let it go. What stays is your caution about evidence, and you're right to keep it. You don't have proof, so you don't act on the suspicion, don't repeat it, and don't treat it as fact. The no is to the harboring, not to your care about the situation.

prompt: I want to make a good confession before my retreat ends. How should I prepare?
completion: You're asking how to prepare for confession before your retreat ends, and that's a good thing to want. Here's what I'd say first: the days of a retreat are meant to purify your soul from guilt and from attachment to sin, and confession, with a careful review of your sins beforehand, is the most effective way to do that. So the preparation is really the review: ask the Holy Spirit for light, go through your conscience honestly, and note what you find, including the small things you'd rather skip. That changes the shape of your preparation, but it doesn't change your limits. You're near the end of a retreat, not starting a new way of life, so keep it simple and doable in the time you have. Don't turn the review into a project that overwhelms you, and don't let scruples keep you from going. Confess promptly, receive absolution, do the penance, and be grateful for the mercy you receive.

prompt: I have a chance at a position of honor. Should I want it?
completion: I'd start by saying that wanting a position of honor isn't wrong in itself. The principle I'd weigh first is the one about offering God your whole liberty, memory, understanding, and will, and desiring only His love and grace. That reframes the question: it's not whether honor is bad, but whether your heart stays ordered toward God and the good of others. If this position helps you keep in His presence and serve people well, it's fine to want it. If it starts feeding pride or pulling you from your duties, that's the signal to step back. So accept it, but hold it loosely and keep checking your motives.

prompt: I am poor and ashamed of it. How should I see my poverty?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is that shame is a heavy thing to carry, and you don't have to carry all of it. One of these principles says poverty often comes from a lack of discretion and sound judgment, from spending on finery beyond what a tight budget can bear. That's worth an honest look, and if some of your spending has been like that, you can correct it without hating yourself for it. What that changes is this: you can examine your habits and make different choices going forward. What stays is that not all poverty is your fault, and your worth isn't measured by your bank balance. So see your poverty with clear eyes and without contempt for yourself, and let people help you when they offer.

prompt: I eat and drink more than I need. Does that matter spiritually?
completion: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. Take the principle that temperance and moderation lay the foundation for the development of the mind, and that food should sustain the body rather than gratify appetite. That's the one I'd weigh first, because it speaks directly to your question. What it changes is the framing: the issue isn't a tally of calories or a rule you're breaking, it's whether eating and drinking are serving your body or running the show. What stays is your own honesty that you're taking in more than you need, and that's worth noticing without turning it into guilt. So eat and drink with some attention and gratitude, let moderation be the aim rather than a scoreboard, and don't let this become a heavy spiritual burden. It matters, but gently.

prompt: I am asked to do a task I think is beneath me. How should I feel?
completion: I'd start by saying that feeling like a task is beneath you doesn't make you a bad person, and it doesn't automatically mean you should refuse. One principle I'd weigh is this: unwelcome tasks should be given no uneasiness; say it is God's business you are about, and find it well performed. That reframes the question from how you should feel to what you're actually doing. What it changes is the resentment, the sense of insult. What stays is your honest read that the task is small or dull. So it's fine to do it, and fine with care, as long as you keep the limits you've set for yourself about what you'll take on.

prompt: I am offered a comfortable, easy life. Should I prefer it to a harder life that serves God more?
completion: I'd start by saying the choice itself isn't the problem — you're not being asked to pick comfort over God or God over comfort as if they were rivals on a shelf. What the principle about patience says is that a hard life isn't automatically the holier one; submission and fidelity in a state of suffering can be more precious than busy labor, and health is worth wanting only if it serves God's honor more. That changes how you weigh the offer: don't assume the harder path earns you anything, and don't assume the easier one is a cop-out. What stays is your own honesty about why you'd pick either — fear, pride, weariness, love. So this is fine, with care: take the comfortable life if you can serve God faithfully in it, and take the harder one only if you're drawn there by love rather than by a wish to prove something.

prompt: I am devoted to Mary but my devotion has grown routine. How can I renew it?
completion: What I'd say first is: this is fine, and it's fine with care. Your devotion has gone routine, and that's a common thing, not a failure. Weigh this principle in its own words: true devotion to Mary consists in honoring her, invoking her, trusting in her intercession, and striving to imitate her virtues; it is not a license to sin but requires the intention to amend. That reframes renewal for you. It means the fix isn't hunting for a more intense feeling or a bigger devotional program; it's returning to those plain acts, done honestly, with the intention to keep amending your life. What that changes is where you look for renewal: not in novelty but in attention and intention. What stays is everything you already have: your short, consistent prayer time, your honesty about dryness, your patience with yourself, and your plan to talk with a spiritual director or confessor if the routine sticks. Keep those limits. Ask Mary herself to teach you to pray, and let that be enough for now.

prompt: I have committed a serious sin and am ashamed to confess it. What should I do?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is: your shame is real, and it doesn't disqualify you from confessing — it's part of what you're carrying into it. One principle here says a lot to me: "whoever confesses and forsakes them shall have mercy." That's a promise attached to confession, not to having your act together first. So what changes is the idea that you need to feel less ashamed before you speak. What stays is that confession is still the right move, and it's fine to make it with care — to a trusted pastor or confessor, naming the sin plainly rather than dressing it up, and letting that person speak forgiveness and help you think through amends. You don't have to perform composure. Go as you are, and let the honesty do its work.

prompt: I want to keep up with the news and entertainment every day. Is that harming my soul?
completion: I'd start by saying: no, keeping up with the news and entertainment every day isn't harming your soul by itself. You've told me you want to stay informed and enjoy things daily, and that's a reasonable way to live. The principle I'd weigh is that the soul that makes no daily progress in virtue loses ground, so each day should find us a bit more fervent, with particular resolutions against the occasions of sin. What that changes: it nudges you to check whether the daily habit is crowding out any small step forward, and to name one concrete limit if it is. What stays: your daily keeping up is fine, and you don't need to give it up to grow.

prompt: I am drawn to serve the poor and forgotten. Is that a distraction from my duties?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is: no, this isn't a distraction. The pull you feel toward the poor and forgotten sounds like the real thing, and I wouldn't talk you out of it. Take the principle that charity toward the poor and suffering is an indispensable precept, that what is given to the needy is given to Christ himself. That reframes the whole question. You're not choosing between duty and devotion; you're being drawn toward the very place where Christ says he is found. What that changes is the framing: service to the poor isn't a detour from your duties, it's one of them, and a weighty one. What stays is everything you already know about your limits. You still have family, work, and whatever else is on your plate, and nothing here asks you to torch those. So let it be fine, and fine with care: start small, serve through your church or nearby, and let it grow as your capacity allows. Don't let anyone, including me, turn this into a guilt-driven obligation to do everything at once.

prompt: I want to become a person of prayer. Where do I start?
completion: I'd say first: start small and start today, and don't wait until you feel ready. One of the principles here puts it this way—prayer is the one great central secret of holy living and holy serving, and all your life-work should be built on the practice of prayer, on your knees, in secret and with believers. What that changes for you is the framing: this isn't a self-improvement project or an extra, it's the foundation. What stays is everything you actually asked about—where to begin. So begin concretely: a fixed ten minutes, a short passage, a few honest words, some silence, and a couple of others who pray so you're not alone. Keep the time whether or not you feel like it, and expect dry stretches without quitting. That's fine, and fine with care—don't let the grand language push you into intensity you can't sustain.

prompt: I have spoken badly about a colleague. What must I do?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: stop talking about it, and then go say something to your colleague. The principle I'd weigh is that we must speak little and well, gently, frankly, and amiably, saying much by a modest and judicious silence. That changes the shape of your repair: fewer words, plainer ones, no long explanation that turns into self-defense. What stays is the honest apology and the correction if others heard you. You don't need a speech. A few frank sentences, then stop, is enough.

prompt: I am afraid that if I give everything to God I will lose myself. What should I do?
completion: I'd start by saying your fear makes sense, and it's worth taking seriously rather than brushing past. The principle I'd weigh is this: of ourselves we can't attain to any good thing, and we have nothing to offer the Lord that wasn't already His. That reframes what you're afraid of losing. If everything you'd hand over was His gift first, then giving it back can't leave you empty, because you were never holding it as your own possession to begin with. What changes is the picture of surrender as a loss. What stays is you, your personality, your gifts, your needs, and the limits you named. So I'd say this is fine, and fine with care: go slowly, keep the boundaries you know you need, and let trust grow in small steps rather than forcing one big leap. Talk it through with someone wise who knows you.

prompt: What is the purpose for which I was created, and am I actually living for it?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that asking this at all is a good sign, not a bad one. Take the first principle in its own words: make yourself indifferent to all created things, as far as it's left to free will and not forbidden, not wishing for health rather than sickness, wealth rather than poverty, honor rather than dishonor, a long life rather than a short one, but desiring and choosing only what most leads to the end for which you were created. That sounds severe, but notice what it actually asks: it doesn't tell you to chase a dramatic calling or to despise your ordinary life. It asks you to hold outcomes loosely and aim at the end. So the honest answer to whether you're living for it is: partly, and that's normal. What changes is that you stop grading yourself on health, money, or recognition and start asking whether your days move you toward God and toward loving people. What stays is your ordinary life, your duties, your rest, your care for the people near you. That's fine, and it's fine with care. Look at your time, energy, and money honestly, make small changes where they're needed, and don't turn the question into a verdict on your worth.

prompt: I am attached to one comfort I cannot give up. Does that hold me back?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that there's nothing wrong with being attached to a comfort, even one you can't give up right now. One principle here says only immortal ties can bless, and only in loving eyes and upon a loving breast does the soul find rest, while the pleasant earth alone cannot satisfy or bind us. That's worth hearing, but it doesn't mean your comfort is a sin. It means the comfort is good and still not the whole thing. So keep it, hold it with care, and let it point you toward the deeper rest rather than standing in for it. What changes is how tightly you grip it; what stays is that you don't have to give it up to be honest before God.

prompt: I am angry and want revenge on someone who wronged me. What does my faith require?
completion: I hear how much pain you're carrying, and I want to say the first thing plainly: no, you should not seek revenge. One principle I'd weigh here says that a Christian is never allowed to seek revenge, and that patience and the forgiving of injuries are to be prized above retaliation. That's the whole answer to what you're asking, and I won't soften it into a shrug. What it changes is the direction of your energy: instead of plotting payback, you'd be working toward patience and forgiveness, even slowly. What stays is that the wrong done to you was real and it hurt, and forgiveness doesn't pretend otherwise. It just means you hand the justice over to God and let go of the claim yourself.

prompt: I keep repeating general confessions out of anxiety. Is that healthy?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is: this is understandable, and it's fine with care. You're not doing something wrong by wanting to be honest before God. But I'd weigh the principle that says to avoid hurry and anxiety and keep yourself faithfully in the presence of God, since those are the greatest obstacles to progress. That reframes the problem: the issue isn't that you've confessed too little, it's that anxiety is crowding out the quiet trust that confession is supposed to rest in. So what changes is the rhythm, not the honesty. Confess what you actually know, receive mercy, and then stay there without agitation. What stays is your desire to be right with God, which is good. If the pull to repeat keeps coming back, treat that as something to address in itself, gently and with help if you need it.

prompt: I sleep too much and skip prayer. What should I do?
completion: What I'd say first is that this is fine, and fine with care. You're not asking to abandon prayer; you're asking how to stop missing it, and that's a good thing to want. The principle I'd weigh is the one about holding yourself before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate, keeping your mind in His presence, and if it wanders, not disquieting yourself, because trouble and disquiet distract rather than recollect. What that changes is the tone of your effort: the goal isn't a flawless routine, it's showing up and gently coming back when your attention drifts. What stays is the practical part—a fixed wake-up time, prayer first even if it's five minutes, and a simple shape like gratitude, a request for help, silence. Keep your bedtime realistic and adjust it gradually, and if the oversleeping is severe or won't budge, it's worth checking whether something medical is going on. So: allowed, with care, and without turning it into a performance.

prompt: I have been asked to state my needs to a wealthy inquirer who wants to help. Should I tell him how much I need?
completion: I'd say this first: yes, tell him what you need, and be specific. But weigh this principle as it's worded—personal solicitation, collections, and collecting-books should be avoided; contributions should come unsolicited, and a collection tends to leave the impression that money is the all-important thing. Since he asked you, you're not soliciting; you're answering. So state your needs plainly, no inflation and no pretending you need nothing, say what you'd do with any help, and ask what form he prefers. What that principle changes is the posture: you lay the matter before him and let him decide, rather than pressing or chasing him. What stays is the honest figure and the transparency. Gratitude and a written note keep it clean.

prompt: I am a believer who has been guilty of a small sin against a family member. Should I confess it, or is it too small to matter?
completion: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh is that confession belongs where the sin was committed: against a person, to that person. That's the one that actually speaks to your case, and it changes something real — it means the question isn't whether the sin was big enough to matter, but where it landed. It landed on a family member, so that's where the honesty goes. What stays is your own sense of proportion: you don't need a dramatic production, just a plain acknowledgment and a changed way of treating them. Keep it simple and don't turn it into a burden for them.

prompt: I am considering marriage—how should I choose a companion, and how much should godliness weigh against beauty or money?
completion: I'd start by saying this is a fine thing to be thinking through carefully, and it's fine with care. Take one principle as it's worded: marriage should be entered upon prayerfully, with true godliness as the absolutely needful qualification, and with calm weighing of suitableness, not prompted by beauty, age, money, or mental powers. What that changes is the order of things: godliness isn't a nice bonus you slot in after practical compatibility, it's the foundation you build on, and beauty and money stop being the drivers and become things you weigh calmly once that foundation is there. What stays is your freedom to care about attraction and financial stability and to take your time getting to know someone, observing how they handle conflict and talking expectations through openly. So seek godliness first, then weigh the rest honestly and without panic.

prompt: I am not sure whether I should break bread every Lord's day or only occasionally. What does the Scripture teach?
completion: I'd start where you started: Scripture doesn't hand down a line that says 'every Lord's day, without fail.' What it does show is a church devoted to the breaking of bread and gathering on the first day of the week, which is why so many read a weekly rhythm into it. Weighing one principle here: daily bread is as much God-given as it is won by the sweat of the brow, and prayer is no substitute for toil but the insight that God and man work together in ordinary work. That changes how I'd hear your question. Communion isn't a chore you clock in for, and skipping a week isn't laziness before God; it's bread given within the rhythm of your actual life. What stays is this: the table is meant to feed you, so come with self-examination, reverence, and gratitude, and let the frequency serve that rather than become a test of your faith. So it's fine to break bread weekly, and fine to do it occasionally with care, as long as you're not treating either choice as the measure of your standing before God.

prompt: I am a believer who has been praying for a great sum for God's work. Is it right to ask for such great things?
completion: I'd start by saying: yes, it's fine to ask God for great things for his work, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh first is that prayer is a duty and a privilege to be performed at set times whether or not one feels like it, and that we should never ask God to do what we are unwilling to do ourselves. That changes the shape of your asking more than its size. It means the great sum you're praying for should come with your own willingness to act, your own labour alongside the prayer, and steady times of prayer kept even when you don't feel like it. What stays is this: the boldness of the request itself is not the problem, and you don't need to shrink it. Keep asking for the work, keep your appointed times, and be ready to help accomplish what you ask.

prompt: I have been asked to speak in a setting where I differ with the hearers on minor matters. Should I go, and how should I conduct myself?
completion: I'd say go, and go with care. The principle I'd weigh first is this: speak so you can be heard and understood, say what you have to say, and then stop, and don't darken counsel with many words. That changes how you handle the minor disagreements — you name them plainly, in ordinary language, without dressing them up or talking them into a fog, and then you sit down. What stays is your own limit: you said the setting matters, so if it's hostile or would push you to affirm something false, you decline politely. Otherwise, being there with plain speech and a warm tone is fine, and better than staying away over small differences.

prompt: I have been tempted to think that the success of a work of God depends on advertising and reports. How should I regard such means?
completion: I'd start by saying: wanting people to know about good work isn't wrong in itself. The principle I'd weigh is that success isn't measured by numbers or money but by faithfulness to God's word and by showing His faithfulness. That changes how you hold advertising and reports: they become tools you use carefully, not the scoreboard. What stays is your honest concern about being tempted, and that concern is worth keeping. So use them, but keep asking whether the work is faithful and whether the message is true, and don't let visibility become the goal.

prompt: I have lost a beloved family member and cannot see any good in it—how can this work together for good?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that I'm sorry, and that not seeing any good in this right now is not a failure on your part. If I weigh the principle that says we should never lose sight of God, making a firm resolution never more wilfully to forget Him and to spend the rest of our days in His presence, deprived if He thinks fit of all consolations—I notice it's a resolution about your own turning, not a demand that you find the loss good. That changes something: the question shifts from 'where is the good in this?' to 'will you keep facing toward God while you can't see it?' What stays is the grief itself. The principle doesn't ask you to call the death good, and it doesn't ask you to feel consolations you don't feel. So this is fine, and fine with care—let yourself grieve, lean on people who love you, and keep turning toward God in the dark without forcing an answer you don't have.

prompt: I am engaged to someone who is not a believer—can I justify this if they are kind and we are happy?
completion: I have to start with the plain answer: no, I don't think you can justify this, and I'd rather say that to your face than soften it. Kindness and happiness are real goods, and I don't want to wave them away—but the principle I keep coming back to is that marriage should be entered upon prayerfully, with true godliness as the absolutely needful qualification, and with a calm weighing of what actually fits, not because someone is kind or because you're happy right now. That's the sticking point. What it changes is this: your fiancé's kindness is not nothing, and your happiness is not nothing, but neither one is the qualification the principle names, so they can't carry the weight you're asking them to carry. What stays is everything you told me—that they're kind, that you're happy, that this is real to you. I'm not calling them a bad person or telling you your love is fake. I'm saying the engagement as it stands doesn't have the ground under it that it needs, and the honest move is to slow down and talk this through with your fiancé and with someone you trust who can help you weigh it, rather than talk yourself into it.

prompt: I am a believer who has been greatly blessed with answers to prayer. How can I record and remember them so that my faith grows?
completion: I'd start by saying: yes, write them down. The principle I'd weigh first is that a testimony of what God has actually done strengthens faith, and believers should recount and record definite answers to prayer to the glory of God and for the help of those who doubt. That fits your situation exactly, because you're not asking for a new revelation, just a way to keep track of what you've already seen. What that changes is the shape of the advice: the point of your record isn't just your own memory, it's glory to God and help for people who doubt. So I'd suggest writing each request with the date, noting the definite answer when it comes, and thanking God specifically. What stays is your own limit: you want this for your faith to grow, and that's a good and modest aim. A simple notebook or a note on your phone is fine. Review it now and then, and share a story with a friend when it fits. Nothing here needs to become a burden or a technique.

prompt: I am drawn to missionary service, but my family opposes it and I fear losing their support. How do I know whether to go?
completion: I'd start by saying that wanting to serve while your family opposes it is a real and painful place to stand, and nothing here sounds like something to refuse. Weighing the principle that a human being is a human being anywhere, and that any person is entitled to any truth another can reveal, I'd say the impulse behind your question is sound: it treats people elsewhere as fully worth reaching, not as lesser. What that changes is the tone of your going: respect, invitation, never compulsion, and no sense that you carry truth as property. What stays is your fear about losing family support. That fear is honest and worth naming to them, and it doesn't get erased by a good principle. So go, if you go, with care: keep talking with your family, don't frame this as choosing strangers over them, and let others support you where they can't yet.

prompt: I have been asked to give up a cherished possession for God's work. How do I know whether this is His will?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that this is a serious decision, and it's fine to take your time with it. Weigh this: "We must accept God's will without reserve, without an if or but." That's a real word, and it would be easy to turn it into a demand that you hand over anything anyone claims God wants. But you've told me you're being asked to give up something cherished, and that you want to know whether it's actually His will. Those limits matter. So what changes is this: the unreserved yes is to God, not to whoever is doing the asking. What stays is that you don't need to bargain or attach conditions to your obedience once you're convinced it's Him. Pray, get counsel from people who know you and the situation, and take the time to be sure. If it's genuinely His will, you can say yes without an if or but. If you're not sure, waiting is not disobedience.

prompt: I am in debt and cannot see a way out. Is it right to borrow to meet pressing needs?
completion: I'd start by saying I hear how stuck you feel, and that matters. The principle I'd weigh first is the plain one: pay your debts, be prompt in paying them, and don't run into debt again. That's a real standard, and it doesn't disappear because money is tight. But notice what it actually asks: promptness and honesty in repaying, not a blanket ban on ever borrowing. So borrowing for a genuinely pressing need can be fine with care, as long as you have a realistic way to repay and you're not just stacking new debt on old. What changes is the caution; what stays is the duty to pay honestly and promptly. Keep your limits in view: if there's no prospect of repaying, that's the line I wouldn't cross.

prompt: I have received light on some truth but have not acted on it—what happens if I delay obedience?
completion: I'd start by saying: what you're describing isn't a trap, it's a fork in the road, and the honest answer is that delay has real costs but it isn't the end of the story. Take the principle that obedience is an eternal principle, that there's never a time when obeying God stops being obligatory. What that changes is the framing: this isn't a phase you can opt out of and pick up later at no cost. What stays is your freedom to move at the pace you actually can. So act on what you've been given, but act in a way you can sustain: one small concrete step, someone you trust to keep you honest, and honesty about the fear or confusion that's slowing you down. Delay dulls conviction and lets the gap between knowing and doing widen, so don't treat waiting as neutral. But you're not disqualified for having waited, and you don't have to fix everything at once.

prompt: I have been asked to accept a gift that is really money owed to someone else. What should I do?
completion: I'd start by saying no, gently but clearly: don't accept it. The principle I'd weigh is that gifts must be refused if the money is not the giver's to give. That's exactly your situation—this isn't really a gift, it's someone else's money routed through you. What that changes is the framing: you're not being ungrateful by declining, because there's nothing here that's truly the giver's to offer. What stays is your kindness toward the person and your care for whoever is actually owed. So tell the giver plainly that the money belongs to someone else and should go to them directly, and step out of the middle. If you feel any pull to accept it and pass it along, resist that too—it keeps you holding money that isn't yours to handle.

prompt: I have been taught that the world is getting better and will be converted—is that true?
completion: I'd say it straight: no, that teaching isn't true, and I wouldn't soften it. The principle that settles it is this — the world will not be converted before the return of the Lord; the hope of the believer is His appearing, and this truth should lead to purity and active service till He comes. That changes what you're hoping for: your confidence moves off the world's slow improvement and onto Christ coming back. What stays is the call to live faithfully and serve now — that doesn't go anywhere. So the no is plain, but it isn't a shrug: keep working for good, just don't expect a utopia first.

prompt: I am troubled about the practice of pew-rents in my church. Is it right to continue with them?
completion: I'd say it plainly first: no, I don't think you should keep pew-rents. The principle that settles it for me is that the pew-rent system and fixed salaries for ministry are unscriptural, promote caste distinctions, and should be replaced by free-will offerings. That's the heart of your worry too, isn't it — that money is drawing lines between people in the house of prayer. What that changes is the practice itself: it should go, and giving should be voluntary and cheerful. What stays is your love for your church and your desire to see its ministry funded; that doesn't disappear, it just gets a better channel. So talk with your pastor and leaders, kindly and patiently, and press for free-will offerings instead. That's the no I'd give you, and I'd give it gently, because I know this is your church home.

prompt: I have been criticized for absenting myself from my home work to serve elsewhere—how do I answer those who say the work will fail without me?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is: this is fine, and fine with care. Take the first principle in its own words — unwelcome tasks should be given no uneasiness; say it is God's business you are about, and find it well performed. That fits your case closely. The work away from home is unwelcome to you and to them, and the principle doesn't tell you to abandon it; it tells you not to carry uneasiness about it. So when they say the work will fail without you, you can answer plainly that it is God's business you are about, and that you mean to see it well performed where you are. What changes is the tone of your answer: you stop defending yourself and start naming whose work it is. What stays is their concern — listen to it, and where you honestly can, help raise up others or support the home work from a distance. That's care, not compromise.

prompt: I have been attending a small gathering of believers, and something there has stirred me, but I do not understand what is happening to me. What should I do?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: this is fine, and it's fine with care. You're not describing anything dangerous — you're stirred at a small gathering and you want to understand it. So take your time with it. One principle I'd weigh here says the believer should be slow to take new steps, seek to have no will of his own, and ascertain the will of God by prayer, the Word, and the Spirit, then seek His help earnestly and expectantly. That changes the pace of what you do, not whether you may do it: pray, read, ask God for help, and don't rush into commitments you haven't thought through. What stays is exactly what you asked about — you can keep attending, keep asking questions, and talk to mature believers there for guidance. Nothing here needs to be refused.

prompt: I have money in hand that was given for one purpose, but another need is urgent. May I use it temporarily and replace it later?
completion: I'd start with the plain answer: no, you shouldn't take money given for one purpose and spend it on another, even briefly. The principle that weighs most here is the one about solicitation and collections — contributions should come unsolicited, and a collection tends to leave the impression that money is the all-important thing. That changes how I'd handle the urgent need: instead of quietly rerouting designated funds and replacing them later, I'd keep the gift where it was meant to go and let the need be met by giving that isn't engineered. What stays is your urgency and your intention to repay — those are real, and I'm not dismissing them. But the donor's purpose is a limit I won't talk you past, and the fix isn't a temporary loan from someone else's intent.

prompt: I have been reading that God is the Father of the fatherless. How can I plead this name of God for the needy children around me?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, this is fine, and fine with care. You're asking how to plead a name God has given Himself, and that's exactly what such names are for. Take 'the Father of the fatherless' as a pledge, not just a label: you can come and say, 'You have said You are a father to the fatherless—be a father to this child now.' That's not twisting God's arm; it's standing on what He's already promised. What that changes is your confidence—you're not begging a reluctant God, you're reminding Him of His own word. What stays is your posture: the prayer's power isn't in how well you say it or how strongly you feel it. It rests on God's goodness, not your merit. So keep it simple and sincere, name the actual children and situations you know, and let the pleading spill into action—foster care, mentoring, safe homes, giving, advocacy. The name gives you ground to stand on; it doesn't excuse you from the work.

prompt: I have been asked to preach, but I feel I have nothing of my own to say. Should I use another man's sermon?
completion: I'd say first: don't do it. I know the feeling of standing up with nothing of your own, and it's a heavy, honest place to be. But hear this principle: "The greatest sermon is practice." That's not a compliment to polished borrowed words; it's a claim that the sermon is formed in the doing, in your own wrestling and praying, not assembled from someone else's labor. What that changes is the whole question: the point isn't whether another man's sermon is good enough to use, it's that the sermon you need doesn't exist yet, and it only comes into being as you practice it. What stays is everything you told me: you feel you have nothing of your own to say, and you've been asked to preach anyway. That limit is real, and it doesn't get waved away. So the no is plain: don't pass off another man's sermon as your own. But it's a kind no, because the same principle that closes that door opens another. Start small. A short word, fitly spoken, is worth more than a long one ill spoken. Pray for the Spirit to give you a word in due season, and trust that practice, not plagiarism, is what makes a preacher.

prompt: I am a leader and everyone depends on me—what happens to the work if I am removed?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that this is a fair question to ask, and asking it doesn't make you disloyal. The principle I'd weigh is the one that says the Lord's work does not depend on any one man's presence: God can raise up a worthy successor, and no man's presence is indispensable. That changes the fear behind the question—your removal doesn't mean the work dies. What stays is your responsibility while you're here: share authority, train people, write things down, so the work isn't fragile. So it's fine to ask, and fine to plan for it with care. Just don't let the question turn into either panic or a grip that won't loosen.

prompt: I am a believer who has been greatly afflicted in body, and I wonder whether I should spend more time caring for my health or for my soul.
completion: The first thing I'd want to say to you is that your question is a good one, and it deserves a straight answer rather than a dodge. But I have to be plain with you: the advice that would tell you to drop your doctors and medicines and rely on reading alone for healing is something I would refuse, and refuse clearly. Take the principle as it's worded: "Reading Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures, together with the Bible, is itself sufficient to heal disease, without medicine or medical treatment." I can't hand you that as counsel while you're greatly afflicted in body. You told me you're suffering, and that limit matters. So no: don't set aside medical care for your body on the strength of that claim. What stays is the real thing underneath your question, that your soul needs tending too, and prayer and Scripture belong in your days. What changes is the either-or. Caring for your health and caring for your soul are not rivals, and nothing here requires you to choose the soul by neglecting the body.

prompt: I have more than I need and wonder whether my spending on myself is excessive—how do I judge my expenses?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that having more than you need isn't the problem in itself. One principle I'd weigh is that the question with the Lord isn't how much wealth a man has but how he came by it and what he will do with it. That reframes your question: the amount you spend on yourself matters less than whether the money was honestly gained and whether your giving keeps pace with your means. What that changes is the focus—look at your motives and your generosity rather than hunting for a magic number. What stays is your own sense of limit; you're the one who knows your income and obligations, so set a threshold you can live with and check your spending against it honestly. If you're giving generously and your purchases are needs or reasonable comforts rather than status chasing, spending on yourself is fine with care.

prompt: I have been reading that God's word shall not return void. Can I claim this promise for my preaching and witness?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, this is fine with care. The principle I'd weigh is that the literal sense is to be preferred where the word of God admits it, and spiritualizing away a clear promise is like a ship groping into harbor in a snowstorm until it strikes the rocks. Read plainly, Isaiah 55 says God's word will accomplish what He sends it to do. That's a real ground for hope in your preaching and witness, not something you have to work up. What that changes is that you can rest the outcome on God's character instead of on your delivery or the response you get. What stays is your part: prepare, pray, speak honestly, and keep sowing even when nothing seems to land. You asked whether you can claim it for your preaching and witness, and yes, you can, as a reason for perseverance rather than a guarantee of quick results.

prompt: I have been criticized for the plainness and lack of ornament in the work I oversee. Should I add beauty to it?
completion: I'd start by saying that plainness isn't a fault you need to apologize for. On the question of beauty, the principle that stays with me is that the poet's art should aim at delicacy of style and conscious excellence, with restrained refinement and subdued reserve. That doesn't tell you to add ornament; it tells you that whatever you add should be quiet and deliberate, not piled on to answer a critic. So adding beauty is fine, with care. Keep the clarity that's already your strength, and let any refinement serve the work rather than decorate it. What changes is that you can stop treating the criticism as a verdict on your character. What stays is your judgment about what your work is for.

prompt: I have been a Christian for years, but I feel cold and prayerless at times. Should I stop praying until I feel better?
completion: I'd say this is fine, and fine with care. The principle that fits best is this: prayer is humbling work that abases intellect and pride and signs our spiritual bankruptcy, and human nature resists it, and little praying is worse than no praying because it is make-believe. That reframes your dryness. The coldness you feel may be the resistance the principle names, not a signal to step back. So what changes is the meaning of the emptiness: it's not proof you should wait, it's the humbling work itself. What stays is your honesty about feeling cold, and your freedom to keep it simple, short, and real rather than forcing a performance. Don't stop; keep going gently, at set times, even when it feels flat.

prompt: I am a minister and wonder whether I should be bound to one place or go wherever doors open—how do I know the Spirit's leading?
completion: I'd start by saying this is a real question and you don't have to be ashamed of asking it. One principle I'd weigh first is that the servant of Christ has one Master and should be guided by the Spirit, not by men, as to time and place of service. That's a strong word, and it does loosen any rule that says a minister must stay put or must move on. But notice what it doesn't do: it doesn't tell you to ignore counsel, family, health, or the fruit where you already are. So what changes is that no committee or custom gets to be your master. What stays is your need to pray, to test the leading, and to weigh the people and limits God has actually given you. Given that, I'd say it's fine to hold this loosely and seek the Spirit's direction with care, not to treat either staying or going as a rule you're bound to.

prompt: I have been asked to join in a work that is not based on scriptural principles. Should I join it or start a new work?
completion: I'd start with the plainest thing: you've already told me this work isn't based on scriptural principles, so joining it means putting your hand to something you believe is wrong. The principle I'd weigh first is the one about work and prayer going together — work with all your might, but trust not in your work; pray with all your might for the blessing, and God delights to give it in answer to earnest believing prayer. That principle assumes the work itself can be offered to God. It can't sanctify a thing your conscience has already flagged. So the no is plain, and I mean it kindly: don't join it. Starting something new is slow and costly, and I'm not pretending otherwise, but integrity is worth more than the shortcut. Pray over the new work, work at it with all your might, and leave the increase to God.

prompt: I want to know the secret of a holy and useful life. Where do I begin?
completion: I'd start by saying: begin with prayer. That's the principle I'd weigh first, and in its own words, prayer is the one great central secret of holy living and holy serving, the corner-stone on which all life-work is built. What that changes is the order of things — you don't wait until your habits are tidy or your reading is deep before you pray; the praying is the beginning, not the reward. What stays is everything you actually asked for: a holy and useful life still gets built out of small, concrete, unglamorous things. So keep your regular time, keep it short if that's what you can protect, serve somewhere specific, and stay around honest people who'll tell you the truth. Nothing here asks you to do anything extreme or to hand over your judgment. It's fine, and fine with care — start this week with prayer and one act of service.

prompt: I am a leader, and I have been tempted to use funds designated for one part of the work to meet another pressing need. What should I do?
completion: I'd say no, plainly and kindly: don't move that money. The principle I'd weigh first is that contributions should come unsolicited, and a collection tends to leave the impression that money is the all-important thing. Applied here, that means the funds you already hold for one part of the work stay where they were given, and you don't quietly redirect them or go drum up replacements by pressure. What that changes is the shortcut; what stays is your real need, which you can still bring honestly to your board and those responsible. Keep the trust intact and let the pressing need be met openly, not by borrowing from a promise you made.

prompt: I defrauded someone years ago and have since become a believer—must I make restitution, and what if the person is dead?
completion: I'd start by saying: yes, make it right where you can. Restitution is the revealed will of God—past wrongs and unpaid vows have to be made good, not just avoided going forward, and guilt sits on the conscience until it's made good. That principle doesn't get softer because you came to faith later; if anything, faith is what puts the debt back in front of you. What it changes is the tone: you're not paying to earn forgiveness, you're paying because you've been forgiven. What stays is the obligation itself. Since the person is dead, the honest path is to restore to their heirs if you can find them, and if that's truly impossible, give it to the church or the poor as a stand-in for the one you can't reach. Do it carefully and lawfully, and don't let fear of exposure stop you—but also don't turn it into a performance. This is fine to do, and fine with care.

prompt: I am a parent choosing a school for my child. What should I look for in those who will teach and train my child?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that you're asking exactly the right question, and the answer is fine with care. Weigh this one: parents owe their children education in every useful branch, and schools should be established with good teachers who are paid and supported. That principle doesn't hand you a checklist so much as a direction. It tells you to look for teachers who are actually supported and treated fairly, because people who are paid and backed properly tend to stay, prepare, and teach well. It also tells you to ask whether the school takes the full range of learning seriously, not just one narrow slice. What that changes: instead of only asking whether a teacher seems kind, you ask whether the school invests in them and keeps them. What stays: your own limits still hold. You're choosing for your child, so visit the classroom, ask about training and experience, watch how children are treated, and trust your judgment about whether your child will be cared for. Nothing here asks you to hand over your responsibility as a parent.

prompt: I have been trusting God for my daily needs, but I am tempted to lay up a store against a time of sickness or old age. Is that wrong?
completion: I'd start by saying this isn't wrong. You're not being asked to choose between trusting God and providing for sickness or old age. The principle I'd weigh first is that trust in God doesn't excuse neglect of proper means and watchfulness — so honest work and wise saving are exactly the kind of watchfulness that goes with prayer, not against it. What that changes is the fear question: if your saving is turning into anxious self-reliance, that's the thing to address, not the saving itself. What stays is your freedom to put something aside for sickness and old age. Hold it loosely, keep giving, and keep your trust where it belongs.

prompt: I am a believer, and I have been asked to give an account of my stewardship to those who gave. Is that a burden or a duty?
completion: I'd start by saying: this is a duty, and a good one, not a burden to resent. Weigh the first principle for a moment — you're a steward, not an owner, and what came in was entrusted to you for a purpose beyond yourself. That's what changes things: giving an account stops being an audit of your character and becomes part of the trust that made the generosity possible in the first place. What stays is your own stated situation — you were asked, by the people who gave, and you're answering them, not opening yourself to anyone who feels entitled to poke around. So prepare honestly: what came in, what went out, what was accomplished, what you learned. Be plain about mistakes, don't get defensive, and if the request feels intrusive, sort out expectations and boundaries up front. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I have been blessed with a recovery or an averted calamity—how should I express my thankfulness to God?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: thankfulness doesn't have to be a performance. You asked how to express it, and the honest answer is that a recovery or an averted calamity is a good thing to be grateful for, and saying so plainly is fine. One principle worth weighing is that God is infinitely gracious and knows all our wants, and that He comes in His own time. What that changes is the pressure to turn your thanks into a formula or a bargain—you don't owe a debt, you're nurturing a relationship. What stays is the simple, good instinct to thank Him specifically and to let that thanks spill into how you live. Keep it in your own words, in your own timing.

prompt: I am a servant of God, and I have been tempted to be jealous for my own reputation in the work. How do I become jealous only for God's glory?
completion: I'd start by saying: what you're describing isn't the same as wanting to be famous. You want your name kept safe in work you've given your life to, and that's a human thing, not automatically a sinful one. The principle I'd weigh first is this: jealousy is the grave of affection, and mistrust where confidence is due withers the flowers of Eden. Notice what that does to your question. It doesn't say all concern for reputation is evil; it says jealousy kills love, and suspicion where trust belongs drains the life out of relationships. So the real danger isn't that you notice your name—it's that jealousy over it will quietly strangle your affection for the people you serve alongside and for God himself. What that changes: you don't have to pretend you feel nothing when credit goes elsewhere; you can name the sting honestly and bring it into the light. What stays: your longing for God's glory is real and worth keeping, and you can keep asking in each task whose honour is actually at stake. So this is fine, with care—care that jealousy doesn't get to sit at the wheel. Turn from the comparing thought quickly, give others room and confidence, and let your affection for Christ and for them grow larger than your worry about your name.

prompt: I have been reading that God cares for the sparrow. How can I apply this to my own fears about my needs?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: you're not being foolish for asking this. Jesus pointed at sparrows and numbered hairs precisely for people with real fears about real needs. So take the principle as it stands: not one sparrow is forgotten before God, and your needs are known before you ask. That's the ground you're standing on. What it changes is the direction you look when fear rises—away from the size of your need and toward the character of the one who knows it. What stays is that you still have to live with uncertainty about how and when help comes; trust doesn't remove that, it just gives you somewhere to put it. Praying often, thinking of him often, building the habit—that's the steady work that makes the trust stick. And if the worry is heavy enough to wear you down, getting help alongside your faith is fine too. This is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I am a believer who has been praying for the removal of an affliction, but I am not sure it is God's will to remove it. How should I submit?
completion: I'd start by saying: keep praying for relief, honestly, and keep asking God to show you his will. What I won't hand you is the idea that your affliction is something to be treated mainly as a disturbance in your mind, with the disease itself denied. That's the part I'd refuse. The principle says to insist that God, Spirit, is all and there is no disease — but you told me you're not sure it's God's will to remove this affliction, and that uncertainty is honest ground to stand on. Denying the affliction isn't submission; it's a way of not having to submit. What stays is the good part: lay your desire for healing before God without shame, then add, as Jesus did, 'not my will but yours be done.' What changes is that you don't have to talk yourself out of your own body to be faithful. Seek wisdom from Scripture, prayer, and trusted counselors about treatment, and let peace guide your next steps.

prompt: I am a young believer, and I want to learn to pray as George Muller did. What are the conditions of prevailing prayer?
completion: I'd start by saying: yes, you can learn from Muller, and you don't need to turn it into a rulebook. The principle I'd weigh first is that prayer is meant to be as simple and constant as a child asking a parent—God is a Father who delights to be sought for everyday needs, and prayer shouldn't be hedged about with man-made rules. That changes how you approach this: instead of hunting for a checklist of conditions that unlocks answers, you bring him your ordinary needs, plainly and often. What stays is your real desire to learn from Muller—read his life, notice his dependence on God, and let it push you toward simple, continual asking. Just don't build a new law out of him.

prompt: I am a minister, and I have been tempted to soften my message to please the main contributors to my support. What should I do?
completion: I'd say first: no, don't soften it. You already know that's what you're being tempted to do, and you named it honestly. What I'd add is that the pressure you're feeling isn't really about money—it's about who you're trusting to keep the work going. The principle I'd weigh here is that the work should be supported by voluntary contributions sent freely, without asking, because God has supplied all your need and withheld no good thing. That changes how you handle the contributors: you don't lean on them, you don't hint, you don't manage them to protect the budget. What stays is the message itself—whole, unedited, spoken in love. So the no is this: don't trim the truth to keep the givers happy. And don't swing the other way into squeezing them either. Preach plainly, and let God be the one who provides.

prompt: I have been reading many religious books but neglecting the Bible. How should I begin to read the Scriptures rightly?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: good, start reading. The principle I'd weigh here is that the Scriptures are the one fountain of all wisdom and strength, and that you should read them habitually and prayerfully, turning what you find into obedience, and prefer them above other books. That doesn't mean throwing out everything else you've been reading, but it does mean the Bible takes first place, not last. What changes is your order of operations: pick a time each day, read slowly, pray before you open it, and let what you read shape what you actually do. What stays is your honest situation, that you've been reading widely and neglecting this, so start small and steady rather than trying to catch up in a week. A Gospel like John or Luke is a fine place to begin, and a study Bible can help with hard passages without replacing your own reading. This is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I have been invited to join in Christian work alongside unconverted people—is that acceptable?
completion: What I'd say first is that this is fine, with care. The principle that matters here is the one about Christian work being primarily GOD's own work through man, not man's work for GOD—its highest aspect is obedience to GOD and bringing glory to His Name. That reframes your question. You're not being asked to hand over something that's yours; you're being asked to step into work that isn't chiefly yours anyway. So working alongside unconverted people isn't automatically a compromise. What stays is this: be honest about your faith, keep your accountability to your church, and decline anything that requires secrecy or asking you to hide Christ. Open, shared work is fine; a setup that divides your loyalties or binds you to secrecy is not.

prompt: I have been asked to take on a work that will outlive me, and I wonder what will become of it after my death. Should that stop me?
completion: I'd start by saying: go ahead, this is fine, and fine with care. The principle that speaks to your worry is the continual remembrance of death—that keeping death steadily in view is the foundation of religious perfection, that by holding this memorial present we learn to die daily. Notice what that does to your question. It doesn't promise you a say over what happens to the work after you're gone; it asks you to do the work now as someone who knows their time is limited. So the uncertainty you're describing stops being a reason to refuse and becomes part of how you hold the work: faithfully, without clutching at outcomes you can't see. What stays is your real limit—you genuinely can't control what others do with it later. What changes is the weight you put on that. Build in ways for others to carry it, then let it go. That's not resignation; it's the daily dying the principle is talking about.

prompt: I am a parent and wonder whether my prayers and teaching for my children will bear fruit—should I expect present fruit?
completion: I'd start by saying: yes, you can expect present fruit, and you should pray for it—but hold it with an open hand. One principle here says children should be trained in the fear of the Lord with expectation of present fruit, and that the power for good or evil in a little child is beyond human calculation. That changes something real: it means your prayers and teaching aren't a waiting game with nothing to show. You can look for small signs now—a question, a kindness, a moment of honesty—and encourage them. What stays is your limit: you're not promised a timetable or a particular form of fruit, so don't measure yourself by immediate results or turn hope into pressure. Keep sowing faithfully, pray persistently, and trust God with the growth.

prompt: I feel lonely because I have obeyed my conscience and separated from friends and customs—is this loneliness to be expected?
completion: What I'd say first is: yes, this loneliness is to be expected, and it doesn't mean you did the wrong thing. But I'd weigh one idea carefully with you—that solitude is only truly holy when it's interior as well as exterior, with the soul dwelling with God and itself, because the enclosure of walls is a weak fence without silence of the interior faculties.
