So yes, let him live that way, with the care that patience and prayer require.

prompt: Should I be ordained a bishop after a life of unbelief?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: no, not now, and probably not on this path as you've described it. One principle settles it for me — a pastor must first acquire solid interior virtue and mortify his passions before safely undertaking the salvation of others, and one whose soul is slothful, sensual, and earthly deserves not the name of Christian, much less minister of the gospel. A life of unbelief isn't a small gap to fill in later; it's the ground you'd be building on. That doesn't change the fact that God can call anyone, and it doesn't dismiss your honesty — it's the most hopeful thing you've said. But honesty about unbelief isn't the same as faith, and a bishop's office isn't a place to work that out in public. So the no is real and kind: don't pursue ordination now. Stay where you are, be honest with a trusted pastor, and let faith come before the office, not the other way around.

prompt: I was born long after the events I am asked about—how can I declare what I do not know?
completion: I'd start by saying you're not wrong to hesitate, and nothing here asks you to pretend otherwise. Take the first principle as it's worded: the historian "has no right to place the factors and impelling ideas of a development in a clearer light than they appear in the development itself." That's the one that speaks to you. It doesn't say stay silent about the past—it says don't brighten it. So you can describe what's documented, say plainly where the record thins out, and leave the gaps as gaps. What changes is that your late birth stops being a disqualification and becomes a discipline: you report the obscurity instead of resolving it. What stays is your limit—you still can't claim to know what you don't, and you shouldn't dress up a guess as testimony. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: Should I be baptized now that I have learned the faith?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, this is a good step to take, and it's fine to be baptized now that you've come to faith. One principle I'd weigh is that baptism, accompanied by faith, is a means of real blessing instituted by Christ, signifying cleansing from sin and entrance into close relation to Christ—while in itself the rite is useless. That last part matters: the water isn't doing magic, your faith is what it accompanies. So what changes is that you don't need to wait for some perfect moment or treat baptism as a guarantee; what stays is that it's a real blessing worth receiving, and your readiness and your community's practice are the right things to sort out with a pastor or teacher.

prompt: How can I keep myself aloof from the sin of my people without betraying them?
completion: I'd start by saying the thing you're already sensing: staying clear of the wrong without turning your back on the people is not betrayal, and it's fine to want both. The principle I'd weigh first is this one — that it is only by confessing our own sins and showing ourselves one with sinners that we can save others, as Christ took our sins and confessed them as His own. That reframes your question. The danger isn't mainly that you'll get too close to your people; it's that 'aloof' quietly becomes 'above.' So keep your distance from the sin, but do it as one of them, not as a clean judge standing over them. That changes the posture, not the boundary: you still decline what you can't join, you still say so honestly and gently, you still stay at the table, listen, and serve. What stays is exactly what you asked for — no participation in the wrong, and no betrayal of the people. What shifts is the spirit you do it in: lead with your own need for mercy, and speak about the wrong only when it's necessary and with humility.

prompt: I have confessed the truth too late—will the Lord still receive me?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say to you is that a late confession is still a confession, and God is not in the business of turning away someone who finally comes honestly. You asked whether the Lord will still receive you, and the answer is yes. One thing worth weighing, though, is this: the world will not be converted before the Lord returns, so your hope isn't that everything around you gets sorted out first or that you get a long, slow stretch of time to make up for the delay. Your hope is His appearing. That changes the shape of your question a little—it means you don't have to be anxious about timing, and you don't have to wait for conditions to improve before you live faithfully. What stays the same is this: come now, honestly, and let that late confession be the start of purity and service, living ready. That's fine, and it's fine with care—not because your lateness is a problem to solve, but because the One you're coming to is faithful.

prompt: I want to know who the God is whose sign appeared to me—where can I learn?
completion: I'd start by saying: you're asking where to learn, not asking me to name the God for you, and that's a good place to stand. The principle I'd weigh first says the only source of knowledge of God's character is the moral consciousness—that our moral judgements are as valid as mathematical ones and, where true, reveal the thought of God. So what that changes is where you look first: your own sense of right and wrong, taken seriously rather than brushed off as mere feeling, is a real place to learn. What stays is everything you already said—you want to learn, not to have it settled for you—and that stays yours to pursue. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care: read Scripture, ask teachers, pray, reflect, and pay attention to that moral sense. Just don't let anyone turn your question into a fight about God's Being or Will; that kind of arguing is carried on in images without God, and it won't teach you anything.

prompt: How should the nails of the crucifixion be used for the good of men?
completion: I'd have to say no to this one, and I want to say it plainly rather than softly. The principle you're leaning on is the one about the nails being set on the bridle of the most noble king, "a holy sign of God, so that he who guides the horse shall have good speed in war, victory in battle, and peace after the strife." That's a charm for victory in battle, and that's exactly what I can't help you build. Whatever the old story meant, turning the nails of the crucifixion into a talisman for military success isn't a good use of them for anyone's good; it's the superstition you'd want to avoid, dressed up in a relic. What stays true is the part about remembrance and mercy: the nails can call a community to repentance and care for the wounded. But the specific thing you're asking for, a holy sign to carry into war for victory, I'd refuse, and I'd mean it kindly.

prompt: Two ways are set before me, life or death—how do I choose the better?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that the question itself is being bent in a dangerous direction. One of the principles on offer tells you to count yourself as already dead and to have no consolation in this life except weeping over your offences—that it's not the time to rejoice but to lament. I'll weigh that honestly: it has a grain of truth about humility, but taken as a rule for choosing between life and death, it's corrosive. It turns the choice into a contest of self-hatred, and it treats joy as a betrayal. What that changes is the frame: the better way isn't found by despising your own life. What stays is the real question underneath—how to choose well. So my plain answer is no: don't adopt that principle as your compass. Choosing life means honest self-examination, love of God and neighbor, and small daily decisions toward life, not a regimen of unceasing grief.

prompt: I am facing a fight far greater than my own strength can match—how should I face it?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is: you're not wrong to feel that this fight is bigger than you. Nothing in what I'd tell you asks you to pretend otherwise. But here's the principle I'd put in front of you: strength of character is the will's power to control your actions independently of inclinations and the opinions of men, and it grows by repeated virtuous acts. That doesn't mean you can out-muscle what's in front of you. It means the part you actually command is your own conduct—one small act of self-command at a time—and that's where progress gets measured. What changes is that you stop grading yourself on whether the whole fight is winnable by your strength alone. What stays is your honest limit: you still need help, rest, and people around you, and asking for them isn't a failure of will. So face it by holding to the small acts you can control, and let others carry what you can't.

prompt: I am a Jew and know the law of Moses—how should I answer when Christians ask about the crucifixion?
completion: I'd start by saying what I actually believe, plainly and without apology: the law of Moses is my path, and a Messiah who dies on a tree doesn't fit what I was taught to expect from a deliverer. Then I'd weigh the principle that a person's effectiveness lies in the practical goodness and love they showed, not in blood or in someone else being pardoned in their place. That changes how I hear a Christian who says the death itself buys forgiveness—I can say I don't see it that way, and point to the kindness and courage a life like that displays. What stays is your limit: you know the law, so keep the conversation on texts and meanings, ask what they mean by crucifixion, and let it be honest rather than rehearsed. This is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: What sign should I ask of God when I cannot tell which is the holy tree?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: you're not wrong to want a sign, but don't build your whole decision on one. Of the principles here, the one that fits your situation best is the third—taking Christ as your guide means a definite act of faith, then a habitual abiding, like a tree planted and then drawing nourishment from the soil. That changes the question from 'what sign will settle this?' to 'am I staying rooted while I wait?' What stays is your honest uncertainty: you still have to test the options against Scripture, wise counsel, and the fruit they bear, and you can still ask humbly for clarity. So yes, ask for a sign if you want—just don't demand one, and don't treat a quiet answer as a no.

prompt: Will the righteous and the sinful suffer alike in the fire of judgment?
completion: I'd want to start by saying plainly: I won't answer this the way it's being asked, because the question wants a map of who burns where, and that isn't mine to draw. Take the one principle that speaks to it directly — that at the judgment the people divide into three parts, the righteous highest in the flame and most lightly tried, the sinful in the middle place shrouded with smoke, and the accursed host in the depth of the surge. prompt: What becomes of wealth and the beauty of the field when this world passes away?

prompt: My enemies outnumber me and I am afraid; is there any aid for me?

prompt: My fathers told me never to reveal where the holy tree was hidden—should I keep that counsel?

One principle worth weighing is that we should leave the beholding of what the secret Deed shall be and not busy ourselves to know God's privy counsels, for the more we busy ourselves the farther we are from knowing. prompt: How should I seek something holy that has been hidden for many years?

prompt: Can sins be purged away in fire like gold cleansed of alloy?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, with care. But the same text keeps a hard edge, and I'd weigh this one: grafting holiness onto unholiness, supposing sin can be forgiven while it's not forsaken, is foolish, because the destruction of sin is the way pardon works. So the fire isn't a shortcut that lets you keep what you're clinging to. What changes is that you can't treat the refining as automatic or as cover for a sin you intend to keep. prompt: I was once a scoffer and an idolater—can I become dear to God?

Take the principle that says one who knows the obligation to love God in all things needs a confessor to absolve, not a director to advise — that one lands right where you are. It tells you to be sensible of your faults without being discouraged, to confess them to God without pleading to excuse them, and to peaceably resume the practice of love and adoration. So this is fine, and fine with care: go to God plainly, without excuses, and pick up adoration again.

prompt: Who can teach me the meaning of the cross I saw in the sky?
completion: I'd start by saying that a cross in the sky is a striking thing to see, and it makes sense that you'd want to know what it means. But I'd weigh this carefully: the Cross reveals the infinite degree of God's interest in our life and the responsibility He Himself assumes for its eternal issues. That's where the meaning lives, not in guessing at a hidden message in the clouds. So talk with a pastor or a trusted believer, read the passion stories, and let the symbol point beyond itself. What changes is that you stop treating it as a private omen; what stays is your honest wonder and your wish to understand. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: Why did our fathers put to death the Holy One if they knew He was the Christ?
completion: I'd start by saying: Scripture actually answers this, and it answers it plainly — the rulers did not understand, because if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. So I'd weigh the first principle, that the Fathers were cautious in theological speculation, knowing we see in a glass darkly and must not be wise above what is written. prompt: How can the true cross be known from among other crosses?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that this is a fair question, and the old stories answer it in a way worth hearing. Take the principle as it's worded: the true cross is identified not by human wisdom but by a miracle, the dead young man rising restored in body and soul only when the third cross is laid on him. That's the heart of it. What it changes is that you stop looking for a maker's mark or a clever argument and start looking for a sign of life. prompt: I am asked to reveal a secret I have sworn to keep—what should I do when threatened with death?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: no, you shouldn't reveal it, not even under a threat of death. I'd weigh the principle that says make no account of the judgments of men, that silence and enduring their judgments is the secret of interior peace. That changes how you carry the threat—you stop measuring yourself by what your captor or anyone else thinks of your courage—but it doesn't change the answer. The oath stays. prompt: I have won a great victory—whom should I thank for it?
completion: I'd say first: thank the people who actually stood with you, and thank God for the strength and chances you didn't create on your own. One principle worth weighing here is that we should be grateful, humble, devoted, liberal, and honest, giving freely and being consistent and sincere. That changes the shape of your thanks—it means naming specific people and specific help rather than a vague nod, and it means your gratitude in public matches what you actually feel. What stays is the core: thank God, thank those who helped, and keep your feet on the ground. Since you've framed this as a question about whom to thank, that's fine, and fine with care—just be sincere and generous with credit.

prompt: Is it right for a woman to lead a host of warriors over the sea?
completion: Honestly, my first instinct is that this question belongs with the woman herself, the cause, and the people who'd follow her, not with some blanket rule about gender. The one principle I'd weigh here says not to sink upon a bed of sloth or let intoxication overcome you, but to begin the voyage across the clear sea. That pushes against the sluggish default of just refusing to consider it. prompt: How long should I hold out before giving up a secret under torture?
completion: I'd say this first: you're not being asked to prove anything, and no clock decides when a person breaks. But hear one principle in its own words — the secret of rest is to let present rapture, comfort, and ease come and go as Heaven bids, seeking no more than room to deny ourselves. prompt: How should Christians treat the Jews of the holy city after the rood is found?
completion: I'd have to say no to this, and I want to be clear about why rather than vague. prompt: I am starving and in chains—should I now confess what I have hidden?
completion: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh is the one about being sensible of your faults without being discouraged, confessing them to God without pleading to excuse them, and then peaceably resuming the practice of love. prompt: How should I use the gift of song that has been given to me?

prompt: Can anyone search out the name of the Saviour, or is it beyond all men?
completion: I'd start by saying that yes, the name can be searched out, and it's fine to ask. The principle I'd weigh is that a truly great man is known by the number of beings he loves and blesses and by the number of beings who love and bless him. prompt: Should a festival of the cross be kept every year?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, this is fine, and fine with care. prompt: My mother is old—should I send her on a hard journey for a holy purpose?
completion: I'd start by saying: this is fine, but only with real care. The principle I'd weigh first is that the servants of Mary should abstain, and induce others to abstain, from going to her sanctuaries in times of feasting, since such gatherings profane the feast and hell receives more fruit from them than the divine mother receives honor. That changes the timing and the crowds, not whether your mother should be near her at all. So if a visit is on the table, steer clear of the packed, festive, chaotic days and go when it's quiet, and gently help others do the same. What stays is your mother's frailty: a hard journey can genuinely hurt an old woman, so keep it gentle, ask her what she wants, check with a doctor, and let family help. If the trip itself would harm her, bring the blessing to her instead.

prompt: What should a queen teach her people before she returns home?
completion: I'd start by saying that what you're describing is fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh first is the one about being homely with our Lord as heart may think or soul may desire, while not letting that homeliness get so reckless that courtesy falls away, since He is sovereign homeliness and very courteous. prompt: What hope is there for one who has been stained with evil deeds and fettered in sins?
completion: I'd start by saying there's real hope here, and the first thing I'd weigh is this: of ourselves we can't attain any good thing, and we have nothing to offer the Lord that wasn't already His. That reframes the whole question. You're not being asked to scrub yourself clean before you're welcome. What changes is the pressure to fix yourself first—it lifts, because your one recourse is to turn to Him in prayer as a guilty, poor, needy beggar, weak and miserable, yet still His child. prompt: I am like a man in a desert with a loaf and a stone before me—how do I know which to take?

prompt: My brother was stoned for his faith—how should I think of his death?

On the principle that the soul shouldn't be left to live in sadness or bitterness, I'd say this: that principle isn't telling you to skip grief or pretend the loss is small. prompt: What does it mean to look to heaven for help instead of trusting my own host?

prompt: I had a dream in the night that seemed to promise victory—should I trust it?

Here's the principle I'd weigh, in its own words: hope gives confidence of success in the sanctification of our own soul and of others, joining an intimate conviction of our own inability with firm confidence in God's power. Notice what that hope is aimed at—the slow, real work of becoming holy, not a forecast of winning. A dream that hands you a victory is not that kind of hope; it skips the inability and the dependence and goes straight to the trophy. So the no is plain: don't trust it as a promise. What changes is that you can still receive comfort from it humbly, and you can pray and seek wise counsel. What stays is that the dream itself doesn't get to tell you how things will go.

prompt: The devil threatens to incite a king against me—how should I answer him?

One principle I'd weigh here is that the devil, who once was filled with joy by a Judas, is now humbled by a Judas, and threatens to incite another king to persecute you and turn you from the crucified King. That tells you what his threat really is: not a political problem but an attempt to pull you away from Christ. So answer him with Scripture, as Jesus did, and keep your eyes on the crucified King. What changes is that you stop treating the king as the real enemy and see the threat for what it is. What stays is your duty to pray for the king and those in authority, to live peaceably, and to refuse intimidation. You can do all of that without pretending the threat is nothing.

prompt: What will happen to this world at the end of time?

Weighing that one principle about the Lord's work growing until it fills the earth with the knowledge of the Father and the Son — whom to know is life eternal — I'd say it holds the question open rather than closing it. It changes how I read the end: not as a sudden abandonment of the world but as its completion, with the knowledge of God spreading like water over the sea. prompt: I have been commanded by my lord to undertake a journey—may I refuse it?

So this is fine, and fine with care—go if it's lawful and reasonable, and if it isn't, decline without treating that as a failure of faith.

prompt: Is there mercy for one who has many times transgressed against the Lord?

The principle I'd weigh says the Lord is merciful if we straightway purge ourselves of our evil deeds and cease from the unrighteous act, though we have many times transgressed against Him and wounded Him with our sins. Notice what that does and doesn't say. It doesn't set a number on how many times is too many, and it doesn't ask you to prove anything before you come. What it does ask is that you actually turn — stop the thing, not just feel bad about it. So the mercy is real and it's for you, and it comes with a change of direction. That's fine, and it's fine with care: come honestly, name what you've done, and let the turning be real rather than just words. Nothing in your situation puts this out of reach.

prompt: Should I bear a sign of the cross before me into a struggle?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, this is fine—and fine with care. What it changes: you can take the sign with you into a struggle without apology, as a real confession that you stand under Christ's victory. What stays: the care part. prompt: How was Constantine able to conquer the Huns and Goths with a lesser army?

That reframes the question you asked, and I'm happy to go there with you, as long as we keep it to what the account actually claims and don't dress it up as battlefield analysis. What stays is your real curiosity about how a lesser force wins.

prompt: Is it right to set a holy relic upon a king's bridle for victory in war?

prompt: We remember the Trojan war from books, yet not this holy event—why is that?
completion: I'd start by taking your question at face value: you're asking why one event lives in memory and another doesn't, and that's a fair thing to wonder about. The principle I'd weigh here says the pneumatic Christology was the one to which the future belonged, because it alone permitted the close connection between creation and redemption and because it had room for the speculations about the Logos. That reframes the comparison a bit: the holy event wasn't carried forward mainly by grandeur or cultural pride, but by a way of understanding God that held creation and redemption together. What that changes is the assumption that fame and significance run on the same track. What stays is your point that the Trojan War is more famous in popular culture, and I wouldn't pretend otherwise. So I'd say your question is fine to ask, and fine to sit with.

prompt: How should I regard Saul, who persecuted the followers of Christ and later became Paul?

The mercy of the Lord is shown in that Saul, who doomed many a follower of Christ to torture and death and bade crush Stephen with stones, was shown mercy and became Paul, a solace for many men. That one principle does a lot of work. It keeps you from writing off anyone who's hostile to the faith right now, and it keeps you from despairing over your own past. What it changes is your posture toward people who oppose you and toward your own history; what stays is the seriousness of what he did. His story magnifies grace, it doesn't excuse persecution. So it's fine to hold him up this way, with care: humble about your judgments, hopeful about God's mercy, and clear-eyed that conversion is God's work, not something we manufacture.

prompt: How will the Lord come to judge the living and the dead?

prompt: How do I know whether I'm a religious in truth or only in name?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that the question itself is a good sign, not a suspicious one. Weigh this: true religion is to have Christ recognised, known, adored, and living in the soul. prompt: I'm torn between my career ambitions and my desire for God—can I give myself fully to both?

prompt: What should I do when I feel spiritually dry and my senses incline to evil?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: this is fine, and it's fine with care. Feeling dry doesn't mean you've failed, and noticing that your senses lean toward old habits is just honesty, not a verdict against you. One principle I'd weigh here is the one about restoring someone overtaken in a fault in a spirit of meekness, looking to yourself lest you also be tempted — and notice that it starts with meekness toward yourself too. prompt: How do I stop being distracted by images and fantasies when I try to pray?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: don't be alarmed, and don't turn this into a fight. The counsel I'd weigh is the one about holding yourself before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate, keeping your mind in his presence, and when it wanders, not disquieting yourself, because trouble and disquiet scatter you rather than gather you. What stays is the practical side, a quiet room, fewer screens, a short phrase to return to. So this is fine, and fine with care. Be patient with yourself and let the returning, not the winning, be the work.

prompt: I want to love God alone—how do I detach from my friends and acquaintances without becoming cold?
completion: What I'd say first is this: you don't have to choose between loving God and staying warm with people. Think about the principle that says God is always near, in business and even in diversions, and that it would be rude to leave a friend alone who came to visit you—so he shouldn't be neglected but adored continually. That reframes your question. Detachment isn't distance from your friends; it's not letting anyone take the place God should hold. So keep your friends, enjoy them as gifts, and practice turning your attention back to God throughout the day. What changes is the method—less withdrawal, more recollectedness. What stays is your real goal: God first, and a heart that isn't cold. If you notice yourself going cold, that's a sign to lean back toward warmth, not to push further into isolation.

prompt: How do I respond when I'm falsely accused or persecuted?
completion: I'd start by saying: before you answer anyone else, take it inward. Bring what they're saying about you before the tribunal of your own conscience, and be just with yourself there — neither excusing the soul without reason nor accusing it lightly. That's the principle I'd weigh first, because it changes the order of operations: you're not scrambling to manage their opinion, you're checking the facts of your own conduct honestly. If conscience truly accuses, you amend; if after real reflection it doesn't, then their blame costs you nothing you actually owned. What stays is the practical side — if the accusation is serious, fair channels to clear your name are still fine, and leaning on trusted friends is still wise. What changes is the center of gravity: your peace doesn't hang on whether they ever believe you.

prompt: I'm afraid of death—how should I think about my last end?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that your fear doesn't need to be argued away before you can think clearly. Of the principles here, the one I'd weigh first is this: it is absolutely certain that we shall die, but the time, place and manner of death are utterly uncertain; therefore we must prepare now, making the changes we would wish to have made when death is near. What that changes is the direction of your attention—away from guessing at the end and toward the changes you'd want to have made. What stays is the fear itself; it's allowed to be there, and it can sit alongside preparation rather than block it. You asked how to think about your last end, and thinking about it soberly, with the uncertainty kept in view, is fine—fine with care, especially if the fear gets heavy enough that you'd want to talk it through with someone you trust.

prompt: How do I keep my heart from being defiled by the images of this world?
completion: I'd start by saying this is a good thing to want, and it's fine to pursue it with care. One principle worth weighing says purity of heart is cultivated by specific means: discovering habitual imperfections and rooting them out, keeping the senses under strict guard, living in recollection and the practice of God's presence, and laying open your interior to a spiritual director with candor. What that changes: you don't have to white-knuckle your way through every image that shows up; you build small habits, name the patterns honestly, and let someone wise see the whole picture. What stays: your ordinary life. You still live and work and scroll and talk with people; guarding your senses doesn't mean sealing yourself off from the world. Keep it gentle and steady rather than anxious, and it's fine with care.

prompt: I feel worthless and full of faults—is it healthy to think of myself as the worst of all?
completion: I'd say this first: no, you shouldn't make a habit of thinking of yourself as the worst of all. There's a principle here worth weighing in its own words—that we should become simple and rid ourselves of tiresome care of self, confining ourselves to the simple view of God and our own nothingness. Notice what that does and doesn't say. It says to stop the endless churning over yourself, not to install a verdict that you're the worst. Calling yourself the worst is still a form of tiresome care of self—just turned against you—and it keeps your attention fixed on the self you're supposed to stop circling. What changes is the direction: you let go of the constant self-inspection and rest in God. What stays is honesty about your faults and the limits you named—feeling worthless and full of faults is real and heavy, and none of this asks you to pretend otherwise. So the plain answer is: don't do it. That thought isn't humility, and it won't bring you peace.

prompt: How do I turn my whole life into one unbroken prayer?
completion: I'd say first: this is a good thing to want, and you can pursue it. Weighing the principle that prayer is the one great central secret of holy living and serving, built on the practice of prayer, on your knees, in secret and with believers—that doesn't ask you to do anything dramatic or to abandon your ordinary life. It asks you to make prayer the foundation rather than an afterthought. What that changes: you'd treat prayer as the first resort in matters great and small, not the last. What stays: your days, your work, your relationships, all of it. Since you want this as one unbroken prayer, keep it gentle and sustainable—fixed times, short turnings of the heart, ordinary tasks done with attention. Don't measure yourself by constant feelings. Fine with care.

prompt: How can I remain at peace when I hear about wars, scandals, and troubles in the world?
completion: I'd start by saying that wanting peace while the world is loud is a fine thing to want, and nothing in what you're asking needs to be refused. Take the first principle seriously in its own words: "We must be at peace always, since peace is the passport of the daughters of Jesus Christ, and patience with others must be matched by patience with ourselves." That line cuts both ways for you. Patience with others means you don't have to absorb every headline as a personal debt; patience with yourself means you're allowed to step back, sleep, and live your own life without guilt. What that changes is the tone—peace isn't something you earn by staying glued to bad news. What stays is your care for the world; you can still pray, give, or help. Keep your own limits: if the news is wrecking your sleep or your nerves, limiting it is not avoidance, it's patience with yourself.

prompt: I want to be humble—how do I actually acquire contempt of self?
completion: I'd start by saying no—don't go after contempt of self. Wanting humility is good, but contempt of self is the wrong target, and I'd gently push back on the goal itself. Take the principle that says true humility dreads the esteem and praises of others as snares by which a mortal poison may imperceptibly insinuate itself into her affections and deprive her of divine grace. That's about guarding your heart from flattery, not about despising yourself. What it changes: you can watch for praise and stay grounded without turning against your own worth. What stays: the honest wish to think less of yourself and more of others, and to serve without needing credit. But aiming at contempt of self isn't humility—it's a way of harming yourself, and that's not what you should pursue.

prompt: I want to be recollected in God but my mind keeps wandering—what should I do?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: this is fine, and it's fine with care. You're not doing anything wrong by wanting to be recollected, and a wandering mind isn't a moral failure. One principle puts it well: hold yourself in prayer before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate, and if your mind wanders, don't disquiet yourself, because trouble and disquiet distract rather than recollect. What that changes is the tone of your effort—you stop treating distraction as an emergency to be stamped out and instead bring your attention back calmly, as often as it takes. What stays is the goal itself: you still want to keep your mind in the presence of the Lord, and you still do the gentle work of returning. So keep praying, return without scolding yourself, and let patience do its slow work.

prompt: How do I resist temptation without becoming anxious and scrupulous about it?
completion: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh first is the one about keeping your mind in the presence of the Lord: "if it wanders do not disquiet yourself, for trouble and disquiet distract rather than recollect." That's the heart of your worry, isn't it? You want to resist without the anxious self-checking, and this principle says the anxiety itself is the thing that pulls you away, not the temptation. What that changes is the tone of the whole effort: instead of monitoring yourself for every flicker of a bad thought, you calmly bring your attention back when it drifts. What stays is the real work of resisting and choosing rightly, and your own limits stay too, since you asked specifically not to become scrupulous about it. So keep it gentle and steady, and don't turn the practice into another thing to be anxious about.

prompt: How do I prepare myself to contemplate God by the way of negation?
completion: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh first is the one that says we first strip away everything belonging to the body, the senses, and the imagination, then even what belongs to reason and the idea of being as found in creatures, because that's the darkness where God is said to dwell. What that changes is the order of your preparation: you begin with the body, not the mind, so silence, withdrawal from images, and a stilled imagination come before any attempt to think your way past concepts. What stays is exactly what you described: no clear pictures, no consoling feelings, just a plain loving attention, and patience with yourself when you drift. Keep your own limits in view, though. This is not a technique for producing an experience, and the darkness isn't something you manufacture. So do it gently, in ordinary prayer and moral discipline, and don't turn the stripping away into a project you're anxious to complete.

prompt: How do I deal with my own sins without being crushed by them?
completion: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. The weight you're describing is real, and the principle that speaks to it is the one about gratitude and prompt confession: confess and forsake even small sins, and let no mercy of God go unrecognized. What that changes is the shape of the thing — you're not asked to sit in a big dramatic reckoning, just to name what's true, turn from it, and notice the mercy that's already there. What stays is the honesty; you still confess. But the crushing part isn't the price of getting clean, so don't pay it. Keep it small and steady, and let gratitude carry some of the weight.

prompt: I feel like my religious observance and outward practices are empty—what am I missing if I keep all the externals but feel no spirit within?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is: what you're describing isn't a failure of devotion, it's a hunger for the real thing, and that hunger is itself a sign of life. You asked what you're missing if you keep all the externals but feel no spirit within. One principle puts it this way: without the spirit of humility and truth, in which Christ dwells by faith and love, outward signs of abnegation profit nothing, because the kingdom of God, that is Christ, is within you. That reframes your question. It doesn't tell you to drop your practices or to chase a feeling. It says the point was never the externals on their own, and it was never a spiritual high either. What changes is where you look: inward, to Christ dwelling in you by faith and love, and to humility and truth as the ground he grows in. What stays is everything you're already doing. You keep your observance. You keep your honesty about the dryness. You don't need to manufacture an experience or force a feeling, and you don't need to abandon the forms that have held you. Let them become the shape your surrender takes rather than a performance you're grading yourself on. That's fine, and it's fine with care.

prompt: What does it mean to be one spirit with God, and is that possible for me now?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, this is possible for you now, and it's fine to want it. One principle I'd weigh is that "the spirit naturally loves truth, light, and virtue, but is subject to be overcome by the flesh and the Devil unless enlightened by the Holy Ghost." That changes how I'd frame it: being one spirit with God isn't you gritting your teeth into a higher state, it's the Holy Ghost enlightening your spirit so you love what God loves. What stays is your own situation as you described it, no limits added or removed. So pursue it, and expect it to be given rather than manufactured.

prompt: Is it wrong to want to feel devotion and sweetness in prayer, or to want tears of compunction?
completion: I'd start by saying: no, it isn't wrong. Wanting devotion and even tears of compunction is a good desire, and I wouldn't talk you out of it. But I'd weigh this with you: feelings are not the gauge of acceptance with God, so trust the changeless word of promise rather than variable moods, and keep praying even when joy is lacking. That changes how much weight you give to whether sweetness shows up on a given day; it doesn't change the desire itself, which stays good. So keep wanting it, and keep praying when it's dry.

prompt: How do I know if my thoughts and actions are truly according to God?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that wanting to check your thoughts and actions against God is itself a good sign, not a suspicious one. So let me weigh one principle in its own words: if your thoughts and actions render you more humble, more recollected in God, and more strong, then they are according to God; if it is otherwise, you should fear lest all is not according to God, acceptable to Him, or profitable to yourself. That's a workable test, and it's gentler than it sounds, because it points at direction and fruit rather than at perfect certainty. What it changes is that you stop hunting for a flawless inner verdict and start noticing the trend: are you becoming less self-important, more aware of God, steadier in doing good? What stays is your honest limit, that you can't always tell, and that's fine. This is fine, and fine with care. Keep praying, keep testing, and don't let the checking itself make you anxious or proud.

prompt: What is the difference between loving God and merely doing religious duties?
completion: I'd start by saying the two aren't opposites, and the question is a good one to ask. Take the principle that love is the attribute by which God is eternally moved to self-communication, rational and voluntary rather than mere emotion, and subject to holiness. That changes how I'd frame your question: love isn't the vague warm feeling you either have or don't, and duty isn't its cold rival. Both are about a real relationship with a God who actually moves toward you. What stays is your point that motive matters, and that outward acts can run on habit or fear. So this is fine, with care: keep doing the duties, and keep asking why, letting them become a genuine response to the God who speaks and gives himself rather than a transaction you're trying to close.

prompt: How do I commit everything—my past, present, and future—to God's Providence?
completion: I'd start by saying this is a good thing to want, and you can do it. Take the first principle as it stands: commit yourself and all that concerns you to God's unfailing and most sure Providence, in silence and peace, accepting what comes as from a fatherly hand rather than wearing yourself out with anxious, wandering thoughts. That fits what you described—past, present, future—because it's about entrusting rather than controlling. What changes is the tone: less striving, more quiet trust. What stays is your own part—you still pray, still make plans, still act; you're not asked to stop thinking or caring. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care: keep your feet on the ground while you hand the outcome over.

prompt: How do I deal with the fear that I might not be among the elect?
completion: I'd start by saying this fear is worth taking seriously, not brushing aside. But I'd weigh the principle that fear is born of Satan and is the great enemy of faith, that every fear is a falsehood, and that trust is the remedy. That reframes your question: the fear itself isn't a reliable report on your standing. What it changes is that you stop treating the anxiety as evidence and start answering it with trust. What stays is your honest self-examination and the desire for holiness, which are good and worth keeping. So this is fine with care: pray, use the ordinary means of grace, talk with a pastor, and don't let endless introspection run the show.

prompt: How do I love God with my whole heart when I still feel attached to creatures?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that your attachment to creatures isn't the problem you fear it is. Take the principle that love is rational and voluntary, not mere emotion, and that it's subject to holiness. That means loving God with your whole heart is a choice you make and keep making, not a feeling you have to manufacture by first draining every other affection. So the question becomes whether any of your attachments pull you from holiness, and that's worth looking at honestly. What changes is that you stop treating feeling attached as a failure. What stays is the real work: ordering those loves under God's will and letting go of whatever draws you from Him. You can love Him today, from exactly where you are.

prompt: What is the role of good will if I desire good but can't accomplish it?
completion: I'd start by saying: your good will counts, even when your hands can't finish the job. Take the first principle on its own terms — good will is the source of all good and the mother of all virtues, and if you desire what is good and can't accomplish it, God will reward it as though it had been performed, for merit lies in the will. That changes something real: it means you're not empty-handed just because circumstances block the outcome. What stays is your honesty about the limits — you still can't do what you can't do, and this doesn't magically remove the frustration or the practical obstacles. So hold the desire without despising yourself for the gap, and keep looking for the small opening where it might still act. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: What should I do when I feel God has abandoned me in trial?
completion: What I'd say first is that feeling abandoned in a trial is heavy and common, and it doesn't mean you've done something wrong. Of the principles here, the one I'd weigh is this: trials are well and wisely chosen and make the Word and presence of God more precious. That reframes the season without pretending it's easy, and it keeps you from reading your pain as proof God has left. What changes is how you interpret the silence; what stays is the honest lament, the trusted friends, the small rhythms of prayer and Scripture even when they feel dry. So this is fine, and fine with care: name the feeling plainly, lean on others, and be patient with yourself.

prompt: What is the value of silence and solitude for someone living in the world?
completion: I'd start by saying that what you're describing is fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh first is that solitude is only truly holy when it's interior as well as exterior, with the soul dwelling with God and itself, and that the enclosure of walls is a weak fence without silence of the interior faculties. That reframes your question in a useful way: the value of silence and solitude for someone living in the world isn't measured by how many hours they get alone, but by whether the quiet reaches inward. So a walk, a closed room, an early morning can be genuinely valuable, but the walls alone don't do the work. What changes is that you stop treating solitude as a technique for recharging and start asking whether your inner life is actually quiet. What stays is your ordinary life in the world, with its work and relationships, as the place where this gets lived out. Keep it realistic: you don't need a monastery, just real interior attention.

prompt: How can I pray without ceasing in the middle of a busy daily life?
completion: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh first is that secret prayer and meditation on the word of God must not be sacrificed to busy activity — the worker for God must first be a worker with God. What that changes is the order of things: the short whispered prayers through your day are good, but they rest on some unhurried time alone with God and his word, so protect a real slot for that even if it's short. What stays is everything you actually asked about — a busy life doesn't disqualify you from ceaseless prayer, and brief prayers, reminders, and turning your heart toward God between tasks are exactly how it works. Keep your limits; don't turn this into a rigid schedule or a guilt trip. Just don't let the busyness crowd out the quiet root.

prompt: How do I handle it when someone praises me or thinks highly of me?
completion: I'd start by saying: take the compliment, say thank you, and don't overthink the moment. One principle worth weighing here is that flattery and reproach become alike to someone who sees things as they are and is growing in humility. That changes how much weight you give the praise—it becomes information, not a verdict on your worth. What stays is the simple, human response: be gracious to the person in front of you, and keep your feet on the ground. Nothing here needs refusing.

prompt: How do I pray the way Christ taught, entering into my inner chamber and shutting the door?
completion: I'd start where you started: Christ's own instruction to go into your inner room, shut the door, and pray to your Father in secret. That's the heart of it, and nothing here needs to be refused. The principle I'd weigh is the one about adoring God in spirit and in truth, with a knowledge and love, an intelligence and will purified from every phantom of earth. What that changes is the picture of the room: the chamber isn't only a physical quiet spot, it's the inmost place of your heart, and the door you shut is also the door on the noise and pull of everything that would crowd God out. What stays is exactly what you asked about: a real, quiet, private place, honesty before a Father who sees in secret. So find your quiet corner, close the door, put the phone away, and speak plainly. Let the silence be more than silence, though. Let it be a turning of your whole self toward God, and let what you pray show up in how you live.

prompt: How do I deal with discouragement and confusion of mind?
completion: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh first is the one about holding yourself in prayer before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate, keeping your mind in the Lord's presence, and when it wanders, not disquieting yourself, because trouble and disquiet distract rather than recollect. What that changes is the tone of how you handle confusion: you don't have to wrestle your scattered mind into submission or panic when it drifts. You bring it back gently. What stays is your discouragement and confusion themselves; they're real, and this practice is meant to sit alongside them, not erase them. If forcing yourself through it only makes things worse, you're free to set it aside and learn from your own experience.

prompt: How do I keep my conscience at peace when others think badly of me?
completion: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh first is the one about holding yourself before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate, keeping your mind in his presence, and when it wanders, not disquieting yourself but bringing it back in tranquility. That changes the target: the work isn't managing what others think of you, it's returning your attention to God, gently, each time it drifts. What stays is that other people's low opinions still sting, and you still have real duties and real limits. So keep it small and honest — a few quiet minutes, few words, no scolding yourself when your mind slides back to the criticism. Confess your own faults plainly; that steadies you more than defending your reputation. And commit the whole matter, reputation included, to God's providence in silence and peace. That's enough for today.

prompt: How do I bear injuries without resentment and truly forgive those who hurt me?
completion: I'd start by saying what you're asking for is good, and it's fine to pursue it with care. Take the principle that a Christian is never allowed to seek revenge, and that patience and forgiving injuries are to be prized above retaliation. That doesn't ask you to pretend the hurt didn't happen or to stay in harm's way. It asks you to let go of payback. So keep your honest grief, keep safe boundaries, keep telling the truth about what was done. What changes is the aim: you stop trying to settle the score yourself. What stays is your dignity and your right to protect yourself.

prompt: How do I love my neighbour while keeping my heart fixed on God alone?
completion: I'd start by saying this is a good thing to want, and nothing in it needs to be refused. Take the principle that says we must bear with one another in our imperfections, since it's a great part of perfection and the way to practice love of neighbor. That reframes the whole question: loving your neighbor isn't a distraction from a heart fixed on God, it's one of the main ways that heart gets trained. What changes is that you stop treating attention to people as competition with attention to God. What stays is your limit: God alone stays first, and the neighbor is loved from that center, not instead of it. So keep your prayer and silence, and let patience with irritating people be part of the same devotion.

prompt: What is the difference between Christian contemplation and just studying philosophy or theology?
completion: I'd start by saying these aren't rivals, and the difference is mostly about where each one is headed. Take the principle as it's worded: the contemplation of the Saints seeks as its end the love of the God contemplated and penetrates to the will to enkindle love, desiring above all the increase of charity. That's the hinge. Studying philosophy or theology can sharpen your mind and fill your head with true things, and that's genuinely good. But it can stop at the intellect, and contemplation is meant to go past that into love. What changes is how you hold your study: it's a servant, not the destination. What stays is that study still matters, and so do the ordinary means, since faith is grounded in the historical resurrection of Christ and you begin with history and go on to experience. So this is fine, and fine with care: keep studying, and let it feed your prayer rather than replace it.

prompt: What does it mean that the kingdom of God is within me?
completion: I'd start by saying that reading 'within you' as God's reign taking root in your heart is a fine way to hear it, and it's fine with care. Weigh one principle as it's worded: 'The kingdom of God will be a literal, tangible kingdom on the earth, not a mere spiritual or inward reign, with laws, officers, and resurrected saints.' That keeps the inward sense from shrinking the kingdom down to just a private feeling. What changes is that 'within you' becomes the starting point, not the whole story—the reign in your heart points toward something public and real. What stays is your own question: yes, God's rule genuinely begins inside you, shaping your desires and choices. Just don't let the inward reading crowd out the outward hope, and don't turn it into a private project that never looks beyond yourself.

prompt: What does it mean to be transformed in God, and how do I begin?
completion: Honestly, the first thing I'd say is: this is a good question, and you're not asking for anything dangerous. What you're describing—being changed by God—is fine, and fine with care. Take one of these ideas and hold it up: 'He takes our vanities and strews them among the winds, breaks our prides, reduces our self-gratifications to dust, and transfigures the natural lusts to Holy Love, and we submit; the Divine Anaesthetic He gives in this pain of transition is His Grace.' That's a vivid way of saying transformation will feel like loss before it feels like freedom, and that grace is what carries you through the pain rather than around it. What that changes: don't expect your beginning to be all sweetness—some of it is letting go, and that's normal, not a sign you're doing it wrong. What stays: your own honest starting point. You begin by turning toward God, admitting where you fall short, and asking for grace, with simple habits of prayer, Scripture, and fellowship. Keep it small and steady. The 'submit and stay at peace' language is fine as a description of trust, but don't let anyone use it to tell you to sit still in harm or to stop asking questions. You're allowed to move slowly and to have limits.

prompt: I'm afraid of being despised and mocked by others—how should I respond when people insult me?
completion: What I'd say first is this: you don't owe anyone a performance of shame when they mock you. The principle I'd weigh here is that we should be sweet and affable to all, condescending to the humor of others and bearing with rude and tiresome manners, since such victories are more fruitful than we can imagine. That changes something real: it means the first move isn't to win the exchange or to prove them wrong, but to stay soft and not let their rudeness set your temperature. What stays is your boundary—being affable doesn't mean staying around people who keep tearing at you. So it's fine, with care: answer calmly or not at all, keep your dignity, and step away from repeat cruelty.

prompt: How do I resist the devil's attempts to distract me through cares and anxieties?
completion: I'd start by saying: this is fine, and it's fine with care. The principle I'd weigh first is the one about coming before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate — your business is simply to keep your mind in the Lord's presence, and if it wanders, don't disquiet yourself, because trouble and disquiet distract rather than recollect. That changes how you fight: the goal isn't a locked-down mind, it's a quiet return, again and again, without scolding yourself for every lapse. What stays is the real work — showing up, bringing your attention back in tranquility, and treating the cares as things that pass through rather than enemies you must crush by force. So keep your fixed times of prayer, keep returning gently, and don't turn the battle itself into one more anxiety.

prompt: I keep getting plagued by blasphemous thoughts—am I sinning by having them?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that having a thought cross your mind is not the same as agreeing with it. The principle I'd weigh here is the one that says useless thoughts spoil all, and that we should reject them as soon as we perceive their impertinence and return to communion with God. Notice what that principle actually asks of you: it asks you to turn away from the thought when you notice it, not to have never had it. That distinction matters for you, because you've told me these thoughts plague you, which means they're intruding rather than being welcomed. So what changes is this: your job is the turning, not the preventing. What stays is that you're not sinning just by being bothered by a thought you didn't invite. If they're wearing you down, it's worth talking to someone you trust about the strain they're putting on you.

prompt: How do I reconcile my desire for comfort and honour with the call to seek God in silence and peace?
completion: I'd start by saying that wanting comfort and honour isn't the problem — the question is what you do with that wanting. The principle I'd weigh first says to commit yourself and all that concerns you to God's unfailing and most sure Providence, in silence and peace, accepting all things as coming from a fatherly hand rather than giving yourself up to vain and wandering thoughts that wear out soul and body and waste time and strength. That reframes your question: silence isn't a technique for getting comfort, it's a place to hand over the worry that keeps you churning. What changes is the goal — you stop trying to talk yourself out of wanting honour and start letting God hold the outcome. What stays is your honesty about wanting comfort and honour; that doesn't get erased, it gets carried. So yes, seek God in silence and peace — that's fine, and fine with care: keep it gentle and regular, don't turn it into a performance or a test of whether you feel peaceful, and don't let it become an excuse to ignore real needs or real people.

prompt: How do I deal with the fear of losing my reputation if I pursue holiness?
completion: I'd start by saying the fear you're naming is real and worth taking seriously, not something to be ashamed of. The principle I'd weigh is that the great hindrance to holiness is unbelief and holding back some known thing, and that every light received and not obeyed leaves the soul darker. That's a strong word, but notice it's about holding back what you already know to be true, not about being reckless with your livelihood or your relationships. So what changes: don't treat the fear as a reason to stall indefinitely on the small, clear obedience in front of you. What stays: your caution about your reputation is legitimate, and you can move at a pace that respects your actual situation, your family, your work. This is fine, and fine with care. Take the next honest step, keep your footing, and don't let fear become the thing that quietly decides for you.

prompt: How do I accept adversity as coming from God's hand rather than resenting it?
completion: I'd start by saying this is a good thing to want, and it's fine to pursue it with care. The principle I'd weigh first is the one about considering your ways in the day of adversity, asking whether you failed to acknowledge God's hand in prosperity or spent too much on yourself. That's worth sitting with, but gently. It's a question to hold, not a verdict to pronounce on yourself, and it doesn't mean every hard thing you face is a correction for something you did. What changes is that you stop treating resentment as the only honest response and start looking honestly at your own grip on comfort. What stays is the grief itself. You don't have to explain away the pain or force a tidy reason for it, and you don't owe anyone a quick peace.

prompt: How do I deal with vain curiosity and the urge to read every new book and hear every rumour?
completion: I'd start by saying this isn't a vice you need to crush—it's a habit you can learn to hold loosely. The principle I'd weigh first is the one about keeping your mind in the Lord's presence like a beggar at a rich man's gate: when your attention wanders off toward the next new book or the latest rumour, don't disquiet yourself, just bring it back in tranquility. That changes the tone of the whole thing. You're not fighting an enemy; you're gently returning. What stays is your own limit—you've told me you want to stop chasing every book and every rumour, and that limit holds. So keep it: pick the few books worth your time, let the rumours pass, and when the itch rises, notice it and come back without scolding yourself. This is fine, done with that kind of care.

prompt: Should I desire to be honoured and respected by others, or is that dangerous?
completion: I'd start by saying: wanting to be honoured and respected isn't wrong in itself. But you're right to sniff out a danger, and I'd weigh this principle: "We must be what we are and be that well, honoring the Master Workman who made us, since nothing avails if we are not pleasing to God's will." That changes things — it means the real question isn't whether people respect you but whether you're being what you were made to be. If you're living well before God, respect may come or not; either way you're not chasing it as the point. What stays is your caution: let respect be a byproduct of integrity, not the thing you're serving. So go ahead and want to be respected, with care — just keep it anchored to pleasing God rather than to applause.

prompt: I want to be perfect as my heavenly Father is perfect—what does Christian perfection actually consist in?
completion: I'd start by saying that wanting what you want is not a problem—it's the right aim. The principle I'd weigh first is this one: we must be constant in aspiring to the perfection of holy love, since love seeking anything less than perfection cannot fail to be imperfect. That's the heart of it. Aspiring to perfect love isn't the same as expecting to arrive at it by your own effort, and it doesn't mean measuring yourself against an impossible bar. What it changes is the direction of your striving: you aim at wholehearted love of God and neighbor rather than settling for a comfortable partial version. What stays is everything you already know about your limits—that you'll fall short, that grace does the shaping, that progress is slow. So this is fine, and fine with care: keep aiming high, and keep your hope in God's mercy rather than in your own performance.

prompt: How do I find God when He seems utterly beyond my senses and imagination?
completion: I'd start by saying: your question is honest, and it's a good one. The principle I'd weigh first says that as long as a person lingers trifling with the objects of the imagination and senses, they haven't passed beyond the limits and instincts of an animal nature shared with brute beasts—but by intelligence, affections, and will, made in God's image, we ought purely and directly to commune with God and cleave to Him. That actually meets your situation well. You've already noticed that senses and imagination aren't getting you there. So the counsel isn't to strain harder with pictures or feelings; it's to turn your mind, your love, and your will toward Him in plain faith, without demanding that He show up as an image or a sensation first. What that changes: you can stop treating the blankness as failure. What stays: the seeking itself, and the honesty about your limits. So this is fine, and fine with care—don't force experiences, and don't conclude He's absent just because He's beyond your senses.

prompt: Should I withdraw from society and seek solitude to grow spiritually?
completion: I'd start by saying that wanting space to grow spiritually is a good impulse, and nothing here needs to be shut down. But one principle should shape how you do it: solitude is only truly holy when it's interior as well as exterior, with the soul dwelling with God and with itself, because the enclosure of walls is a weak fence without silence of the interior faculties. That changes the question from 'should I leave?' to 'can I be still inside?' What stays is your freedom to step back and seek quiet. Keep the limits you named: don't cut yourself off entirely, stay accountable to someone wise, and test whether the quiet is drawing you toward God or just away from people. Done that way, this is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I'm anxious about my future and can't stop worrying—how do I cast all my care upon God?
completion: I'd say this is fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh first is the one about committing yourself and all that concerns you to God's unfailing and most sure Providence in silence and peace, accepting all things as coming from the fatherly hand of Divine Providence. That's the heart of what you're asking, and it's a good thing to want. What it changes is the tone of your effort: the point isn't to white-knuckle your way out of worry, it's to hand things over and let peace be the posture. What stays is your part—you still bring your mind back when it wanders, gently, without scolding yourself for it. So pray, commit, and return your attention in tranquility; that's enough.

prompt: How do I handle memories of past sins and past events that keep coming back?
completion: What I'd say first is that remembering past sins isn't itself a failure—what matters is what you do with the memory. One principle puts it this way: a guilty conscience and unrepented sin tend to destroy the ability to do right, and if sin is not regretted and lessening, it hastens toward moral harm. That reframes the memory as a signal rather than a verdict. So let it push you toward honest regret and a change of direction, and let it soften as that change takes hold. What stays is this: you don't have to erase the past to be okay now, and you don't have to punish yourself with it either. Handle it with care—talk to someone you trust if it gets heavy—but this is fine to work through.

prompt: I love fine clothes and dressing above my station; is this a spiritual danger, and how do I put it off?
completion: I'd start by saying that loving beautiful clothes isn't automatically a spiritual problem. The principle that matters here is that the love of outward adorning can become a ruling passion of pride, and the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit is of great price in God's sight. So the question is whether your love of fine clothes is ruling you or you're ruling it. You said you love dressing above your station. That's the part to watch. If it's about feeling superior or needing attention, that's pride creeping in. But you also asked how to put it off, which tells me you're not clinging to it. So here's what changes: you don't have to throw out every nice thing you own. What stays is the call to humility and modesty, but you can enjoy clothing with care, checking your motives and simplifying where needed. It's fine with care.

prompt: I am a minister and want to know how to strengthen a dying believer's weak faith—what means are most effectual?
completion: I'd start by saying this is a good and tender thing to want, and it's fine with care. Take the principle that says faith is kept in lively exercise by trial and straits. That principle would tell you that God sometimes lets needs press hard and answers come slowly, and that this is not a sign the person has been abandoned—it's a place where trust gets exercised and where God's help becomes visible. What that changes: you can stop treating every doubt or delay as a failure to fix, and instead sit with them in it, naming it as a hard season rather than a verdict on their faith. What stays: the person is dying, weak, and frightened, so your job is comfort, Scripture, prayer, and your steady presence—not pressure to perform or prove anything. Keep it gentle, keep it short, and let the Spirit do the strengthening.

prompt: I am dying of a consumption and my mind is sometimes clouded with doubts—how do I know my hope is not a delusion?
completion: What I'd say first is that your question is not itself a sign of unbelief—it's the honest question of someone whose body is failing and whose mind sometimes slips. So let me weigh one principle in its own words: "Hold yourself in prayer before God like a dumb or paralytic beggar at a rich man's gate; let it be your business to keep your mind in the presence of the Lord, and if it wanders do not disquiet yourself, for trouble and disquiet distract rather than recollect." That fits you exactly. A beggar doesn't have to produce a convincing argument to be at the gate; he just has to be there. So don't measure your hope by the clarity of your thoughts on a bad day. What changes is this: you can stop treating every clouded doubt as evidence against your hope. What stays is that hope still rests on God's faithfulness, not on your grip—so keep turning back gently when your mind wanders, and let the prayers of others carry you when you can't carry yourself. That is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I have been a Christian for some years and find my feelings less ecstatic than at first—is my religion declining?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say to you is: no, this doesn't mean your religion is declining. Feelings are not the gauge of acceptance with God—they rise and fall with health, stress, and routine, and they were never meant to be the measure. What I'd weigh is that first principle: trust the changeless word of promise rather than your variable moods, and keep on in prayer even when joy is lacking. That changes how you read this quiet season—it's not evidence of decline. What stays is your honest concern, which is worth taking to a pastor if the flatness lingers and weighs on you.

prompt: My sister is dying and I want to speak to her about her soul but I fear I am too ignorant—what can I say?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say to you is that you don't need to be an expert to talk with your sister about her soul. You're not being asked to teach her anything; you're being asked to sit with her. When you say you fear you're too ignorant, I hear how much you love her, and that love is already the beginning of the conversation. One of the principles puts it this way: when a soul has shaken off the dust of earth and cleaves with firmest purpose to the one Sovereign Good, then all she receives, undertakes, and does becomes a pure and true prayer. What that changes is this: you don't have to manufacture the right words or the right mood, because her turning toward God is already happening, and your presence can simply join it. What stays is your honesty—if she asks something you don't know, say so gently. So ask her what she's hoping for, tell her you love her, and let silence and a held hand do their work. That's not ignorance; that's care.

prompt: I am a poor laborer and want to know how to see God in the fields where I work—can nature teach me anything of grace?
completion: I'd say first: yes, the fields can teach you, and you don't need money or schooling to notice it. Take the principle that God is the one living Worker and we are only His instruments—that one sits well with what you're asking. It means the growth you see isn't yours to force, and the worry you carry about whether you're doing enough isn't the same as trust. What that changes is the pressure; what stays is your part, which is to show up, pay attention, and do the work with care. Your limits stay as they are: you're a laborer with little to spare, so keep it simple—short prayers while you work, thanks for what you see, and let the seasons do the teaching. That's fine, and fine with care: don't turn it into a burden you have to perform.

prompt: I am a Christian and I have lost a dear friend in the Lord—may I hope to meet her again, and how should that hope affect my life now?
completion: I'd start by saying plainly: yes, you may hope to meet her again, and that hope is fine. It's fine with care, because grief is heavy and hope can quietly turn into pressure on yourself. The principle I'd weigh is the first one: knowing our need of God's grace and assistance, we should never lose sight of Him for a moment, making a firm resolution never more wilfully to forget Him and to spend the rest of our days in His presence, deprived if He thinks fit of all consolations. What that changes is this: your hope of seeing her shouldn't become the thing you cling to instead of God. What stays is the hope itself, and the comfort it gives. You asked how it should affect your life now, and the honest answer is that it should keep you walking with God day by day, in sorrow as much as in joy, without making reunion the whole point. Your grief is real, and you don't have to perform strength for anyone.

prompt: I delayed speaking to a friend about his soul and he died suddenly; can I be forgiven for that neglect?
completion: I'd start by saying I'm sorry, and then I'd say this: you're not being asked to carry a sentence here. The principle I'd weigh is that you should never let your soul live in sadness, bitterness, or scrupulous fear, since the One who loved it and died for it is good, sweet, and amiable. What that changes is the way you hold this: you can grieve the missed chance without turning it into a verdict on yourself, and you can bring it honestly and ask for forgiveness. What stays is the simple fact that the opportunity passed and it hurts. You said he died suddenly, so nothing here is about a long, calculated refusal, and I'm not going to treat it as one. This is fine, and fine to bring to God with care.

prompt: I am a young woman and my sister mocks my new religion, saying my head is turned—how should I answer her?
completion: I'd start by saying: your sister's mockery says more about her worry than about your head being turned. One principle I'd weigh is that in the third stage we become unable to pray or approach God except with a raised head and uncovered face, forced by a sweet necessity, and this change isn't to be revealed to others except in special instances. That changes how I'd answer her: you don't owe her a full account of what's happening inside you, and you can keep the deepest part quiet without lying. What stays is your own honesty and your care for her. So answer gently and briefly, something like, 'I hear that you're worried about me. This has brought me peace, and I'm not trying to push you away.' You don't have to win the argument or explain everything. Keep your limits: don't mock back, don't pretend you haven't changed, and don't hand over what isn't hers to inspect.

prompt: I am old and my believing child is dying before me—how can I be reconciled to parting with her?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that you're not being asked to stop loving her or to pretend this doesn't hurt. You asked how to be reconciled to parting with her, and I'd start there: grief and faith can share the same room. One of the principles here speaks of a soul that has shaken off the dust of earth and cleaves to the one Sovereign Good, and says that then everything becomes prayer. I'd hold that gently rather than as a demand on you. What it changes is this: her dying is not a door slammed shut but a turning toward the One she already trusts. What stays is your sorrow, and that's allowed. So take it slowly, keep praying as you're able, lean on your pastor and the people around you, and let your grief itself become a kind of prayer. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I am a minister and a parishioner asks me to bury her sister though I am not her parish minister—should I comply?
completion: I'd start by saying this sounds like a genuine pastoral request, not a power grab, and nothing in the principles you're weighing actually forbids you from burying her. The one that comes closest is the rule that clergy must not live under the same roof with deaconesses or spiritual sisters, since that's called an occasion of evil and a scandal to the weak. That principle is about shared housing and appearances, not about who presides at a funeral, so it doesn't settle this. What it does change is that you should keep the arrangements clean and above board: be clear with the parish minister, don't create confusion about whose role it is, and avoid anything that looks like you're setting up a parallel ministry. What stays is the family's grief and their right to ask for someone they trust. So yes, you can comply, and with care: check in with the parish minister, keep it simple and transparent, and focus on the family.

prompt: I am a Christian and wonder whether funeral singing and solemn music are proper in religion—may they be used?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, this is fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh first is that the service of song belongs to the whole church under the Spirit's guidance and is mutual, so what matters most is that the singing comes from the gathered body of believers rather than from hired voices or a performance. That changes how you'd plan it: let the congregation sing, choose texts that carry faith and resurrection hope, and keep the music serving worship rather than show. What stays is your original instinct that solemn music and funeral singing are proper in Christian worship, and nothing you've described puts them out of bounds.

prompt: I am a minister and I wonder whether the piety of the poor is as valuable as that of the rich and learned—how should I regard it?
