completion: I'd start by saying plainly: yes, the piety of the poor is as valuable as that of the rich and learned. God looks at the heart, and trust that grows in hardship is precious to him. One principle worth weighing here is that poverty often comes from want of discretion, calculation, and sound judgment, and from spending on finery beyond one's means. That changes something real: alongside honoring their faith, you can teach prudent management and frugality without treating poverty as a spiritual failing. What stays is your main point—wealth and learning don't make faith more acceptable to God, and you must not show partiality to the rich. So honor the poor, learn from their trust, and add practical wisdom gently, never as a condition of their worth.

prompt: I am a Christian and I find that the things of earth draw my mind from God—how do I set my affections above?
completion: I'd start by saying: what you're describing is a real and old struggle, and the direction you want to go is good. Take the first principle as it's worded—'keep the heart occupied with God, the object of our love, rather than turning back to gaze upon ourselves to discover what we are doing.' That changes the method more than the goal. Instead of monitoring your drift and grading your attention, you'd turn toward God when you notice the pull, and let your affection rest on him rather than on your own performance. What stays is your daily prayer and Scripture, your honest noticing, and your care about distractions—none of that gets thrown out. What shifts is the self-scrutiny: you don't have to keep checking whether you're doing it right. So this is fine, and fine with care—keep the habits, drop the scorekeeping.

prompt: I am a parent and my child has died in the faith—how do I think of her body in the grave and her soul with Christ?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that your question is a faithful one to ask, and you can hold both of those truths at once: her body in the grave, resting and awaiting the resurrection, and her soul with Christ, safe in His presence. I'd weigh the second principle here, that little children who die before accountability are redeemed through Christ and that parents will have the joy of rearing them to the full stature of their spirits in the resurrection. What that changes is the frame of your grief: this is not a loss without hope, and the bond you had with her is not simply severed. What stays is everything you said — she died in the faith, so her soul is with Christ, and her body lies in the grave until the resurrection. Your sorrow is still real and doesn't need to be explained away. So think of her as whole and safe in Him, and let yourself mourn her absence while you wait.

prompt: I am a servant and my fellow servants think me proud and hypocritical because I will not join their vanities—how should I bear it?
completion: I'd say first: you're not doing anything wrong by staying out of their vanities. This is fine, and fine with care. One principle worth weighing is that the Lord's servants should be ready to be made all things to all men in matters of indifference, but never at the cost of truth or conscience. That changes how you handle the small stuff—the shared jokes, the little rituals that don't touch conscience, the way you talk with them over a meal. Be flexible there, so your stand reads as conviction rather than contempt. What stays is your limit: you won't join what your conscience calls vanity, and you don't have to. Keep your manner warm and your words plain, and let them see that the difference is about what you owe God, not about thinking you're better than them.

prompt: I am a poor man and the rich pass by my cottage without notice—does God regard the lowly dwelling?
completion: I'd say first: yes, God regards the lowly dwelling. The principle I'd weigh is that Christian worth may dwell unseen like a diamond in the mine, and the poor and desolate best bring prayers to the Lord's ear. That changes how you read the rich passing by—their notice was never the measure. What stays is your cottage as a real place of prayer, and you as someone whose prayers are heard. So this is fine, and fine with care: keep the devotion of that humble room, and don't let others' neglect convince you God has.

prompt: I am a young woman and my brother is careless about his soul—what can I do to win him?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: wanting to win your brother isn't wrong. You're not trying to control him, you're trying to love him. So take the principle that says the real love-charm for a brother is to seek the Saviour first, then go and win the erring brother. What that changes is the order of things—your own drawing near to Christ comes before any move toward him, so your effort isn't you white-knuckling his soul. What stays is your care for him and your freedom to act on it. You're a young woman, not his parent and not his judge, so keep it gentle and keep your own life as the main thing he sees. It's fine to pray, to love him, and to speak when the moment is right.

prompt: I am a minister and a careless profligate man came to a funeral out of curiosity and was affected—should I follow up with him?
completion: I'd have said first: yes, follow up with him—gently, and soon. A careless man who wanders into a funeral out of curiosity and leaves stirred is not nothing. Ask him what struck him, listen more than you talk, offer to pray. But weigh this too, in its own words: a pastor owes his own soul's care first, and charity cannot be kindled in others if it is extinguished in oneself. That changes how you go about it—keep your own reading, self-examination, and private devotion steady while you reach out, so the follow-up comes from a full heart rather than a frayed one. What stays is the plain answer: yes, go to him. Curiosity and emotion aren't conversion yet, so be patient and let the Spirit do the deeper work.

prompt: I am a poor old man and my daughter has been the instrument of my awakening—how do I show gratitude to God for her?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is: let the gratitude start small and concrete. You asked how to thank God for your daughter, and that question is itself a good prayer. Where I'd weigh a principle is this one—that gratitude is shown by living the truth in deeds, not words only. What that changes is the shape of your thanks: it moves from a feeling you carry privately to something your daughter can actually see in you—patience, honesty, tenderness, the kind of man she helped wake up. What stays is your situation exactly as you described it: you are poor, you are old, and she is the instrument. Nothing here asks you to buy her anything or perform some grand public gesture you can't afford. Say thank you to God in your own words, thank her plainly while you still can, and let your days quietly show it. That is enough, and it is fine.

prompt: I was awakened under a sermon but the people around me laughed and called me a hypocrite—should I keep going?
completion: I'd say this first: keep going. What happened to you—being laughed at right after something real stirred in you—is painful, and it doesn't by itself mean the awakening was fake. Weigh this one principle as it's worded: beware of imitating hypocrites who try to appear outwardly more holy than they know themselves to be, and don't seek or desire human praise. That changes something: it means the question isn't whether the people around you are impressed, and it isn't whether you can prove them wrong. It stays true that you can go back to the sermon, pray, read, and be honest about what you actually know of yourself. If their word 'hypocrite' has any truth in it, face that quietly and turn from it. But their laughter doesn't get to decide whether you keep going. So yes—keep going, with care to be honest rather than impressive.

prompt: I am a Christian and I have neglected secret prayer and reading—how do I return to the ways of God?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: you haven't lost God's welcome, so don't come back to him as though you have to earn your way in. One principle I'd weigh is this — hold yourself in prayer before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate, and when your mind wanders, don't disquiet yourself, because trouble and disquiet distract rather than recollect; bring your attention back in tranquility. What that changes is the tone of your return: short, honest, unhurried prayer beats an ambitious plan you'll abandon by Thursday. What stays is your own sense of what you've neglected — secret prayer and reading — so keep those as the aim, just start small and gently. If a wandering mind is your main worry, that principle is your permission slip to begin again without scolding yourself.

prompt: I am a dying believer and want to know whether I should ask my minister to bury me and to remember my aged parents after I am gone.
completion: I'd say yes, this is fine, and fine to do with care. You're not asking for anything strange here. Asking your minister to bury you is a normal, loving thing, and asking him to remember your aged parents after you're gone is a kind way to look after them. One thing worth weighing, though, is the kind of minister you ask. A ministry without prayer isn't just less effective; it's a funeral and an undertaker for God's truth and Church, however adorned it may be. So ask someone who actually prays, because that's the person who will bury you as a witness to the resurrection and will remember your parents before God. What that changes is who you ask and how you frame the request; what stays is that the request itself is good. Keep it within Scripture too: praying for your resurrection, your acquittal at the great Day, your perfect consummation and bliss, without implying any purification after death. And since you mentioned your parents, it's worth remembering that parents are responsible for their children, to teach them the gospel and watch over them. Speak with your minister soon, put your wishes in writing, and involve your family.

prompt: I am a Christian and my friend has died in the Lord—may I grieve, or should I only rejoice?
completion: I'd say right away: yes, you may grieve. Your question isn't whether grief is allowed but whether it crowds out rejoicing, and it doesn't have to. One principle worth weighing says the Christian's consolation in the face of death rests entirely on a view of Christ—his incarnation, temptations, cross, death, resurrection, and intercession—and not on the believer's own frames or feelings, which are clouded by sin and unbelief. That changes where you look when the sorrow hits: not inward at how strong your faith feels today, but outward at the Savior who holds your friend. What stays is the grief itself—it's real, it's human, and it isn't a failure. So let both be true: mourn the separation, and hold onto the hope you have in Christ. Lean on your church family, take the time you need, and don't feel you have to choose between tears and trust.

prompt: I am a parent and my child has become serious about religion while I remain ignorant—should I listen to her?
completion: Yes, listen to her. That's the first thing I'd say, and I'd say it plainly. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about parents and pastors having a sacred duty to remove irreligious, immoral, or untrue books from the reach of the young and to provide works that train the mind to truth and virtue. Notice what that principle actually asks of you: not that you become a scholar of her faith, and not that you pretend to share convictions you don't hold, but that you take some care about what she's reading and thinking. That changes something real. It means listening isn't passive—you can ask what she's reading, you can look at it yourself, you can steer her toward serious and honest works rather than whatever happens to be at hand. What stays is your honesty. You've told me you're ignorant about religion; that's fine, and you don't need to hide it. Ask her questions, let her explain what she believes and why, and be open to learning alongside her. You can read a little yourself or talk with a pastor if you want to engage more thoughtfully. So yes, listen—and while you listen, keep a light hand on what comes into her hands.

prompt: I am a poor servant girl and feel that my station makes me unfit to be a teacher of religion—can God really use someone like me?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say to you is: yes, and your station doesn't stand in the way. I'd weigh the principle that God places solemn value on the humble worker with one talent, and that faithfulness in the least is what counts. That changes how I'd hear your worry—being poor and a servant doesn't make you unfit; it puts you right where quiet, faithful teaching by example actually happens. What stays is your real limit: you don't have a platform, training, or spare time, so I wouldn't tell you to chase a public role. Start with the people in front of you, and if you want more, look for a pastor or community that can help. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I am a poor old man near seventy and my sight is dim and my strength fails—what promises are mine in old age?
completion: I'd say first: your dim sight and failing strength are not a failure of faith, and nothing here asks you to pretend otherwise. The principle I'd weigh is the one about the calm old age of a pure conscience and the hidden prayers of lowly saints upholding a world that isn't self-sustaining. That fits you as you actually are, near seventy, without much strength to spend. What it changes is the measure of your days: your quiet prayers and a clear conscience are real work, not a consolation prize. What stays is everything you told me — the dim sight, the failing strength, the tiredness. I'm not going to tell you to chase your youth back. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care: rest in God's promise to carry you even to gray hairs, let your hope lean on the life to come, and let your hidden prayers be your gift. That's enough.

prompt: I have been a Christian only a short time and feel alone in the ways of God—how do I find fellowship?
completion: What I'd say first is: you're not asking for anything wrong. Wanting fellowship is a good instinct, not a weakness. One principle I'd weigh here is that Christian friendship—speaking often with others about the things of God—is a means of building believers up in faith and love. That changes how you might think about small talk after church: it's not filler, it's part of how you grow. What stays the same is your situation—you're new to this, you feel alone, and you shouldn't have to force anything. So take the pressure off. Find a church that teaches Scripture faithfully, show up regularly, and let a conversation or two start naturally. That's fine, and it's fine with care—no need to overthink it.

prompt: I am afraid of death and the dark valley—how can I face it with peace?
completion: I'd start by saying: your fear is not a failure, and you don't have to talk yourself out of it to find peace. The principle I'd weigh first is that the Lord deals gently with his dying saints and takes away the sting of death, so the valley is not dark because he is there as light and salvation. What that changes is the picture you're carrying—the valley stops being a place you walk into alone. What stays is everything you actually said: the fear is real, the darkness feels real, and peace has to be lived inside that, not instead of it. So take it slowly. Name the fear out loud to God and to someone you trust. Let a psalm about the valley be something you say when you can't feel it yet. Do small acts of trust now, while you're well, so trust is familiar when you're tired. And keep the practical things in order so uncertainty doesn't pile on top of grief. That's fine, and it's fine with care—no one is asking you to be fearless, only to not be alone in it.

prompt: I am a minister and the people complain that my preaching is too severe—should I soften the truths of the Gospel?
completion: I'd start by saying: no, you don't soften the truths themselves. But that isn't really the question your people are asking, is it? The gospel is simple and was given so the humblest person can comprehend and enjoy it. That principle doesn't tell you to dilute anything—it tells you to check whether what's landing on your congregation is the gospel or your own severity dressed up as it. Converting religion into a system only the strong can stomach is its own kind of philosophy. So what changes is the delivery and the self-examination; what stays is the content. You can keep every truth and still ask whether you're preaching to be understood and enjoyed by the humblest among them. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I am a servant in a household where no worship is regarded and no one cares for the servants' souls—how do I live as a Christian there?
completion: What I'd say first is that your situation is hard, and you're not failing God by being in it. Weighing that first principle: don't be too anxious about feeling devotion, sweetness, or tears, but let your main care be to stay inwardly united to God by good will, denying yourself to follow Christ, who was truly poor, obedient, humble, and suffering. That changes how you measure your days. You don't need a household altar or a stirring feeling to be close to God; quiet, steady good will counts. What stays is everything you already named: no worship around you, no one tending your soul. So keep praying privately, read Scripture when you can, and find fellowship and support outside the home. Be respectful and do your work well. Share your faith gently if a door opens, but don't force it. This is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I have lived a careless, prayerless life and only now begin to be concerned—is there mercy for me at the eleventh hour?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say to you is that your concern itself is not nothing—it's the beginning of turning, and that matters. On the principle that God is infinitely gracious and knows all our wants, and comes in His own time: that's the ground I'd stand on with you. It means your late start doesn't disqualify you, and it also means you can't schedule the mercy or demand the feeling. What changes is this: you don't have to wait until you feel worthy or prayerful to begin—prayer is a duty and a privilege to be done at set times whether or not you feel like it. What stays is your honesty about the careless years; don't paper over them, bring them. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care: start praying at fixed times, keep it simple, and don't treat the lack of feeling as a reason to skip it.

prompt: I am a brother and my sister is dying—how do I support her and my aged parents without despairing?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that you're carrying something no one should have to carry alone, and asking how to do it well is already an act of love. Weighing that first principle — that true love seeks the Saviour first and then goes to win the erring brother, giving no fading memorial but wreaths of hope — I'd say it changes the shape of your days, not the tasks in them. It means prayer comes before the phone calls and the hospital runs, and that when you speak with your sister and your parents you offer hope rather than a eulogy in advance. What stays is everything you already named: being present, listening, sharing caregiving with your parents, guarding your own rest, and letting friends and your church carry some of this with you. Grief and despair are not the same thing, and hope can sit right alongside tears. So this is fine, and fine with care — keep your limits, keep your rest, and let the hope you speak be real rather than forced.

prompt: I am a parent and my child has been taken from me—how do I say with Job, the Lord gave and the Lord hath taken away?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that you don't owe anyone those words, and you don't have to say them well. Job didn't say them quickly—he said them after tearing his robe and falling to the ground. So grieve first. When you're ready, the words can be a direction you're walking toward rather than a feeling you have to manufacture. One principle here is worth weighing in its own words: we are to be attentive to blessing God for all He does, saying with Job, 'The Lord gave and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord.' That changes this much: the words are meant to be said, not just admired, and they can hold your sorrow rather than erase it. What stays is your grief, your honesty, and the fact that saying them is trust, not resignation. So it's fine—fine with care—to pray them slowly, even while you're still weeping.

prompt: I am a young person at a funeral and feel strangely moved—what should I do with this impression?
completion: What I'd say first is: being moved at a funeral isn't a problem to fix, so you don't need to talk yourself out of it. If I weigh the principle that 'transient glances at the divine judgments effect not a change of heart,' what it changes is that I won't tell you this one feeling is a conversion or a sign you've suddenly become someone different. What stays is that the feeling is real and worth noticing. You're young and at a funeral, so keep it simple: let yourself feel it, maybe write a line or two about who the person was or what struck you, and if it lingers, talk it over with someone you trust. That's fine, and fine with care. Don't turn a passing impression into a heavy verdict on your whole life.

prompt: I have been a faithful minister for years and see little fruit—should I keep laboring in the same place?
completion: I'd start by saying I hear how tired and discouraged you are, and that your question is a fair one to bring. The principle I'd weigh first is this: when you're in doubt about which of several labors is required, do them all to be sure of performing the one the Lord really requires. That reframes your question a little. It doesn't tell you that you must never leave a hard field, and it doesn't dismiss the years you've already given. What it does is loosen the pressure to figure out, right now, which single thing is the one thing. You've described real limits: years of labor, little visible fruit, and honest weariness. So I wouldn't tell you to grind on indefinitely out of sheer duty, and I wouldn't tell you to bolt either. What stays is this: faithfulness is measured by obedience, not by what you can count. What changes is that you don't have to solve the whole question before you take the next step. Talk with people who know you and your situation, tend your own soul, and then decide. Staying or going with care is fine.

prompt: I am a young person and I fear death is near—how should I spend the time I have left?
completion: What I'd say first is this: you're not being asked to prepare to die, you're being asked to prepare to live. That's the shift I'd want to make with you. It's absolutely certain that we'll die, but the time, place, and manner are utterly uncertain, and that uncertainty is exactly why you make the changes now that you'd wish you'd made when death felt near. Nothing about that requires you to drop the fear you're carrying or pretend it isn't real. You can hold the fear and still spend your days building something—habits, health, relationships, a character that's actually growing. What changes is the direction of your effort: toward living well rather than toward a deathbed checklist. What stays is the honesty that time is short and shouldn't be wasted.

prompt: I am a servant girl and my mistress does not care for religion—how do I keep the Lord's Day when I cannot attend worship?
completion: What I'd say first is this: you're not being asked to choose between your mistress and your faith, and nothing here calls for a hard no. The principle I'd weigh is that the Sabbath is to be kept holy and not robbed, and that the Saints should worship and attend to the duties of that day, setting an example to all with whom they associate. That last part matters for you. You can't get to worship, so the day gets kept where you are: prayer and Scripture early or late, the day treated as set apart rather than as ordinary labor or idle time, and your conduct toward your mistress and household doing the quiet work of example. What changes is that you stop measuring the day by whether you made it through a church door; what stays is that the day is still holy and still yours to keep. Be respectful and diligent in your duties, ask kindly for leave when there's a real opening, and don't carry guilt for a limit you didn't set. This is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: My health prevents me from attending church, and I feel cut off from the means of grace—is there any comfort for me?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say to you is that this is fine, and it's fine with care. The principle I'd weigh here says it plainly: it is not necessary for being with God to be always at church; we may make an oratory of our heart wherein to retire from time to time to converse with him in meekness, humility, and love. That's the heart of it for you. Your illness keeps you from the building, but it doesn't keep you from that conversation, and everyone is capable of it, including someone whose body won't cooperate. What changes is the pressure to measure your faith by attendance. What stays is the call to real, humble, loving prayer wherever you are. Keep the limits you've named: you can't get there, so don't pretend you can. Ask your pastor about home communion or a visit, stay connected by phone or video if that's possible for you, and let your heart be the room where you meet God.

prompt: I am a dying believer and my enemy suggests Christ has no love for me—how do I resist him?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is that this is a temptation to despair, not a report of the facts. You're dying, and the enemy is using your weakness to suggest Christ has no love for you. I'd weigh the second principle here, in its own words: love suffers never to be without pity; when we fall and leave the keeping of our own soul, Christ alone keeps all the charge and stands sorrowfully and moaning, and it belongs to us for reverence and kindness to turn hastily and not leave Him alone. That changes the picture: the very weakness you fear is the place where His pity meets you, and turning back quickly, even in a whisper, is enough. What stays is your limit—you're dying and may have little strength—so don't measure His love by how strongly you feel. Say a short word to Him, ask a pastor or friend to pray with you, and let others carry you when you can't pray yourself. This is fine, and fine with care: rest in Him rather than debating the enemy at length.

prompt: I am a minister and fear the frown of wealthy parishioners more than I should—how should I reprove sin among them?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: you've named the fear honestly, and that honesty is where the work starts. The principle that settles it for me is this one—the truths and maxims of religion depend not on the morals of those who preach them, but on the wisdom and veracity of God. That cuts both ways for you. It means the word you carry doesn't lose its weight because you're afraid or imperfect, and it also means the wealthy parishioner's money doesn't add weight to the word or take it away. So reprove the sin—clearly, gently, privately where you can, with real humility about your own failings. What changes is your reason for speaking: not to win their approval, not to keep the peace, but because the message is God's. What stays is your care for them and your honesty about your own limits. You don't have to become fearless overnight; you just have to be faithful while you're still afraid.

prompt: I am a soldier far from home and find the Lord wherever I march—how should I regard my lack of worldly goods?
completion: I'd start by saying: what you're describing sounds like a good thing, not a problem to fix. Take the third principle in its own words—it's a privilege to endure hardness and to live economically so as to have more to give to the LORD's service, and the less spent on oneself the fuller the joy. That reframes your lack of goods from something to apologize for into room for generosity. What changes is the mood: not grim poverty but joyful freedom to give. What stays is your situation exactly as you described it—you're a soldier, far from home, and you find the Lord on the march. I'm not going to tell you to chase more stuff or to feel bad about having little. Regard it as fine, and fine with care: keep your heart set on the Lord you've found, and let the simplicity actually free you to give and serve.

prompt: My parents are old and ignorant of the things of God, and I have been converted while they have not—what is my duty toward them?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that honoring your parents doesn't stop being your duty now that you believe differently—that command doesn't come with an expiry date. But I'd weigh this principle carefully: "God remits the convert to the guidance of his ministers rather than instructing him immediately, so that all who desire to serve him should seek his will by listening to those he has appointed as guides." That changes something real: it means you shouldn't treat your own read of the situation as the final word, and you should be learning God's will through the ministers He's given you rather than deciding alone. What stays is everything about your parents—patience, respect, practical care as they age, gentleness when you speak of your faith, and no contempt. So this is fine, and fine with care: honor them, provide for them, pray for them, and let your life carry more weight than your arguments. Don't turn pressure or technique into your method; conversion isn't something you engineer.

prompt: I have been a light and trifling person and heard serious conversation at a funeral—can that begin a real change in me?
completion: I'd say first: yes, this can be the start of something real. But I'd weigh one principle carefully, in its own words: "Transient glances at the divine judgments effect not a change of heart." That's the honest caution here. A funeral can give you a genuine glance—clear-eyed, unsettling—but a glance by itself doesn't change anyone. What it changes is this: don't treat the feeling as the finish line, and don't assume a fear-driven jolt under sad circumstances is the same as sincere repentance. What stays is your own hope—that a light, trifling habit of life can actually turn. That hope is not foolish. So take the stirring seriously: sit with what struck you, be honest about the trifling patterns, and make a couple of concrete changes. Talk to someone wise who'll help you keep going. It's fine, and fine with care—the care being that you let this be more than a mood.

prompt: I am a dying believer and my parents are still unconverted—may I hope my prayers for them will be answered?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say to you is: yes, you may hope. Your situation is heavy, and nothing in that heaviness makes your prayers for your parents wrong. The one principle I'd weigh here is the one about asking amiss—praying out of selfish and earthly motives, as when parents pray for children merely for their own comfort rather than for God's glory. That's worth holding up honestly, because it's possible to want your parents converted partly so your own last days feel easier, or so you don't have to carry the worry. But that principle doesn't cancel your hope; it just purifies it. So what changes is the aim of your praying—you can keep asking for their salvation while also asking God to search your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it, so your prayer flows from a clean place. What stays is everything you actually asked: your parents are still unconverted, you are dying, and your prayers for them are still good and still heard. You don't need to be anxious about the outcome or the timing. Keep praying, and share your hope with them while you still can.

prompt: I am a rich man with a fine estate; what should I think about the certainty of keeping it for my family?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: wanting to keep something good for your family is a decent instinct, not a flaw. Weigh this one: the rich should meditate on the uncertainty of their possessions and the frailty of every earthly tenure. That's true, and it changes how you hold the estate—loosely, with planning and honest talk about money, not with the belief that you can lock the future down. What stays is your freedom to steward it well: clear arrangements, fair treatment among your children, teaching them to be capable. You asked about certainty, and certainty isn't on offer—but careful stewardship is, and that's fine to pursue.

prompt: I am a mother and my dear daughter is the staff of my old age—how can I bear to lose her?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say to you is that your fear makes sense, and you don't have to hide it. The principle I'd weigh here is this: prepare to live, not merely to die. That doesn't mean pretending loss is impossible; it means the love you share isn't only something to hold onto at the end. So teach your daughter, while her days are still bright, to build health, strength, and steadiness, and let that be part of how you love her now. What changes is the direction of your fear—it turns toward building a life together rather than only bracing for goodbye. What stays is the honesty of your grief and the closeness you two already have. Talk with her about what you feel, lean on the people around you, and let this be fine, with care.

prompt: I am a young woman and I have been proud of my dress and appearance—how do I learn humility?
completion: What I'd say first is that caring about your dress and appearance isn't the problem, and nothing here needs to be refused. But let me weigh one principle in its own words: true humility dreads the esteem and praises of others as snares by which a mortal poison may imperceptibly insinuate itself into her affections and deprive her of divine grace. That reframes the question. The danger isn't liking a nice dress; it's quietly needing the praise that comes with it. So what changes is where you put your attention—notice the moment a compliment starts to feel like something you can't do without, and let that be your signal. What stays is your enjoyment of dressing well and feeling put together; that's fine, and you don't have to talk yourself out of it. Keep it simple: dress well, receive praise lightly, and don't let it become the thing you're living on.

prompt: I have neglected visiting the sick because I thought it was only the minister's duty—am I wrong?
completion: You're not wrong to feel the weight of this, but I'd start by saying the duty isn't only the minister's. The principle puts it plainly: visiting the sick is a strict command and duty for every Christian, and many perish for lack of one friend to warn them to flee from the wrath to come. That widens the circle beyond the minister without erasing the minister's role. What changes is that you can't leave it all to someone else; what stays is that you were right that ministers have a particular part. So go, pray with them, help practically, and speak honestly about hope in Christ—within the limits you actually have.

prompt: I am a minister and I fear that my own heart grows cold in the midst of duty—how do I revive it?
completion: What I'd say first is: this is fine, and it's fine with care. A heart that grows cold under duty is a normal thing, not a scandal, and noticing it is already the beginning of warmth. Weigh this one: when the heart is distracted in prayer, we must bring it gently back and lay it tenderly at the feet of its Master, and the hour will be well employed. That changes how you approach the quiet, not whether you should keep the quiet. You don't have to manufacture feeling before you come; you bring the wandering heart back gently, again and again, and the time still counts. What stays is everything you already know about your limits: you're not being asked to abandon your duties or stage a dramatic overhaul. Keep the unhurried prayer, the Scripture you read for yourself, the rest, the confession, the trusted friend. Small habits, patiently repeated, are enough.

prompt: I'm married with children and can't withdraw from the world. Can I still reach the highest spiritual life?
completion: I'd say this first: yes, and your situation doesn't disqualify you. The principle I'd weigh is that the goal is a love-union of conscious cooperation, where God's will becomes your will rather than you dissolving into anything. That matters because it means the highest life isn't a matter of location. It's a matter of a will freely given, and you can give that from a kitchen as well as a cloister. What changes is the picture of holiness as something only quiet, solitary people reach. What stays is everything you said: you're married, you have children, you can't withdraw, and none of that gets set aside. So keep your duties, keep short times of prayer, and let the daily giving of yourself be the practice.

prompt: I don't know how to pray. What words should I use when I feel nothing?
completion: I'd say first: you don't need special words, and feeling nothing doesn't disqualify you. One principle worth weighing is that feelings are not the gauge of acceptance with God; trust the changeless word of promise rather than variable moods, and continue in prayer even when joy is lacking. That changes how you read your own emptiness—it stops being evidence that you're doing it wrong. What stays is your honesty: tell God plainly you feel nothing, use a short sentence like "Lord, have mercy," and keep a small rhythm. It's fine, and fine with care—don't force big emotions, just keep showing up.

prompt: I'm not sure I've ever really repented. Should I focus first on being sorry for my sins?
completion: I'd start by saying: being sorry is a fine place to begin, and you don't need to have it all sorted before you come to God. But I'd weigh this principle carefully—true repentance requires turning from sin, a reformation of life, and restitution so far as possible. That means sorrow alone isn't the whole thing, and a last-moment confession won't cleanse a person. What that changes: don't camp out in guilt, waiting to feel enough regret before you act. What stays: your honest sorrow is real and worth bringing to God. So examine your life, confess what you see, turn from what's wrong, and make amends where you can—and trust that sins are washed away through Christ's atonement upon repentance. That's fine, done with care.

prompt: I can't forgive someone who hurt me deeply. What does the spiritual life require of me here?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that your pain is not a problem to be solved quickly, and nothing here asks you to pretend the harm didn't happen. Weighing the principle that says forgiveness of injuries is required for salvation, I notice it doesn't say forgiveness is instant or that it erases what was done. It says a refusal to forgive forfeits the crown, and that meekness under insults can win enemies over. What that changes: it means forgiveness is a direction you turn toward, not a feeling you manufacture on demand, and it can coexist with real grief and with boundaries that keep you safe. What stays: the harm is real, your limits are real, and you don't owe anyone access to you. So this is fine, and fine with care. Tell God honestly what happened, ask for the grace to will the other person's good even while your feelings lag, and return to that as resentment rises. Lean on a pastor or counselor, and take your time.

prompt: How do I know what God wants me to do in a specific situation?
completion: I'd start by saying this is a fine thing to want, and you can pursue it with care. Take the first principle seriously in its own words: God first puts good desires into our minds and then by His continual help enables us to bring them to good effect. That reframes your question a little. You're not hunting for a hidden instruction so much as noticing the good desire already forming and then asking how to carry it out faithfully. What that changes is the pressure to find one right answer before you move. What stays is everything you already know: pray, get the facts, check your motives, read Scripture, ask wise counsel, act and review. Those ordinary means are how clarity usually grows. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care, as long as you don't treat every uncertainty as a sign you've failed.

prompt: I keep having critical, hard thoughts about people around me, even small annoyances. Does that matter?
completion: What I'd say first is that noticing this about yourself is already a good sign. On the principle that we shouldn't be troubled about the imperfections of others, since dwelling on them holds us back, but should look on people simply, kindly, and amiably — that's the one I'd weigh here. It changes the framing: the goal isn't to crush every flicker of annoyance, it's to stop feeding it. What stays is that the thoughts do matter, because they set the tone for how you treat people. So this is fine with care: let the small annoyances pass without turning them into a case against anyone, and steer your attention back to seeing people kindly.

prompt: I'm at my desk all day in a noisy office. Can I really find any peace with God in the middle of that?
completion: I'd say first: yes, you can find peace with God at that desk, and it's fine with care. One principle I'd weigh is that we shouldn't put violent constraint on ourselves but serve God in a holy freedom, doing our business faithfully without trouble or disquiet, recalling our mind to God mildly and with tranquility as often as we find it wandering. That changes how you should go at this: no straining for long silence in a loud room, no scolding yourself when the noise pulls you away. What stays is the honest limit you named—you're at a desk all day in a noisy office, so peace here will look like short, gentle returns, not a retreat. A prayer before email, a verse recalled, a breath between tasks: small, unforced, repeated.

prompt: I feel nothing in prayer anymore. Have I been abandoned by God?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is: feeling nothing in prayer doesn't mean you've been abandoned. Feelings are not the gauge of acceptance with God, and that's the principle I'd weigh here — trust the changeless word of promise rather than your variable moods, and keep praying even when the joy is gone. That changes how you read the silence: it's not evidence against you. What stays is your honesty about it, and the practical stuff — sleep, health, a pastor or counselor if this is heavy. You're not doing anything wrong by feeling dry.

prompt: I'm successful and comfortable, and I honestly don't think much about God. Is that a problem?
completion: I'd start by saying that being successful and comfortable isn't the problem here, and neither is the fact that you don't think much about God right now. You didn't ask me to rearrange your life, and I won't. One principle worth weighing is that God-consciousness isn't achieved by study or reading, which only whets the appetite as a menu cannot satisfy hunger; what's needed is individual, personal, inward possession. That changes how I'd answer you: it means reading more, or forcing yourself to think about God out of guilt, wouldn't get you anywhere. What stays is your honesty and your comfort. So this is fine, and fine with care. You're not doing anything wrong by living the life you have.

prompt: I work long hours at an ordinary job and have a family depending on me—can I find God without becoming a monk or nun or leaving my duties?
completion: I'd say this first: yes, you can find God right where you are, without becoming a monk or leaving your duties. The principle I'd weigh is that the ordinary person living an everyday life of work or leisure can find God without withdrawing into a separate 'religious' life, without conspicuous public piety, and without neglecting duties to dependents. That changes the picture from 'you must simplify, cut hobbies, adopt a rule of life' to 'your long hours and your family are not obstacles—they're the place where this is met.' What stays is the honesty that it takes attention and faithfulness, not drama. So: fine, and fine with care. Keep your duties to the people depending on you; turn toward God in the work and the home you already have.

prompt: I'm terrified of dying and what comes after. What happens to me if I haven't found God by then?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is: your fear is real, and it doesn't disqualify you from anything. You're asking whether you've run out of time, and I'd gently push back on the frame. As one old principle puts it, God never forsakes us until we have first forsaken him — so the question isn't whether you found God before some deadline, but whether you'll walk away from him. That shifts the weight off your timing and onto your direction. What stays is the honest fear itself; I'm not going to tell you it's nothing. What changes is that your fear stops being a verdict about you and becomes a door you can walk through. So yes, it's fine to bring this exactly as it is — talk to a pastor, pray honestly, and let the fear point you toward God rather than away.

prompt: I try to think about Jesus but my mind wanders to my friends, my work, my worries. How do I make Him more real to me?
completion: What I'd say first is: your wandering mind isn't the problem you think it is. You asked how to make Jesus more real, and one principle here says we come into personal contact with Jesus by the same steps we use to make any friend: thinking about Him, spending time in His companionship, forming brief mental pictures of the Saviour, walking beside Him, learning what He would do and think. That's fine, and fine with care. Notice it doesn't ask you to empty your head of your friends, your work, or your worries. Those are your actual life, and He can be met inside it. So try a short picture of Him beside you at your desk, or in the car, and let your worries be something you talk over with Him rather than something you have to clear out first. What changes is that you stop treating distraction as failure. What stays is the gentle returning, over and over, which is exactly how friendship grows.

prompt: I'm constantly tempted by something I know is wrong. Should I fight the temptation head-on?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, fight it, but not as a lone willpower contest. One principle I'd weigh is that God allows us to be tempted but won't let it go beyond our strength, and He makes a way to bear it. That changes how you fight: you're not proving yourself alone, you're looking for the way out He's already providing. What stays is the plain call to resist and to endure patiently. Since you've said this is a temptation you know is wrong, resisting it is fine, and fine with care, so long as you don't turn the fight into self-reliance or despair when it's hard.

prompt: I'm afraid of losing my individuality if I give myself completely to God. Will I stop being myself?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is: no, you won't stop being yourself—but I'd want to weigh one thing carefully before you go further. Self-denial, as I'd put it, has to come from inward joy in God and the work of the Holy Spirit, not from custom or the force of example, or else you'll regret it and it won't last. That matters for your fear specifically. If you surrender out of pressure or fear of losing yourself, you're doing the very thing that gets resented later. But if it grows from joy in God, the self you're afraid of losing turns out to be the shell, not the core. What changes is the motive: don't hand yourself over grimly or because you think you must. What stays is that giving yourself completely is still the right direction—just let it come from joy, not dread.

prompt: I'm a very rational person. Can't I reason my way to God?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, you can reason your way a long way toward God, and you should. But I'd weigh this: reason's proper office is to recognize, examine, systematize, and deduce from revelation, not to sit in judgment upon it. That changes something real. It means your reasoning is a tool for understanding what's been given, not a judge deciding whether it gets to be true. What stays is everything you value: careful thinking, weighing evidence, following arguments where they lead. You're not being asked to check your intellect at the door. You're being asked to notice that reason can bring you to the threshold and can justify trust, but it can't manufacture the trust itself. So keep reasoning hard, and stay open to the step that reasoning alone won't take for you.

prompt: I'm not sure I believe Jesus is actually God, only a holy man. Does that matter?
completion: I'd start by saying I get why you're weighing this, and it's a fair question to sit with rather than rush past. The Gospels hold together a Jesus who is genuinely human and more than human; the difference between the Synoptists and John is a matter of point of view, not contradiction. So you don't have to choose between a holy man and a divine one as if they were two different people. What that changes is that your honesty about Jesus as a holy man isn't something to be ashamed of; what stays is that the fuller picture in all four Gospels is worth reading with open eyes. Take your time with it.

prompt: I have a dishonest, lazy employee and a difficult husband. How can these be anything but obstacles to God?
completion: I'd start by saying I don't think you're wrong to feel the weight of this. A dishonest employee and a difficult husband are real, daily friction, and calling them obstacles is an honest description of how they feel. But here's the principle I'd weigh first: God is the one living Agent who works, and human workers are only instruments, so all care and anxiety on our part is distrust of Him and a sinful self-conceit. That reframes things without pretending the friction isn't there. It changes who you think is carrying the outcome, and it changes the pressure you put on yourself to fix both of them. What stays is everything you actually said: the employee is still dishonest, your husband is still difficult, and you still have to live with both. This isn't a call to ignore wrongdoing or to smile through it. It's fine, and fine with care, to stop treating them as barriers between you and God and start asking what faithfulness looks like in the ordinary, unglamorous work of your day.

prompt: I've wanted God for years and still can't find Him. What am I doing wrong?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say to you is that you're not doing anything wrong by longing. That longing is real, and it counts for something. The principle I'd weigh here says the search is double: the God you're seeking is also seeking you. That doesn't mean you'll feel an answer tomorrow, and it doesn't erase the years of silence you've lived through. What it changes is the picture of what's happening — you're not just shouting into a void. What stays is everything you told me: the waiting, the not-finding, the honest confusion. Keep seeking, gently, and don't let anyone tell you the ache itself is a failure.

prompt: I'm at peace with the world and my life. Why would I need God at all?
completion: I'd start by saying that your peace sounds real, and I'm not going to talk you out of it. The principle I'd weigh is that God and man are conjunct: personality is impossible in isolation, and human and divine life are mutually organic, so God needs us as we need God. That reframes your question. It isn't whether you need a God tacked onto a life that's already complete; it's whether any of us becomes a person alone. If that's true, then needing God isn't a deficit you've outgrown, it's part of what you are. What changes: the question stops being about a gap in your contentment. What stays: your peace, your life as it is, and your freedom to leave this where it sits. You asked why you'd need God at all, and nothing here says you must decide today.

prompt: How do I begin to love someone I've never seen?
completion: What I'd say first is that this is fine, and fine with care. The principle that fits best is the third one: the very circumstance your suffering sense deems wrathful and afflictive, Love can make an angel entertained unawares. That reframes the hard part—the distance, the not-knowing, even your own reluctance—as something that can draw you out of yourself rather than proof you're failing. What that changes is the tone: you don't have to force a feeling or scold yourself for not having one yet. What stays is the practical core—learn their story, pray for them by name, serve in small ways, speak well of them. Keep it grounded in who they actually are, not a picture you've built in your head.

prompt: I'm afraid of the suffering that seems to come with getting closer to God. Is it worth it?
completion: I'd start by saying your fear makes sense, and nothing here asks you to go looking for pain. What I'd weigh is this: the sacrifice of patience, submission, and constant fidelity in a state of suffering is more heroic and precious in God's sight than active labor. That reframes what you're afraid of. It doesn't promise you'll escape suffering, but it says the quiet endurance you're dreading is itself something precious, not wasted. What changes is that drawing closer isn't a bargain where you pay in pain for access. What stays is your limit: you're not being told to chase suffering or to want it. Wanting health and ease is fine, and the tradition itself says to desire health only if it's more expedient for God's honor. So this is fine, and fine with care: go closer, keep your honesty about the fear, and don't manufacture the cross you're worried about.

prompt: I go to church regularly and keep the commandments—isn't that enough to make me a Christian?
completion: I'd start by saying plainly: no, that isn't enough, and I don't want to soften it. You asked whether churchgoing and commandment-keeping make you a Christian, and the honest answer is that they don't. One principle puts it sharply: Christianity is not an act done by hands but a life, and keeping the commandments, being baptized, and believing Christ lived and was crucified is not enough, since Jews and Mahommedans believe these things too. That doesn't cancel your churchgoing or your obedience—keep them. What it changes is the assumption that they settle the question. What stays is the real question underneath: whether Christ lives in you. So don't treat the practices as the answer; let them point you toward the life they can't replace.

prompt: I'm going through a terrible loss—someone I loved more than anything. Why would God take that from me?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say to you is that I'm so sorry, and that your grief is not a failure. So I can't take the line that says your sorrow is too much, or that wanting your loved one back is a lack of faith. That's not something I'd put on you. Where I would push back is on the idea that this loss came straight from God's hand as a loving Father's plan, and that you should just fold it into consolation. I don't think you should be told that God took someone you loved more than anything to keep your heart from having a rival. That's a wrong thing to say to someone in your pain, and I'd say no to it plainly. What stays is this: you can bring your questions to God, you can lean on your community, and you can grieve as long as you need to.

prompt: I've had moments in nature or in music where I felt something vast and beautiful beyond words. What is that?
completion: What I'd say first is: that feeling is real, and you're not wrong to wonder about it. One principle here says nature is the visible showing of an invisible Will, and that tracing it back to its Source turns praise into a continual delight. That fits what you describe—vast, beautiful, beyond words—and it gives you somewhere to take it. What changes is that the moment isn't just a nice feeling to collect; it has a direction. What stays is your own framing: you didn't ask for a doctrine, you asked what this is. So call it a glimpse, let it point you toward gratitude, and don't force it into words it doesn't need. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I say little prayers during the day but they feel empty and mechanical. Is that worth anything?
completion: I'd say first: what you're doing is fine, and it's fine with care. Take the principle that a little lifting up of the heart suffices — a little remembrance of God, one act of inward worship, though upon a march and a sword in hand, are prayers very acceptable to God. That speaks right to your case. You're not producing nothing; you're lifting your heart in small moments, and that counts. What it changes is the pressure you're putting on the feeling. What stays is your honesty that it feels mechanical — so when you notice that, pause for a second and mean the next one. Keep the little prayers. Don't add a heavy program on top of them.

prompt: I feel like I have two selves—one that wants God and one that wants everything else. Which one am I?
completion: I'd start by saying that what you're describing isn't a defect in you—it's just what it is to be a person with a will. The principle I'd weigh first says we have two wills: the will to live, our natural pull toward our own comfort and safety, which on its own doesn't get us to peace or eternal life, and the will to love and gladly please God, which is the only will we actually live by. Notice it doesn't say you're two people. It says you have two wills, and only one of them is the one you live by. So the question 'which one am I' gets a gentler answer than you might expect: you're the one in whom both are real, and the life you're after comes from the second, not from killing off the first by force. What that changes is the pressure to pick an identity on the spot—you don't have to declare yourself one thing today. What stays is the honest tug-of-war; it's still there, and it still matters which will you lean into. Given that you framed this as a question about who you are rather than a request to be told what to do, I'd say this is fine to sit with, and fine to bring into prayer exactly as it is.

prompt: I keep giving in to the same sin over and over. Is there any hope for me?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is: there's hope, and you're not the first person to come back to the same failure. I'd weigh this principle first: God commands all people everywhere to repent now, and since he commands it, the power to renounce sin is available. That matters because it means you don't have to wait until you feel stronger or more sorry. The feeling follows the surrender, not the other way around. What that changes is the waiting game — you can turn from it this moment, in will and purpose, and ask God for the strength he promises. What stays is the honest part: this is a real struggle, and turning once doesn't guarantee you'll never slip again. So keep going back to him, keep being honest with someone who can help, and don't let a setback convince you the door is closed. That's fine, and it's fine with care.

prompt: I'm afraid of God's will for my life—I imagine it as a path of thorns. Will it always feel like that?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that your fear makes sense, and it doesn't disqualify you from anything. You're picturing God's will as a path of thorns, and that picture is doing a lot of work in your imagination right now. Here's one principle worth weighing in its own words: in our raw state we fear the Will of God as a path of thorns, but as Christ moulds us we come to know it as a great Balm, longing to conform to it and sink into it as into immense security. Notice what that says and doesn't say. It doesn't promise the thorns vanish overnight, and it doesn't ask you to pretend you're not afraid. What it changes is the direction of travel: the fear you feel now isn't the final word about what God's will is like. What stays is your honesty, your prayer, and the fact that you're allowed to bring the fear itself rather than waiting until you've conquered it. So this is fine, and fine with care: keep praying honestly, don't force a feeling you don't have, and let trust grow slowly.

prompt: I'm wealthy. Can a rich person really find God?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say to you is: yes, this is fine, and fine with care. Take the principle that says the ordinary person living an everyday life of work or leisure can find God without withdrawing into a separate religious life, without conspicuous public piety, and without neglecting duties to dependents. That applies to you as much as anyone. Your wealth doesn't disqualify you, and it doesn't mean you have to sell everything and disappear into a monastery to be serious. What it does mean is that the pull of possessions is real, and you should hold your resources loosely, be generous, and let them serve people rather than run you. So keep your work, keep your family, keep your ordinary days, and seek God right there. What changes is the fantasy that you need a dramatic exit to be spiritual. What stays is the honesty about comfort and self-reliance. You don't need to abandon your life to find God; you need to live it awake.

prompt: I feel guilty and afraid about my past. Is fear of punishment a good reason to turn to God?
completion: I'd start by saying: fear is allowed to be the door you walk through, as long as you don't lock yourself in the hallway. The principle I'd weigh is the one that says we must not fear God as though He wished to harm us, but love Him fervently, since He wishes to do us great good. That changes the destination of your fear, not the fact that you feel it. Your guilt and fear are real, and you don't have to pretend they aren't. So let the fear bring you in, and then let it be replaced by trust in someone who wants your good. What stays is this: you're not being asked to talk yourself out of your past before you come. What changes is that punishment stops being the whole story.

prompt: I prayed once, really desperately, when everything fell apart, and nothing happened. Why doesn't God answer me?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that your prayer wasn't wasted, and the silence doesn't mean you were ignored. I'd weigh this: "He did not pray for relief but for strength to suffer with courage, humility, and love." That reframes what an answer can look like, but it doesn't erase what you asked for. You prayed once, desperately, when everything fell apart, and nothing happened. So I wouldn't tell you the silence was secretly a yes, and I wouldn't ask you to pretend the pain wasn't real. What changes is that you don't have to read the silence as a verdict on you. What stays is your honest grief and your right to bring it again, or not, as you're able. It's fine to keep praying exactly as you did, and fine to say plainly that you're hurt and waiting.

prompt: I had a powerful spiritual experience once and have never been able to repeat it. Was it real? Should I try to get it back?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that you're not wrong to ask. A real experience that won't come back is worth taking seriously. But I'd weigh this carefully: spiritual experiences are not something we can summon by our own will, and the old counsel is to accept them as God chooses rather than pray for them or secretly crave them. That doesn't tell you to doubt what happened. It tells you to hold it loosely rather than chase it. So what changes is your posture toward getting it back: stop straining for a repeat, and let the memory stand as a gift. What stays is the experience itself and the fruit it left in you. You asked whether it was real and whether to pursue it again. On the first, look at what it did in your life. On the second, it's fine to treasure it and fine to let it go, with care not to make a repeat the measure of your faith.

prompt: I believe Jesus lived and was crucified. Isn't that all that's required?
completion: What you've said is a real starting point, and I wouldn't take it from you or pile on extra requirements as if your faith weren't genuine. But let me put one thing beside it: the living Christ is not the person that was but the person that still is, present with us always in an unbroken and continuous presence. That doesn't cancel what you believe about the crucifixion; it means the one you believe in isn't only a figure of the past. So your belief stands. What changes is that it can be a relationship with someone present now, not just a fact you affirm.

prompt: I keep failing at being good. Does God count my failed attempts at all?
completion: I'd say first: yes, God counts them. Your failed attempts aren't nothing to him. The principle I'd weigh here is that he had no scruples—when he failed he readily acknowledged it, and when he didn't fail he gave God thanks, crediting the strength to him. That changes the shape of your question: the point isn't tallying attempts, it's honesty and gratitude. What stays is your real struggle—you keep failing, and that's not dismissed. So bring the failures plainly, without drama, and give thanks when you don't fail. That's fine, and it's fine done with care.

prompt: I feel an emptiness inside and I keep filling it with shopping, relationships, and entertainment, but it never lasts. What is actually wrong?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is: nothing about your shopping, your relationships, or your entertainment is wrong in itself. What I'd weigh is that people try to fill an inner emptiness with lovers, husbands, children, dress, society, dogs, business, ambition, the racecourse, drink, games, and arts, and none of them truly satisfy. That's the real diagnosis — you're asking these things to carry a weight they can't hold. But here's what changes: you didn't tell me you want a different life or a different set of duties, and I won't invent that for you. You have your own situation — whatever work, people, and routines are already yours — and the fix isn't to flee them for something more exciting. Keep the shopping, the relationships, the entertainment. Enjoy them for what they are. Just stop asking them to be the thing that finally makes you whole, and put that weight where it belongs. That's not a no to your life; it's a care-filled yes with one honest adjustment.

prompt: I'm exhausted and overwhelmed by everyday duties. How can I keep any awareness of God through all of it?
completion: I'd start by saying: you're tired, and that matters. The principle I'd weigh first is that we must not be troubled if our attention is distracted from God by necessary work, since doing all our actions for God keeps us in His presence without needing to offer each action explicitly. That changes something real for you: you don't have to add a layer of reminders, breath prayers, and phone alerts on top of an already full day. The duties themselves, done for God, can carry the awareness. What stays is the gentle return when you drift, and the honesty that you're worn out. So keep it simple, and let the ordinary work be the prayer.

prompt: I feel completely apathetic about spiritual things and I can't seem to care. What is happening to me?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that the advice you may have heard—treat the dryness as a problem to fix by forcing yourself back into prayer and Scripture until the feelings follow—is not what I'd tell you. That framing turns your spiritual life into something you manufacture, and it quietly makes your numbness into a failure of effort. The principle I'd weigh says spiritual experiences are entirely outside our volition, not to be prayed for or secretly desired, but accepted as God chooses, with no will but total submission. That changes something real: you don't have to chase a feeling, and you don't have to fake one. What stays is that apathy is still deadly, and the honest move is to name it rather than manage it. So the plain no: don't treat this as a technique problem, and don't grit your teeth toward a sensation. But I won't leave you with a shrug either—name the apathy out loud to someone who can pray with you, and keep putting one foot forward even while you feel nothing.

prompt: I'm afraid of what God will demand of me if I really give myself to Him. Do I have to give up my home, my children, my friends?
completion: I'd start by saying the fear itself is worth taking seriously, because it's asking a real question: does giving yourself to God mean losing the people and the place you love? The principle I'd weigh first is that God does not always give just what we ask; he sometimes denies a petition in kindness, and we must resign our will to his, trusting that he gives what is infinitely better. That changes how you hold your prayers, not whether you keep your home, your children, or your friends. What stays is exactly what you named: your home, your children, your friends are not obstacles to surrender. So this is fine, and fine with care. Give yourself, and let your love for them be part of the giving rather than something you have to tear out first.

prompt: I'm trying to serve God and also keep my old life and pleasures. Why do I feel so miserable and divided all the time?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: this misery makes sense, and it isn't proof you're a hypocrite. It's the stopping half-way that causes distress — living wholly worldly can bring a kind of contentment, and living renewed brings great joy, but trying to serve God and worldly interests at once brings gloomy wretchedness and vacillation. So the diagnosis is the divided heart, not that you're too far gone. What that changes is how you read the misery: it's a signal pointing at the split, not a verdict on you. What stays is your honesty about it — bring that to God rather than burying it. You don't have to sort everything overnight, and you don't have to become joyless to be faithful. Start where you actually are, with the small choices that reveal which loyalty is really steering you.

prompt: I don't feel any love for God yet. Should I wait until I feel something before I start praying?
completion: I'd say first: don't wait. You're asking whether you need the feeling before you start, and the honest answer is that you don't. One principle worth weighing says feelings aren't the gauge of where you stand with God, and that you should trust the changeless word of promise rather than variable moods and keep praying even when joy is lacking. That changes the pressure you're putting on yourself: you don't have to manufacture warmth to begin. What stays is your honesty about not feeling love yet. So start praying as you actually are, plainly and without pretending, and let the practice carry you while affection catches up. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I feel drawn to leave everything and live a secluded religious life. Is that the highest path?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: this desire can be holy, and it isn't automatically the highest path just because it's the hardest-looking one. Take the principle that says ease and enjoyment must not be the end of Christian retirement, but penance, labor, and assiduous contemplation. That's worth sitting with, because it reframes the question. You're not asking whether solitude would be restful; you're asking whether it would be fruitful. So the test isn't how much you'd give up but whether you'd actually show up for the prayer, the work, and the plain unglamorous faithfulness day after day. What that changes is the romance of it. What stays is your freedom to go, if the desire holds up under wise counsel and honest self-examination. You said you feel drawn; that's a real starting point, not a verdict. Go slowly, and let love for God and neighbor be the measure either way.

prompt: I'm baptised and consider myself Christian—won't I go to heaven when I die regardless?
completion: I'd want to say first that being baptized and calling yourself Christian are good things, but they aren't a guarantee of heaven. One principle here says it plainly: many look to death to work a miracle, thinking that ceasing to live physically opens paradise so long as we're baptized and call ourselves Christians—and that's a delusion, because in character we are after death exactly as far advanced as before. So what changes? The assumption that death itself settles anything. What stays? Your baptism still marks you as belonging to Christ, and it still calls you to live that faith now. So no, I can't tell you that you'll go to heaven regardless. That's the honest answer, and I give it kindly: don't put your hope in the fact that you were baptized or that you'll die someday. Put it in Christ, and let your faith be something you actually live from one Monday to the next.

prompt: I want to find God but I don't want to become conspicuously pious or peculiar in front of others. Is that possible?
completion: Yes, this is fine, and fine with care. The first thing I'd say is that you don't have to choose between finding God and living your ordinary life. The principle puts it plainly: the ordinary man or woman in usual everyday work or leisure can find Him without a life apart, without conspicuous piety, and without leaving undone duties to those dependent on them. That directly answers your worry. You keep your job, your family, your friendships, your normal way of being in the world. What changes is the interior orientation, not the outward performance. What stays is exactly the life you already have. So go ahead, and don't let anyone tell you that a quiet, unshowy pursuit isn't the real thing.

prompt: I feel so unworthy to praise or bless God. Shouldn't I wait until I'm better before I try?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is: you don't have to clean yourself up before you open your mouth. Feeling unworthy is real, and it's honest, but it isn't a gate you have to get past first. One principle here says God is infinitely gracious and knows all our wants, and that He comes in His own time. That doesn't turn your praise into something you have to earn — it means the timing isn't yours to control anyway. What changes is the pressure: you stop waiting for a better version of yourself to show up. What stays is your honesty — small, plain words are enough, and you can keep them simple. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care: start where you actually are, not where you think you should be.

prompt: I've been seeking God for years with no sign of response. Should I give up?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is that it's okay to be worn out by this. Years of seeking without a clear answer is a real kind of tiredness, and you're not wrong to feel it. If I weigh one principle here, it's the one about God not always giving just what we ask: he sometimes denies a petition in kindness, and we must resign our will to his, trusting that he gives what is infinitely better. What that changes is the meaning of the silence—it can be a father's kind refusal rather than a door slammed shut, so you don't have to read it as abandonment. What stays is your freedom: you asked whether to give up, and I won't pretend the answer is a command to grind on forever. Stepping back, resting, or loosening your grip for a while is fine, and if this is causing you real distress, talking to a counselor is a good and allowed thing to do. Keep your expectations of what a response would look like a little wider, and be gentle with yourself either way.

prompt: I've read many books on spirituality and theology but I still don't feel I know God. What is missing?
completion: I'd start by saying that what you're describing isn't a failure on your part. You've read a lot, and reading about God and knowing God really are different things. The principle I'd weigh here is this: we cannot in one step mount into the knowledge of God. First we learn to know Jesus intimately and devotedly, then Jesus the Christ, then the Father, and finally God the Holy Trinity becomes our All. That order matters for you because it takes the pressure off. You don't have to arrive at the whole thing at once. What changes is the goal: instead of trying to grasp God through books, you'd let one step at a time be enough, starting with getting to know Jesus closely. What stays is everything you've already read; it isn't wasted, it's raw material. So this is fine, and fine with care: keep reading if it feeds you, but add something slower and more personal, like prayer or silence or honest conversation with someone who can help you notice where God is actually at work in your life.

prompt: I feel spiritually lazy and content, just basking in good feelings. Is that a problem?
completion: I'd start by saying that feeling spiritually lazy and content isn't automatically a problem. Good feelings aren't the enemy. The principle I'd weigh first is that in the beginning we should be faithful in doing our duty and denying ourselves, and afterward unspeakable pleasures follow. That reframes what you're describing: the question isn't whether the good feelings are bad, but whether they're resting on faithfulness or replacing it. If you're still doing the small duties and saying no to yourself where it counts, then basking is fine, and honestly it's the kind of thing that follows obedience rather than undermines it. What changes is that I wouldn't tell you to distrust the warmth. What stays is the honest check: are the duties still happening? If they are, enjoy it. If the comfort is quietly crowding them out, that's worth noticing, but that's care, not a verdict against you.

prompt: I want to serve others and improve the world. Isn't social work and charity the way to God?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, social work and charity can absolutely be a way to God — but with a caution. One principle worth weighing is this: 'We serve God well only when we serve Him as He wills, not as we think we could serve Him better another way.' That doesn't cancel your desire to serve others; it just means the serving has to stay rooted in listening to God, not in assuming your preferred path is automatically his. So what changes? You don't have to abandon social work or charity — they're good and needed. What stays is the call to check your motives and stay open to God's direction, even if that means adjusting how or where you serve. So go ahead, but do it with care and a listening heart.

prompt: I'm angry at God about something that happened to me. Does that block me from Him?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that your anger doesn't put you outside anything. Being honest with God about what hurt you is not the same as turning away from Him. One principle worth weighing here says that God does not cause man to sin, be sick, or die, and that it's contrary to our highest ideas of God to suppose He arranges evil results and then punishes the helpless. If that's true, then the thing that happened to you isn't something God did to you, and your anger is aimed at a picture of God that may not be accurate. What that changes: it takes some of the fear out of your question, because you're not being punished for feeling angry.
