What stays: the hurt is real, and the anger is real, and it still needs somewhere to go. Bring it to Him honestly rather than letting it harden into bitterness, and talk to someone you trust about what happened.

prompt: My spouse is not spiritual and my friends think I'm becoming strange. How do I deal with the loneliness of this path?
completion: What I'd say first is that this loneliness is real, and it doesn't mean you're doing something wrong. On the marriage piece, I'd weigh this: husbands and wives should not separate if there is no Christian demand for it; mutual compromises, tender solicitude, and patience maintain the union. That doesn't tell you to hide your inner life or pretend, and it doesn't ask you to drag your spouse along. It means the patience runs one direction for now, toward staying kind and close in ordinary ways while you carry this yourself. What changes is that you stop treating your spouse's distance as a verdict on the marriage. What stays is your need for people who get it, so keep finding that community, and keep your friends who mock you at arm's length without writing them off.

prompt: How do I respond when someone asks me why God saved me and not others who were killed?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that you don't owe anyone a tidy explanation, and you're allowed to say plainly that you don't know why you were spared. That's honest, and it's kinder than a theory. One of the principles here says that when we've drifted from God we shouldn't tie ourselves in knots about it, but should acknowledge our need and come back to him with more trust. That fits this question: the mystery of why you lived doesn't have to be solved for your answer to be faithful. What it changes is the pressure to justify yourself or hint that you deserved it. What stays is the grief, the real absence of an answer, and the freedom to point to Christ who shares our death and promises resurrection. So it's fine, with care: be honest, don't rank yourself above the dead, and let gratitude and service carry part of what words can't.

prompt: How do I find the fulness of the Holy Spirit in my life?
completion: I'd start by saying: this is a good thing to want, and you can go after it with confidence. The principle I'd weigh first is that the Spirit is a divine Person, the Paraclete, Christ's other self, who came at Pentecost to dwell in the church as his successor and vicar. That means you're not chasing a force or a mood—you're asking a Person to make himself at home in you, and he's already committed to that. So pray and ask him to fill you, read Scripture with an open heart, worship, obey what you sense him prompting, and confess sin quickly rather than letting it pile up. What that changes is the tone: it's relational, not a technique to master. What stays is your own situation—if you've been hurt by church structures or feel burned out on institutions, you don't have to force yourself back into them to find him; he's not confined to a building. Take the gradual path, expect character to grow over time, and be patient with yourself.

prompt: I've been praying for a family member's salvation for years. Should I keep going?
completion: I'd say first: yes, keep praying. That's fine, and it's fine with care. One principle I'd weigh is that prayer should be our main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, and that we should pray for God to help us search out our own hearts and reform what's amiss in them. What that changes: some of your praying for your family member can turn toward your own heart too, so the years of waiting don't just wear you down. What stays: you keep bringing this person before God, honestly, for as long as you want to. You've named no limits here, so I won't invent any. Keep going, and let the praying do its work in you as well.

prompt: Is it wrong to plan my own life instead of leaving it open to God's leading?
completion: I'd start by saying that planning your own life is not the problem. The principle I'd weigh here is that God's commands always imply promises, and the ideal of walking worthy of the Lord is not put before you unless it can be realized by grace. That tells me God isn't asking you to drift and call it trust. He's asking you to walk, and walking involves choosing a direction. What that changes is the fear that making plans is somehow a lack of faith. What stays is the posture: hold your plans with an open hand, pray over them, and be willing to turn if He prompts you. So plan, and plan prayerfully. That's fine, and it's fine with care.

prompt: How do I find the right person to care for my children when I have to travel for ministry?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that this is a fine thing to be thinking through carefully, and there's no reason you shouldn't look for a good caregiver. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about bringing every matter, great and small, before the Lord in prayer, taking no step without first asking counsel of the Scriptures and seeking guidance, and waiting until the will of God is clear. That changes the tone of your search: it means you don't have to rush a decision out of anxiety, and you can pray specifically about the hours, the duties, and the person. What stays is everything practical you already know you need — asking trusted friends and church members for recommendations, interviewing people, checking references, and making sure the caregiver shares your values and treats your children well. You're traveling for ministry, not abandoning your kids, and seeking God's guidance alongside a careful search is exactly the right posture.

prompt: Is it right to give away my best workers when other missionaries ask for them?
completion: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it for me is this: believers should be transparent with fellow laborers in the work, sharing the knowledge of needs so that they may share in prayers, faith, and reward. That means when another missionary asks for one of your best workers, the honest move is to talk plainly with them about what you actually need and what you can actually spare, rather than quietly hoarding or quietly resenting the ask. What that changes is the tone of the whole thing: it becomes a conversation among fellow laborers, not a tug-of-war over scarce goods. What stays is your own stated limit, that your work can't collapse, and that the worker is a person with a calling, not a piece of equipment to hand over. So release when you can spare someone, decline or offer another when you can't, and keep the worker free to say what they sense God is asking of them.

prompt: My husband and I disagree about trusting God for our finances. How should I respond?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that this is a fine thing to work through together, and it's fine with care. One principle worth weighing in its own words: God is the one living Agent who works, and human workers are only instruments, so all care and anxiety on our part is distrust of Him. That reframes the argument—neither of you is the one holding your finances together, so the question isn't whose plan wins but how you both stop gripping so hard. What that changes is the tone: less debate about who trusts God more, more honesty about where each of you feels afraid. What stays is everything practical—you still need a budget, still need to talk calmly, still may need a pastor or advisor. Your limits are real: you disagree, it's stressful, and you don't have to resolve it in one conversation. Keep listening to your husband without judgment and share your concerns plainly.

prompt: I'm afraid to go where God is leading because of the risk to my family. What should I do?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is: your fear for your family is not a failure of faith. It's love, and love counts the cost. So I wouldn't rush you past it. Weigh this: God's protection in danger is real, and you can commit yourself and your family to His keeping, finding His Word sweet in times of peril. That doesn't mean the risk disappears or that you skip wise precautions. What it changes is who holds the outcome. What stays is your responsibility to pray together, seek counsel, and make real provision for the people in your care. Going where God leads is fine here, and fine with care, taken one honest step at a time.

prompt: How do I handle it when the home church tells us to retrench and cut back the work?
completion: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh first is the one about being meekly and mightily fastened to our Mother Holy Church, since the whole Body was never broken even when a single person often is. That changes how you carry the disappointment: you don't treat the cutback as a betrayal or start something on your own to keep the work alive. What stays is your honest grief and your questions, and the freedom to ask leadership what they're seeing. Stay fastened, stay humble, and let the decision be theirs to make.

prompt: What does it mean to rest in Christ instead of struggling on my own?
completion: I'd start by saying that resting in Christ isn't the same as doing nothing, and your question already assumes that. Take the first principle on its own terms: the real secret of perfect rest is to be jealously, habitually occupied with Jesus, and failure often comes over a trifling thought or word. That's worth weighing, but notice what it doesn't ask of you. It doesn't ask you to police every stray thought until you're exhausted, which would just be struggling on your own under a different name. What it changes is the direction of your attention: instead of white-knuckling your own effort, you keep turning back toward Him, even after a small distraction. What stays is the ordinary stuff you mentioned, prayer, Scripture, fellowship, and the honest work of daily life. So this is fine, and fine with care. Rest is trust, not strain.

prompt: I prayed for a specific sign from God about a decision. Is that acceptable?
completion: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh first is the one about watching our prayers as well as their answers, using the light God has already given rather than demanding signs. That principle doesn't forbid asking for a sign; it warns against treating a sign as something God owes you or using it to dodge a decision you could already make. So what changes is the posture: you can bring your specific request honestly, but hold it loosely and keep acting on the Scripture, counsel, and plain good sense you already have. What stays is your freedom to ask. You said this is about a real decision, so the practical test is simple: if no sign comes, will you still move forward with the wisdom in front of you? If yes, your prayer is in good shape.

prompt: How do I pray when I'm in danger and afraid for my life?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: pray right now, however you can, and don't worry about getting the words right. One of the principles here puts it well — 'a little lifting up of the heart suffices; a little remembrance of God, one act of inward worship, though upon a march and a sword in hand, are prayers very acceptable to God and serve to fortify courage in danger.' That fits your situation exactly: you're not in a quiet room with time to compose yourself, you're afraid for your life. So a short cry — 'Lord, help me,' 'Lord Jesus, have mercy' — is a real prayer, not a lesser one. What that changes is the pressure to pray at length or in a certain form; what stays is that you can turn to God honestly in the middle of the fear. Keep it simple, keep it short, keep doing it as long as the danger lasts.

prompt: Should I take a job or a position that keeps me from the mission field?
completion: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh first is that we must not desire another vocation or another kind of service, since nothing prevents attaining the perfection of our vocation like desiring another. That doesn't tell you the mission field is off-limits or that a job is second-best; it tells you not to let a longing for a different field hollow out the one you're actually in. So the question shifts: does this position truly shut the door, or does it just make mission involvement less convenient and less glamorous? You've said it keeps you from the mission field, and I'll take that at face value as a real limit, not something to wave away. What changes is the guilt — taking the job isn't a betrayal if you serve God honestly in it. What stays is your calling to witness, give, pray, and stay open if a door reopens. What also stays is your duty to care for your own life and responsibilities, which a paycheck may serve. So take it, with care, and don't let the desire for another field sour the one you're in.

prompt: How do I know whether an answer to prayer was really from God or just happened anyway?
completion: I'd start by saying this is a fair question, and you don't have to resolve it before you keep praying. The principle I'd weigh first is the one about answers depending on meeting conditions the Bible records—contrite humility, forsaking sin, faith, obedience, asking according to God's will. That's worth taking seriously, but notice what it does and doesn't do. It tells you to examine your own heart and ask whether you're asking rightly; it doesn't hand you a test that sorts events into 'from God' and 'just happened.' So what changes is your focus—less on auditing the outcome, more on the honesty of the asking. What stays is your original instinct: keep a record, notice fruit like gratitude and humility, ask trusted people, and hold it loosely. You're allowed to live with some uncertainty here.

prompt: I'm afraid of dying and of the suffering that might come before death. How do I find peace?
completion: What I'd say first is that your fear is not a failure, and you don't have to get rid of it to find peace. The principle I'd weigh here says we should be at peace always, since peace is the passport of the daughters of Jesus Christ, and patience with others must be matched by patience with ourselves. That last part matters most for you: patience with yourself. It changes the goal from erasing fear to meeting it gently, day by day, without scolding yourself for feeling it. What stays is that peace is still the aim, and that it's fine to pursue it with care—through breathing, prayer, trusted people, and professional help if the fear gets heavy. You asked how to find peace, and this is fine, done gently.

prompt: I prayed for something and God gave me something different and better. How should I understand that?
completion: What I'd say first is that this is fine, and it's worth sitting with rather than rushing past. The principle I'd weigh is that prayer is an absolute faith that all things are possible to God, a spiritual understanding of Him, and an unselfed love; it doesn't inform or change God but brings us into harmony with the unchangeable divine Principle. Read that way, your experience makes sense: you didn't talk God into a different answer, and nothing in God shifted. What changed was your alignment with what was already true. So the 'different and better' gift isn't a sign that your first request was wrong or that you earned an upgrade. It's an invitation to trust the giver more than the wording of the request. What stays is your honest asking, which was real and good. What changes is how tightly you hold the specific outcome. Keep your limits in view here: you prayed for something particular, and you're allowed to grieve the thing you didn't get even while you're grateful for what came. Both can be true at once.

prompt: I prayed for something for three years and God never gave it to me—does that mean my prayers don't work?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that three years of praying is not nothing, and the fact that you didn't get what you asked for doesn't mean your prayers are broken. I'd weigh this principle: prayer is 'an absolute faith that all things are possible to God, a spiritual understanding of Him, and an unselfed love' — and notice what it says prayer does not do. It doesn't inform God or change God's mind. So the question 'do my prayers work' is quietly asking prayer to be a lever, and that's the part I'd gently set down. What changes is the scorekeeping: no answer arriving isn't a failed transaction. What stays is your desire, honestly held, and the fact that you're still talking to God after three years. That's not a malfunction. Keep praying, and keep the disappointment in the conversation too.

prompt: I'm a missionary and I feel like a failure at learning the language. Should I give up?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: don't give up. Feeling like a failure at language learning is common, and it doesn't mean you should quit. One principle worth weighing here is that missionaries must have their own testimony and teach with simplicity and humility rather than oratory or contention. That changes how you study and speak, not whether you keep going: you're not trying to impress anyone with fluent speeches, just to speak plainly and humbly. What stays is that language learning takes years and progress often feels invisible before it becomes real. So give yourself permission to be a beginner, set small steady goals, find a patient tutor, and celebrate modest wins. Your worth and calling don't rest on fluency. Rest when you need to, lean on colleagues who've walked this road, and if health or circumstances genuinely block progress, reassessing isn't failure. Before quitting, ask whether you're discouraged rather than truly blocked. Keep going gently.

prompt: I feel guilty that I prayed for my child's healing and she died. Did I do something wrong?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is that praying for your child's healing was not wrong. You asked out of love for her, not out of selfish or earthly motives—you weren't praying for your own comfort, you were praying for her life. One principle worth weighing says many pray and don't receive because they ask amiss, out of selfish and earthly motives, as when parents pray for children merely for their own comfort rather than for God's glory. That principle is about prayers bent toward our own convenience, and yours wasn't that. So the guilt you're carrying doesn't fit the facts. What stays is that her death is not a punishment for a faulty prayer, and what changes is the story you're telling yourself that your prayer somehow caused this. Be gentle with yourself, let people support you, and if the guilt keeps pressing hard, talk with a pastor or counselor.

prompt: Should I be praying for converts from the very beginning of a work?
completion: I'd have said yes right away, and I'd still say it: pray for converts from the very beginning. What I'd weigh is this line — no conversion ever takes place save by the almighty power of the Holy Ghost, and the great need of every worker is to know God. That changes the ground you stand on when you pray: you're not asking God to bless your technique, you're asking him to do what only he can do, and to make himself known to you while he does it. What stays is the timing — you start on day one, not once the work is up and running. Nothing in what you've described gives me a reason to hold back.

prompt: I keep failing to meet the conditions for answered prayer. Does that mean God has rejected me?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say to you is this: failing to meet conditions doesn't mean God has turned away from you, and it doesn't mean you're rejected. But I'd also weigh one principle carefully, in its own words: answers to prayer depend on meeting Bible-recorded conditions, including contrite humility and forsaking sin, seeking God wholeheartedly, faith, obedience, and asking according to his will. That's real, and it's worth examining honestly. What it changes is that prayer isn't automatic, and you can look at your heart and your life with God about those things. What stays is this: your standing with God isn't measured by whether every condition is perfectly met, and it certainly isn't measured by your moods. So keep praying, confess what needs confessing, and don't read your struggle as rejection.

prompt: Can God heal someone today the way he did in Bible times?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, God can heal today, and I wouldn't want to fence that in. The principle I keep coming back to is that Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever, so healing isn't locked in the past. That changes how I'd pray with you: I'd pray expecting God to act, not just asking him to make us peaceful about being sick. What stays is that the outcome is genuinely in God's hands, and a no isn't a failure of your faith. So pray boldly, keep using the doctors, and leave the result with him.

prompt: How can I trust God with my children's safety when I feel called to a dangerous place?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that your fear isn't a failure of faith—it's the shape love takes when you're responsible for small, vulnerable people. So let me weigh one principle honestly: "the safest place for oneself and one's children is the path of duty; God must come first, and one can safely trust children to him wherever he leads." I think that's true in its core, but it's often used too quickly, as if trusting God cancels prudence. It doesn't. What it changes is this: you don't have to treat safety as the ultimate god, and you can hold the call seriously even when it frightens you. What stays is everything you already know—your children are entrusted to you, not discarded by you, and the danger being real means safeguards, timing, and wise counsel still matter. So go, if you're truly called, but go with care: go first alone, arrange trustworthy care, test the call in community. That's not unbelief. That's faith with its eyes open.

prompt: I feel ashamed of my lack of faith when I see how God has provided in the past. How do I grow?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is: don't let the shame sit on you. The principle I'd weigh here is that when you haven't thought of God for a while, you shouldn't disquiet yourself—just acknowledge your wretchedness and return to Him with greater trust. That reframes your shame as a nudge back toward God rather than a verdict against you. What changes is the tone of your growth: you're not trying to punish yourself into more faith, you're turning around and leaning in. What stays is the real work—reflecting on how God has provided, thanking Him for it, and stepping out in small trusts. You asked how to grow, and that's fine, with care: let the remembering feed trust, not self-scolding.

prompt: Should I tell others about the specific answers to prayer in my life, even the very personal ones?
completion: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh first is the one about prayer being unselfish and full of sympathy—that intercession for others is the heart of prayer, and that our own blessings grow as we pray for others. What that changes is the frame around your question: the real question isn't only whether to tell, but whether the answer you'd tell about was ever sought with others in view, or just for yourself. That reframes your motive without forbidding anything. What stays is exactly what you said: some answers are very personal, and you get to keep those between you and God, or share them with one trusted person. So tell the ones that would lift someone's eyes to God, keep the intimate ones where they belong, and let humility, not a rule, decide.

prompt: How do I teach my children to trust God when we live in hard conditions?
completion: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh first is that children should be educated spiritually and formed in obedience to moral and spiritual law, and that they should be allowed to remain children in knowledge rather than indulged into fretfulness and frivolity. That's the one that actually speaks to your situation. It changes the tone of what you teach: keep the moral and spiritual basics clear and steady, but don't load a small child with adult-sized weight. What stays is the heart of your instinct, that trust is caught more than taught, so let them see you bring worries to God honestly and keep doing the next right thing. Answer their questions truthfully without pretending hard things are nothing, keep simple routines of prayer and gratitude, and let them be children while they learn. That's care, not pressure.

prompt: How do I deal with the fear that my children will get sick in unsanitary conditions?
completion: I'd start by saying your fear makes sense, and nothing here needs to be refused. Take the principle that says the sick are not helpless victims, that a person can resist disease and ward it off as positively as they can resist temptation to sin. That changes the tone of the thing: instead of hovering over your kids as if illness is fate, you teach them that clean hands, safe food and water, and steady habits are something they can actively do. What stays is everything you actually asked about: keep the practical steps, keep vaccinations current, see a doctor when something appears, and don't let the fear run your household. What also stays is your limit, that you're not looking to hand your children's safety over to fate or to anyone else's say-so. So this is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I'm worried about my son who is going off to war. Can I pray for his protection?
completion: I'd say first: yes, of course you can pray for your son's protection. Nothing about your fear disqualifies the prayer. One principle worth weighing says that "a little lifting up of the heart suffices"—that a brief, inward turning toward God, even in the middle of a march with a sword in hand, is a prayer he accepts and that it steadies a person's courage in danger. That's a comfort here: you don't need long, polished prayers, and neither does your son. A short, honest plea for his safety counts. What that changes is the pressure to pray perfectly or at length; what stays is the simple fact that your prayer is welcome. Keep praying in whatever moments you have, and take care of yourself too.

prompt: Is it wrong to ask God for small, everyday things like a hat or a coat?
completion: I'd say right off: no, it's not wrong. Nothing is too great for God's power and nothing too small for his love, and that's the principle I'd weigh here. If he cares about the trimming of a hat, then a hat or a coat is not beneath his attention. What that changes is the worry that small requests are somehow beneath God or a sign of weak faith. What stays is this: asking doesn't mean he hands over exactly what you name. He may say no in kindness, and trusting his wisdom is part of the asking. So bring the hat, the coat, the ordinary stuff freely, and leave the answer with him.

prompt: I'm afraid to speak in public and my voice fails me. Can God help me?
completion: I'd say yes, and it's fine with care. Take the principle that says talking to God for men is greater than talking to men for God: if you've never learned to talk to God for the people you'll be speaking to, you won't talk well to them for God. That changes the center of gravity — your fear of the room gets answered first by turning toward God on behalf of the room, not by hunting for a technique. What stays is everything you told me: the fear is real, and your voice actually fails. So this is fine with care — pray for the people you'll speak to, prepare simply, speak so you can be heard and understood, and if your voice goes, pause and breathe rather than force it. Nothing here asks you to pretend the fear isn't there.

prompt: I want to serve God but I have no money and no help. Can I still go forward?
completion: I'd start by saying: yes, you can go forward, and the fact that you have no money and no help doesn't shut the door. The principle I'd weigh first is that the Lord's people should be willing in the day of His power to offer themselves and their substance for His work without salary, trusting God to supply their needs. That doesn't mean you should be careless with real obligations, and it doesn't mean money and help don't matter. What it changes is the idea that you have to wait until you're comfortable before you can serve. What stays is your actual situation: no money, no help. So go forward with what you do have, your time and willingness, and keep your duties to anyone who depends on you. That's fine, and it's fine with care.

prompt: I feel God is calling me to a life of prayer and obedience, but I'm afraid of what it will cost. What should I do?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: your fear doesn't disqualify you, and it doesn't need to be argued away before you start. I'd weigh this principle: prayer is a duty and a privilege to be performed at set times whether or not one feels like it. That changes something real — it means you don't have to wait for the fear to lift or for a clear picture of the whole cost before you begin. You can set a fixed time, keep it, and let faithfulness carry you on the days you feel nothing. What stays is exactly what you named: the cost is real, and I'm not going to pretend it isn't. So keep it small and concrete, be honest with God about the fear, and talk with a pastor or a trusted friend who can help you see the next step. You don't need the whole road mapped out — just the next faithful one.

prompt: What should I do when I'm too exhausted to pray?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: you're not failing at prayer, you're exhausted, and those are different things. So the principle I'd weigh is the one about holding yourself before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate — just keeping your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, not disquieting yourself, because trouble and disquiet distract rather than recollect. What that changes is the pressure to produce words. You don't have to. Sitting there half-asleep, bringing your wandering attention back gently, is prayer. What stays is that you're still turning toward God rather than away — but that turning can be wordless and small. So this is fine, and fine with care: rest, be quiet, let a short honest sentence be enough.

prompt: How do I know God's will when two paths lie before me and I can't decide?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: you're not doing anything wrong by standing there with two good paths and no clear sign. That's not a failure of faith. The principle I'd weigh is that the will is mistress of all our faculties and must recall them and carry them to God as their last end. Notice what that does and doesn't do. It doesn't promise you a decoded answer before you move. It says your mind will rove endlessly between the two options unless your will gathers it up and turns the whole thing toward God. So the roving isn't the sin; letting it run unsupervised is just exhausting. What changes: you stop waiting for your mind to settle it and instead decide to aim the choice at God, then gather the facts, ask wise people, and check your motives honestly. What stays: you still have to choose, and you may never get certainty. That's fine. If both paths are morally good, you have real freedom here, so decide prayerfully and don't paralyze yourself.

prompt: How can I help someone who is bound by an addiction that they can't break?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: yes, you can help, and it's good that you want to. But I'd start with the principle that says if you're yourself lost in the belief and fear of disease or sin, and knowing the remedy fail to use it for yourself, you can exercise little or no power for others' help. That doesn't mean you have to be perfect before you lift a finger. It means check your own fear and your own habits first, because a helper who's panicking or secretly contemptuous transmits that. What that changes: you lead with your own honesty and calm, not with a rescue plan. What stays: everything practical you already thought of, encouraging real treatment, offering to help find resources, setting boundaries so you don't get consumed, being patient, and accepting that you can't force anyone to change. So this is fine, and fine with care. Keep your limits, protect your own life, and be a steady presence rather than a fixer.

prompt: How do I deal with the criticism of others about how I dress as a missionary?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is: this is fine, and it's fine with care. The principle I'd weigh here is that a missionary shouldn't pull down their predecessors but should speak of them as brothers and sisters who did the best they knew, and should invite rather than compel. That changes how you handle the critic. If someone's criticism is really about the people who came before you, you don't need to defend yourself by running them down. You can say a good word about them and still make your own choices. What stays is your freedom to dress as you see fit where it's just preference, and your willingness to adjust where there's a real question of fitting in or giving offense. You're not compelled to win the argument, and you don't have to compel anyone else either.

prompt: How do I know if a burden to pray for someone far away is really from God?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: bring the burden itself to God and ask Him plainly whether it's from Him. That's not a dodge, it's the actual answer, because nothing is too small to hand over to Him, and taking even a small impression out of His hands is the wrong move. So weigh that: you honour God by asking His guidance in small things. What that changes is that you don't have to settle this by your own analysis first; what stays is the testing, by Scripture and by the counsel of mature believers, and the honest check on whether the burden moves you toward God's glory and the good of the person far away rather than toward your own comfort. You can pray in faith, nothing wavering, and trust that He understands your innermost thoughts even when the person is far off. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care: keep bringing each impression to Him rather than deciding it alone.

prompt: My child is very sick and the doctors say there is no hope—should I keep praying for healing?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: keep praying. You're not doing anything wrong by asking God for your child's healing, and you don't need to feel guilty about it. One principle worth weighing here says God can heal in answer to prayer, especially when doctors have done all in their power. That doesn't promise you a particular outcome, and it doesn't ask you to pretend the doctors are wrong. What it changes is this: your praying isn't futile or naive, even now. What stays is everything you told me—the doctors' prognosis, your fear, the possibility that healing doesn't come. So pray, and also hold your child, accept help, and let people be with you. If asking for healing gives you strength, keep asking.

prompt: I lost something important and I'm panicking—should I pray about it?
completion: I'd say first: yes, pray—right now, before you do anything else. One principle I'd weigh is this: 'we cannot pray without being with Him, cannot be with Him but by thinking of Him often.' That's not a demand to be saintly in the middle of a panic; it's a reminder that prayer is company, not a technique. What it changes: you don't need polished words or a calm heart to start—just turn toward Him mid-panic. What stays: you're still panicking, and that's okay; the practical steps still matter, so retrace your steps, check the usual places, ask someone to help you look. Prayer and searching aren't rivals. So yes, it's fine—pray, and let it steady you while you look.

prompt: I'm overwhelmed by the work before me and I don't have enough helpers. What do I do?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: you're not failing by feeling overwhelmed. The load is real, and the helpers aren't there. So let's take the principle seriously — "doing everything for the love of God with prayer upon all occasions for His grace to do the work well makes even naturally aversive work easy." What that changes is the spirit you carry the work in: pray before you start, do the next task as something offered rather than something crushing you. What stays is everything you told me — the work is still too much, and the helpers are still too few. So alongside that, triage honestly: what must happen, what can wait, what can be dropped, and who specifically you can ask for concrete help. Rest matters too; exhaustion makes everything look impossible. This is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: Should I keep a record of the times God answers my prayers?
completion: I'd say yes, go ahead and keep that record. The principle that stands out to me is this: a testimony of what God has actually done strengthens faith, so recounting and writing down definite answers to prayer honors God and helps people who doubt. That fits what you're describing. What it changes is the purpose: the record isn't a scorecard or a way to twist God's arm, it's a witness. What stays is your own good sense about keeping it private where it needs to be and not turning it into something you obsess over. So keep it, and keep it as worship.

prompt: I have bitterness toward someone who wronged me and I can't forgive them. Will that affect my prayers?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that your bitterness is real and it's not a small thing, so I'm not going to brush past it. Here's the principle I'd weigh: forgiveness is not a gift falling from the skies in return for a request; it is an inward condition that can come only to a forgiving spirit, and the blessing depends on us as much as on God. What that changes is this: your prayers aren't being blocked by a God who's keeping score and waiting for you to say the right words. The blockage, if there is one, is in your own spirit, and that's something you can actually work on with God's help. What stays is that the bitterness does affect your communion with God, and forgiveness is a process, not a switch you flip. You told me you can't forgive right now. That's honest, and it's where you are. So keep praying, ask for a heart that's willing even if it isn't able yet, and don't pretend the wrong didn't happen. That's fine, and it's fine with care.

prompt: How do I know God will provide a home for us when we have nowhere to go?
completion: I'd start by saying I'm sorry you're in this spot, and I don't think there's anything wrong with asking the question. One principle I'd weigh is that God supplies all our need, often through unexpected and timely gifts from others, and that man's extremity is God's opportunity. What that changes is the shape of the answer: you don't have to force certainty about a specific house or timeline, because provision often arrives through people and timing you can't predict. What stays is your honest fear and your practical next steps, like calling churches and local organizations. So it's fine to hold hope and ask, as long as you're not treating the question as a guarantee you can pin down.

prompt: How do I deal with the temptation to take pride in a successful sermon or talk?
completion: I'd start by saying this is a fine thing to work on, and you're not doing anything wrong by noticing it. Take the principle that says God permits evil inclinations and temptations to make us humble. That reframes the whole thing: the temptation itself isn't the failure. What matters is that it stays displeasing to you. So when pride shows up after a talk that went well, you don't have to panic or flagellate yourself. Despise the temptation, but don't be crushed by it. What changes is the tone of your response: less shame, more honest prayer. What stays is your instinct to take it seriously, which is good. Keep doing what you're already doing, noticing it and turning it over, and let it push you toward prayer rather than toward self-punishment.

prompt: I've struggled with the same sin for years and keep failing. Is victory over sin really possible for me?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that yes, victory is possible for you — and I'd say it before anything else, because you asked a real question and deserve a real answer. The principle I'd weigh here is this one: the secret of victory is Christ himself indwelling the believer, and the life of victory is summed up in resting in him. That changes the shape of the answer: it means the years of failing don't disqualify you, and it means the fix isn't a bigger effort. What stays is your honesty about how long this has gone on — I'm not going to pretend that's nothing. But resting in him isn't a loophole, and it isn't passivity either; it's dependence. So this is fine, and fine with care: keep bringing the actual sin into the light with someone who can walk with you, and don't treat 'resting' as a reason to stop fighting. But no, your struggle doesn't put victory out of reach.

prompt: How do I deal with fear when I'm facing a mob or real danger?
completion: I'd start by saying: fear in the face of a mob or real danger is not a failure, and the first thing I'd tell you is to get to safety and use your judgment. One principle worth weighing is that God tenderly comforts our fears, saying 'It is I, be not afraid'; He is the antidote to fear and the substance of deliverance, so we should keep our eyes fastened on Him. That changes the inner ground you stand on, but it doesn't cancel the practical steps, the caution, or the limits you set. So keep your eyes on Him and still take the sensible precautions you already know to take.

prompt: Is it right to ask God for money when our mission funds are low?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, it's fine to ask God for money when your mission funds run low. Scripture itself teaches us to pray for daily bread, so bringing a real need to God isn't out of line. One principle worth weighing is that if there were a lack of funds to carry on the work, then to that degree, in that development, or at that time, it could not be the work of God. That's a serious thought, and it should make you pause and ask whether this particular shortfall is a sign to stop, wait, or rethink. But it doesn't forbid prayer. What it changes is the confidence with which you assume the work must continue exactly as planned. What stays is this: you can still ask, honestly and with an open hand, and you can still seek wise counsel and steward what you already have. Asking isn't the problem; assuming is.

prompt: I was criticized by someone who said I don't live as I preach. How do I change?
completion: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. Your question is honest, and wanting to close the gap between what you say and how you live is a good thing to want. One principle I'd weigh says that when a chance to practice some virtue comes along, you should say to God, 'Lord, I cannot do this unless you enable me,' and then strength more than sufficient is given. That changes how you approach the change: you're not white-knuckling your way to consistency, you're asking for help and trusting it's there. What stays is the practical part—don't get defensive, ask the person what they actually saw, pick one real thing and start on it. Keep it modest and specific, and don't let this turn into a project of proving yourself to anyone.

prompt: I feel like God is silent and I haven't seen an answer to prayer in months. What's wrong?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that nothing here sounds like something you need to be refused or corrected for. Feeling like God is silent for months is a heavy place to be, and it doesn't mean you've done something wrong. One principle worth weighing says prayer is humbling work that abases intellect and pride and signs our spiritual bankruptcy, and that human nature resists it. That's honest about how hard prayer can feel, but notice it doesn't say dryness is a verdict on you. What that changes is this: the flatness you're feeling may be part of the work itself, not evidence of failure. What stays is exactly what you said, months without a clear answer, and I won't pretend that's easy or explain it away. Keep talking to God, and let someone you trust pray alongside you.

prompt: Is Christ's presence in my heart just a feeling or an idea, or something more?
completion: I'd start by saying the question itself is a good one, because it takes seriously that Christ's presence isn't just a mood or a mental picture. One principle I'd weigh is that Christ bids us live in an atmosphere of love, believing He ever loves us and claiming His approval, rather than living in thought, sensuality, or mere duty. That reframes your either/or: the presence is a relationship you trust and rest in, not a sensation you chase and not a concept you file away. What that changes is that you stop grading your days by how strongly you feel Him. What stays is your honest experience, including the flat, numb stretches, which don't cancel His love. So it's fine to hold this as more than feeling and more than idea, and fine with care, as long as you don't turn inward monitoring into the whole thing.

prompt: Does the coming of Christ have any real bearing on how I live day to day?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, it does, and then be careful about what kind of bearing it has. The principle I'd weigh is that the Christian life is a life of hope: the vision of the future keeps hope alive, showing the Lamb upon the throne without helping us calculate times and seasons. That changes how you hold the question. It means the return of Christ isn't a date to work out or a countdown to manage; it's a horizon that steadies you. What stays is the practical shape of your days: hope that makes you patient in ordinary work, honest in small dealings, and steady when things are hard. So it's fine to let this shape how you live, as long as you don't turn it into a timetable.

prompt: I have peace with God but still feel anxious day by day—what is the peace of heart I'm missing?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that this is a real and honest question, and there's nothing wrong with asking it. You've named something many people carry quietly: peace with God settled, but the heart still restless day to day. One principle I'd weigh here is that feelings are not the gauge of your acceptance with God—you should trust the changeless word of promise rather than variable moods, and keep on in prayer even when joy is lacking. What that changes is how you read your own anxiety: it's not evidence that something is broken between you and God. What stays is the anxiety itself—it's still real, still worth tending, and still worth bringing honestly to God and to a trusted person. So this is fine, and fine with care: don't let a flat or fearful day become a verdict on your standing, and don't ignore the practical side of worry either.

prompt: Is consecration something I do for God, or something God does in me?
completion: I'd start by saying: yes, it's both, and that's not a dodge. Take the first principle in its own words — we are no longer our own, and we should keep ourselves free from binding engagements because we don't know when the LORD may call. That reframes what your part is. Your consecration isn't a contract you sign and lock in; it's a keeping-free, a yielding to a claim that's already on you. What changes is the tone of your commitment — less a vow you enforce on yourself, more an open hand. What stays is that you really do act: you dedicate, you yield, you respond. And God's side stays too — He's the one setting you apart and making you holy. So it's fine, and fine with care: don't turn your dedication into a cage you built.

prompt: What does it mean to be sanctified wholly—is any part of my life allowed to be held back?
completion: I'd start by saying: yes, whole sanctification does mean nothing held back—but hear that as gift, not as a demand you grind out. The principle I'd weigh is that sanctification is the gift of the Holy Ghost and the grace of Christ, a divine holiness received by faith, not human self-improvement or painful mortification. That changes the tone of your question: the point isn't you white-knuckling every corner of your life into order, it's consenting as God shows you what's closed. What stays is the honesty—there really is no compartment you get to keep as a private reserve. So it's fine, and fine with care: don't turn it into self-punishment, and don't let 'it's a gift' become an excuse to hold something back.

prompt: My love for Christ feels stagnant—how does love grow?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that this is a fine thing to be asking, and nothing here needs to be refused. Take the principle that says love is to abound yet more and more — abundant, increasing, progressing, with the motto 'more and more.' That's the one I'd weigh, because it speaks directly to your feeling of being stuck. What it changes is the assumption that stagnant means finished; it reframes where you are as a place to grow from, not a verdict on you. What stays is your honesty about the dryness and whatever limits you've named — the tiredness, the schedule, the sense that feelings aren't cooperating. Those aren't obstacles to the principle, they're the ground it works on. So keep the small spaces you actually have, think on Him there, and let 'more and more' be a direction rather than a demand. This is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: Can God really count me worthy when I know I'm not worthy in myself?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is: yes, and your honesty about not being worthy in yourself is not a problem for God—it's the right starting place. The principle I'd weigh here is that God counts the believer worthy of his calling not for any personal worthiness but for the worthiness wrought by grace, while the believer remains responsible for his use of grace. That changes the question from 'am I worthy?' to 'am I trusting the grace that makes me worthy?' What stays is your own honest sense that you're not enough on your own—that's true, and grace doesn't ask you to pretend otherwise. So this is fine, and fine with care: keep being honest about your lack, and keep using the grace you've been given rather than sitting still.

prompt: I want to obey God's commands but feel I have no power to do so—what does the Gospel offer me?
completion: What I'd say first is that this struggle isn't a sign you're outside the Gospel — it's the very place the Gospel meets you. Take one principle, in its own words: God's commands are promises, and what He requires He gives, so His precepts are assurances that He will keep you from the sin He warns against. That reframes your question. You're not being asked to dredge up power you don't have; you're being asked to treat each command as a promise to lean on. What that changes is where you look when you feel weak — not inward for willpower, but to the God who supplies. What stays is exactly what you said: you don't have the power in yourself, and that's still true. The Gospel doesn't tell you to pretend otherwise; it tells you to bring that inability to God and trust Him for the strength to obey. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care — hold the commands as promises, and let your lack of strength be the reason you turn to Him rather than the reason you give up.

prompt: Is it really possible to love everybody, including people I find thoroughly unlovable?
completion: I'd say yes, with care, and I'd start with the distinction that makes it possible: loving and liking aren't the same thing. You can love someone with the love of compassion even when you can't love them with the love of complacency—wishing them good, bearing with them, without pretending you enjoy them. That distinction changes what's being asked of you: it's not a demand to feel fondness for people who've hurt you, it's a direction of the will. What stays is your honesty about who you find unlovable and your right to keep real distance from people who are harmful. Loving someone in this sense doesn't mean handing them access to you.

prompt: How do I direct my heart into the love of God when I feel distant from Him?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is: the distance you feel isn't the same as being abandoned, and you don't have to fix it by sheer effort. One of these principles says that for the right practice of the presence of God the heart must be empty of all other things, because God will possess the heart alone and cannot act in it unless it be left vacant to Him. That's worth weighing, but notice what it does and doesn't mean. It doesn't mean you must clear your heart before you're allowed to come near; it means the competing loves—the noise, the busyness, the disappointments you're clinging to—are what crowd out the sense of His love. So what changes is the direction of your effort: less straining to feel something, more gently setting aside what fills the space. What stays is everything ordinary—honest prayer, Scripture, the Psalms, fellowship, confession, serving others. You asked how to direct your heart; that's a fine thing to want, and it's fine to pursue it with care, at the pace of a season rather than a verdict.

prompt: How can I be sincere in my motives when I can't even fully know my own heart?
completion: I'd start by saying: you're not alone in this, and the fact that you're asking the question is already a kind of sincerity. One principle here says purity of heart grows through specific means—rooting out habitual imperfections, guarding your senses, living in recollection, and laying your whole interior open to a spiritual director with candor. What that changes is the assumption that sincerity is something you generate by introspection. It isn't; it's cultivated, and part of the cultivation is letting someone else see what you can't. What stays is your limit: you still won't fully know your own heart, and that's fine. The point was never perfect self-knowledge. So this is fine, with care—be candid with someone trustworthy, keep watch over the small habits, and don't demand of yourself a clarity you were never promised.

prompt: How does the Lord actually guide a person—through feelings, through Scripture, through circumstances?
completion: I'd start where you're already leaning: yes, God can guide through feelings, Scripture, and circumstances, but they don't carry equal weight. Take the principle that the Lord directs hearts by His Word, by His Holy Spirit dwelling within, and by His Providence in daily circumstances. That's a wide, generous picture of guidance, and it fits your question well. What it changes is that feelings aren't dismissed outright—the Spirit does incline the heart—but they're never the judge on their own. Scripture stays the clearest test, circumstances are read with humility, and feelings get weighed rather than obeyed. What stays is your instinct to ask the question at all: pray for wisdom, stay in the Word, seek mature counsel, and treat guidance as a process you can adjust along the way. So this is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: What does it actually mean to be holy—is it about being purified or about something else?
completion: What you're really asking is whether holiness is just cleanup or something more, and I'd say it's more—but purification still belongs inside it, not before it. Take the principle that sanctification is the gift of the Holy Ghost and the grace of Christ, a divine holiness received by faith, not human self-improvement or painful mortification. That changes how you pursue it: you're not grinding yourself clean by willpower, you're receiving a gift and learning to walk in it. What stays is your instinct that purification matters; it's just not the whole picture. Holiness is belonging wholly to God and letting that belonging shape your days, and that's fine—fine with care, because it's easy to turn a gift into a project.

prompt: I'm facing prolonged trials and feel like giving up—how do I find the patience of Christ?
completion: I'd start by saying: what you're carrying sounds heavy, and feeling like giving up after a long stretch is human, not shameful. One principle worth weighing is that the soul must be patient and wait upon the Lord, taking whatsoever befalls it from his hands as intended for its highest good. That reframes your trial as something received rather than something you have to white-knuckle through alone, and it gives you a reason to keep going that isn't just willpower. What it changes is the posture: patience becomes trust rather than gritted teeth. What stays is everything practical you already know helps, prayer, one day at a time, people who can pray with you, rest, and professional help if the weight gets too much. So this is fine, and fine with care, especially the care of not isolating yourself.

prompt: I'm surrounded by attractive but questionable teaching—how do I discern what is dangerous?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: you're not being paranoid, and wanting to tell the difference is itself a good sign. Of the principles in front of me, the one that fits your situation is the one about teaching in the name of Truth but contrary to its spirit being dangerous quackery, while strict adherence to the divine Principle and its rules is what secures anything real. That changes how I'd look at the teachers around you: I'd stop grading them on charisma and start asking whether what they say actually holds together with the truth they claim to serve, or just borrows its language. What stays is your own judgment—you still have to weigh each claim, and you're allowed to ask hard questions and walk away. So this is fine to do, with care: test the teaching, not the personality, and don't let attractiveness do the work that discernment should.

prompt: Can love and clear-eyed judgment coexist, or does love mean suspending discernment?
completion: I'd start by saying no, love doesn't require you to switch off your judgment. The principle I keep coming back to is that love 'abounds in full knowledge and all discernment' so you can tell things apart and hold onto what's genuinely good. That reframes the whole question: clear sight isn't the opposite of love, it's part of how love works. What changes is the picture of love as blind surrender; what stays is your instinct that love should be warm and generous rather than cold and calculating. Both can be true at once, and you don't have to choose.

prompt: What is the difference between knowing God's will and knowing God Himself?
completion: I'd start by saying these aren't rivals, and you're right to hold them together. Take the first principle as it's worded: the will of God known and done is the secret of all true living, and the prayer is that you'd be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding. That lifts knowing his will above a checklist of decisions—it's something you're filled with, and it grows. What that changes is the framing: it's not will versus Person, it's the Person's will shaping how you live. What stays is your instinct that knowing him is the deeper thing, because that's where the filling comes from. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care—keep asking both questions, and don't let the search for specific direction crowd out the relationship.

prompt: I've been toiling for a long time without seeing fruit and am tempted to think it's in vain—what should I do?
completion: What I'd say first is that your weariness is not the same as failure, and you shouldn't let it talk you into quitting on its own. Weigh this one: "The nearer we come to Christ the more willing we are to be lost sight of in our fruit, letting others be prominent while we hold up their hands by silent love and prayer." That reframes what you're looking for—fruit you can see and count versus faithfulness that may stay hidden. What it changes is your measure of success; what stays is the honest question of whether the work itself is sound. So it's fine to keep going, and fine with care: check your methods, get real feedback, rest, and let some of the fruit be invisible without deciding that means nothing is happening.

prompt: I've been hindered from returning to friends I long to see—should I pray about something so ordinary as travel and open doors, or is that too small for God?
completion: I'd say first: yes, pray about the trip. The principle I'd weigh is the one that calls prayer sober, matter-of-fact business with God, who answers prayer for supplies and protection. That's the whole point here—travel and open doors are exactly the kind of ordinary thing that fits. What it changes is the tone: you don't have to dress it up or wait for a crisis to make it worthy. What stays is your situation as you described it—you're hindered, you long to see friends, and you're asking whether this is too small. It isn't. Name the hindrances plainly, ask for clear passage and safety, and keep planning and saving alongside. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: How do I distinguish between what is good and what is best in the choices before me?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that you're not really asking for a rule, you're asking how to weigh things, and that's a fine thing to ask. Take the first principle in its own words: to be great is to be good before the heavens and before all good men. That reframes your question. You're not sorting options into impressive and unimpressive; you're asking which one lets you be good, plainly and in front of people who can see you. What that changes is the pressure to pick whatever looks biggest or most impressive. What stays is that you still have to choose, and some good options will simply be smaller than others. So test each choice by whether it keeps you honest and kind when no one is clapping. That's a fine way to decide, and it's fine with care, because it takes time and you may not get a clean answer.

prompt: Why does fellowship with other believers matter for my spiritual growth if my faith is personal?
completion: I'd start by saying your faith being personal is not the problem, and nothing here asks you to give that up. One principle puts it this way: the vague impulse to reach beyond our isolated self gives place, when God is known as Father in Christ, to actual social fellowship with a personal Friend and Companion. That's what changes: the pull you already feel toward other believers isn't a distraction from a private faith, it's that impulse becoming real and shared. What stays is your own relationship with God, which fellowship supports rather than replaces. So this is fine, and fine with care. Keep the personal side; let it grow into company rather than stay alone.

prompt: How can Christ be glorified in an ordinary life like mine?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, this is fine, and it's fine with care. The principle that settles it for me is the first one: Christ is to be glorified in us and we are to be glorified in Christ, a reciprocal glory, so that people around us see something of Christ as they associate with us. That means your ordinary life is exactly the place this happens. It doesn't need to be dramatic to count. What changes is that you stop measuring your days against grand gestures and start seeing faithfulness in your work, your relationships, and your duties as the actual arena. What stays is the caution: keep the focus on Him shining through you rather than on your own performance, and don't let smallness become an excuse for coasting. Your limits are real, and they don't disqualify you from this.

prompt: How do I keep a moment of consecration from fading into ordinary life?
completion: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. The principle that helps most is the first one: consecration means we are no longer our own, so we keep ourselves free from binding engagements because we don't know when the Lord may call. That reframes your worry. You're not trying to keep a feeling alive; you're trying to stay available. So what changes is the goal—less about preserving the high, more about not cluttering your life with things that would make you slow to answer. What stays is your ordinary life, which is exactly where that availability gets tested. Keep the moment in memory, sure, but let it show up as freedom and readiness rather than as a shrine you maintain.

prompt: I've become morbid and self-focused in my pursuit of holiness—how do I get out of that?
completion: I'd start by saying: what you're describing sounds less like a spiritual problem to be refused and more like a trap you've noticed and want out of, and that noticing is itself a good sign. The principle I'd weigh first is that being occupied unduly with yourself in the matter of holiness makes you self-centred, morbid, fearful, and weak, while being occupied with God makes you restful, quiet, strong, confident, and growing in grace. That reframes the fix: it isn't more self-scrutiny, it's a change of what you're looking at. What that changes is the direction of your attention—toward God's faithfulness rather than your own fluctuating state. What stays is your real desire to grow; that doesn't get thrown out, it just gets re-homed. Keep the limits you've set: don't turn this into another project to manage, and don't let anyone push you into harsh self-denial as a cure for self-focus, since that would just feed the same loop. Talk to someone you trust, keep it simple, and let service and prayer pull you outward.

prompt: Is prayer supposed to be easy? Mine feels like a struggle and I wonder if I'm doing it wrong.
completion: What I'd say first is: no, you're not doing it wrong. Struggling in prayer doesn't mean you've failed at it. One principle worth weighing here is that prayer is a duty and a privilege to be kept at set times whether or not you feel like it — so the dryness you're describing isn't the measure of whether it's working. What that changes is the pressure to feel something profound every time; what stays is that you keep showing up, gently, at whatever rhythm actually fits your life. Try different forms if it helps — written prayers, silence, a walk — and be patient with yourself. If it keeps feeling heavy, talking to a trusted friend or spiritual leader is a good idea.

prompt: I feel weak and want to know the power of God in my life—what is that power like?
completion: What I'd say first is that you're not asking for something out of bounds—wanting to know God's power in your weakness is a good and honest thing. Weigh this: "the exceeding greatness of God's power toward believers is the same power wrought in Christ at the resurrection, the ascension, the subjection of all things under His feet, and His headship over the Church—man needs not merely a philosophy or ethic but a dynamic." That changes how you picture power: not a mood you work up, but the same strength that raised Jesus and set him over everything, and it's turned toward you. What stays is your weakness—it isn't a disqualifier, and I'm not going to tell you to grit your teeth and feel strong. So this is fine, and fine with care: ask God to open your eyes to what he's already given, and let it show up in courage, love, and hope rather than in claims.

prompt: I long for peace of conscience but my past still weighs on me—where does that peace come from?
completion: I'd start by saying: your longing for peace is good, and it's fine to pursue it with care. One principle worth weighing says that a guilty conscience and unrepented sin tend to destroy the ability to do right, and that sin not regretted and lessening hastens toward moral and physical ruin. That changes something real: peace isn't found by skipping past what you've done. It stays true that the weight you feel may be pointing at something you haven't yet faced honestly. But it doesn't mean you're trapped, and it doesn't mean peace depends on you fixing yourself first. So begin with honest repentance, and let the dread of your own unsureness keep you meek rather than presumptuous, while the mercy shown to you keeps you from sinking into despair. What stays is this: peace comes not from your virtue but from love received by a repentant heart, and the memory of your past may remain without condemning you.

prompt: Can I have real peace with God while being at odds with fellow believers?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, you can have real peace with God even while a relationship with another believer is strained, and that's worth saying plainly before anything else. The principle I'd weigh here is that war and contention come from wickedness and the lack of God's Spirit, not from God's design. That reframes your question: the conflict itself isn't proof you've lost peace with God, but it does ask you to look honestly at where the strife is coming from in you. What changes is that you stop treating the tension as a verdict on your standing with God; what stays is that unresolved conflict still deserves honest attention, forgiveness where you've been wronged, and repentance where you've wronged others. So this is fine, with care.

prompt: How do I pray for people I've never met and don't know?
completion: I'd start by saying: you don't need to know someone to pray for them, and you don't need details to pray well. The principle I'd weigh is the one about habit: we cannot pray without being with God, cannot be with Him but by thinking of Him often, and cannot think of Him often but by a holy habit. That reframes your question a little. It says the praying for strangers grows out of a life of prayer rather than a technique you deploy. So what changes is that you don't have to hunt for information or feel guilty about not knowing them; what stays is that this is still real prayer, offered to a God who knows them better than you do. Ask Him to give them what they most need. Keep it regular rather than occasional, and let it be short. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I keep failing and doubting God will finish what He started in me—what can I rest on?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that you're not being asked to manufacture a feeling of certainty before you're allowed to rest. You asked what you can rest on, and the honest answer is not your record. Take the principle that says the real secret of rest is to be jealously, habitually occupied with Jesus. That's the one I'd weigh, and notice what it does: it moves your attention off the scoreboard of your failures and onto Him. It doesn't deny the failures are real. What it changes is where you're looking while you keep going. What stays is your honesty about doubting, and the plain fact that growth is slow and uneven. So this is fine, and fine with care: keep turning your attention back to Him when the doubt spikes, confess what needs confessing, and don't measure how it's going by how you feel on a given day.

prompt: Is it enough to know Bible facts, or is there something more I need?
completion: I'd start by saying: no, facts alone aren't enough, and that's fine to admit. Take the principle that the Scriptures must be read as a whole, not piecemeal, and that the aim is to know Jesus, not merely to know about him. That reframes your question without dismissing study. What changes is the goal of your reading; what stays is that learning facts is still good and worth doing. So keep studying, but read expecting to meet the person behind the pages, and let what you learn move you toward trust and love rather than just a fuller notebook.

prompt: I've been trying to grow in holiness but feel unsettled about whether I'm truly accepted by God—where should I start?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: you don't have to earn your way into being accepted. What you're describing sounds less like a holiness problem and more like a loop of self-inspection, and I'd gently point you away from that. One principle puts it this way: being occupied unduly with yourself in the matter of holiness makes you self-centred, morbid, fearful, and weak, while being occupied with God makes you restful, quiet, strong, confident, and growing in grace. That changes where you start—begin with God's character and faithfulness rather than with a ledger of your own sins and motives. What stays is real growth in holiness; this isn't a pass on that. But the assurance you're chasing comes from resting in God, not from intensifying the introspection. So start there, and let the unsettled feeling settle as you look at him instead of at yourself.

prompt: How do I keep my devotion from becoming thoughtless, or my study of theology from becoming dry and fruitless?
completion: I'd start by saying: you're not asking how to choose between devotion and theology, you're asking how to keep each from hollowing out. That's a good instinct, and it's fine to pursue it with care. Take the first principle in its own words: beware of untheological devotion and of undevotional theology, since it is the heart that makes the theologian. That reframes your question. Thoughtless devotion isn't fixed by adding more feeling; it's fixed by devotion that actually thinks. And dry study isn't fixed by adding more study; it's fixed by study that carries the heart with it. What changes: you stop treating prayer and reading as two separate tracks that compete for your time, and you stop measuring either by intensity alone. What stays: your ordinary habits still matter, and you still have to show up to both. So keep praying before you study, keep letting what you learn push you toward God, and don't be alarmed when some seasons feel drier than others. That's fine, and it's fine with care.

prompt: I'm clever and well-educated but feel spiritually dull—why is that?
completion: I'd start by saying this isn't a strange thing to feel, and it isn't a sign you've done something wrong. One principle worth weighing says that wisdom and revelation come through the full knowledge of God in personal fellowship, and that spiritual insight is due solely to fellowship with God—independent of intellectual conception and verbal expression—so that believers of slight natural education may have uncommon spiritual perception. What that changes: your education isn't the problem, and it isn't the cure either. What stays: the dullness is real, and it points toward fellowship rather than more information. So this is fine to bring up, and fine to work on with care—turn toward God Himself, not just ideas about Him.

prompt: How do I let Christ actually rule in the deepest parts of my life?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that this is a good thing to want, and nothing in it needs to be refused. If I weigh the first principle in its own words—Christ dwelling within conquers what we never could overcome, so the question shifts from what is the best I can do to what is the best Christ can do—that reframes your effort without canceling it. What changes is the pressure: you're not white-knuckling your way to a surrendered heart. What stays is everything you actually named: the hidden desires, the habits, the honest work of paying attention to where you still grip the wheel. So keep praying, keep examining, keep acting on what obedience asks—just stop treating your resolve as the engine. Let it be the response to something already at work in you.

prompt: I have good desires but never seem to bring them to good effect—what am I missing?
completion: What I'd say first is that you're not missing a trick—the desire itself is a gift, and the help to carry it through comes with it. Take the principle that God first puts good desires into our minds and then by His continual help enables us to bring them to good effect. That changes the frame: you're not manufacturing effort from nothing, you're cooperating with something already underway. What stays is the practical part—name the desire, pick one concrete next step, set a time, cut the friction, review it weekly. So this is fine, and fine with care: don't turn the practical steps into self-generated striving, and don't expect the whole thing to land in a day.

prompt: I find it easy to pray for my own needs but rarely for others—does that reveal something wrong with my spiritual life?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is: noticing this about yourself is not the same as being caught out. You asked whether it reveals something wrong, and I'd say it reveals something human more than something broken. Take the principle that prayer is a duty and a privilege to be kept at set times whether or not you feel like it, and that we should pray with our families and never ask God to do what we're unwilling to do ourselves. That principle doesn't accuse you of a scandal; it just says prayer is a practice, not a mood. What that changes is the framing: instead of hunting for what's spiritually defective in you, you can put a few names on a list and bring them at a fixed time, and let the habit carry you when the feeling doesn't. What stays is your honesty—you're not pretending your prayers are broader than they are, and that honesty is worth keeping. So this is fine, and fine with care: keep praying for your own needs, and add others by name, small and steady.

prompt: How do I keep love from being just a warm feeling and make it real and practical?
completion: What I'd say first is that you're asking the right question, and the answer isn't to distrust every warm feeling you have. One principle worth weighing says self-love never dies, it sleeps like a fox and springs suddenly, so we have to be constantly watchful and patiently defend ourselves against it. That's true, but notice the word patiently. It doesn't ask you to sit and dissect your motives all day. So what changes is this: you can stop trying to purify your feelings before you act, and you can stop treating every mixed motive as a crisis. What stays is the practical part, the kind word, the quiet help, the quick forgiveness, the showing up when it costs you. Do those, and when you catch yourself acting for your own credit, set it down gently and get back to the person in front of you. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: How can I be sure I'm actually being guided by God and not just following my own preference?
completion: I'd start by saying this is a fine thing to want, and fine to pursue with care. Take the first principle on its own terms: "when Word, Spirit, and Providence agree we may be sure the guidance has been given." That's the test I'd hand you, and it's a real one, not a mood check. What it changes is that you don't have to sit in permanent uncertainty about whether it's just your preference — you have three things to line up, and you can actually look at whether they do. What stays is your honesty about the difficulty: agreement across all three is the aim, and where they don't yet agree, you wait rather than force it. So yes, this is fine — go slowly, check your desires against Scripture, watch how circumstances unfold, and don't demand certainty before you've done that work.

prompt: I want to live to the glory and praise of God until the day of Christ—what does that look like day by day?
completion: I'd start by saying this is a good thing to want, and nothing in it needs to be refused. The principle I'd weigh first is this: Christ in you is the hope of glory, the secret hidden from ages—if Christ is in you, the 'I' goes and He becomes your purity, grace, and strength.
