That changes the shape of your day more than it changes your goal. Instead of measuring each morning by how well you performed, you'd begin by acknowledging He's already living in you, and let obedience flow from love rather than duty. What stays is everything you described: prayer, Scripture, gratitude, serving your family and church, confessing when you fail. What shifts is the pressure—you're not striving to manufacture a life that glorifies God, you're resting in the One who does. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care: keep the direction, drop the scorekeeping.

prompt: How do love and holiness fit together in a daily Christian life?
completion: I'd start by saying this is a good question, and the short answer is that it's fine to hold love and holiness together in your daily life, with care. Take the first principle seriously on its own terms: holiness is the fundamental attribute of God, and love must have a norm, and that norm is found only in holiness. That means your love isn't self-defined; it's shaped by what God calls good. What that changes is the order of your thinking, so you don't treat kindness as the whole story and let boundaries slide. What stays is everything you already sensed: love without holiness goes soft, holiness without love goes cold, and both belong in ordinary habits like honesty, purity, forgiveness, and service. Keep your limits in view, stay humble about your own failures, and return to grace when you stumble.

prompt: I'm not intellectual but I long to know Christ deeply—is that possible for me?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is: yes, this is fine, and your longing itself is a real beginning. I'd weigh the principle that says wisdom and revelation come through fellowship with God, so that believers of slight natural education may have uncommon spiritual perception. That changes things for you—it means deep knowledge of Christ doesn't depend on being clever or well-read. What stays is this: it's still knowledge of a person, grown through honest prayer, reading the Gospels simply, and actually doing what you understand. So keep your longing, bring it to Christ, and don't let the lack of a scholarly mind hold you back.

prompt: I don't want my life to be a stumbling-block to others—how do I become a stepping-stone instead?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that wanting your life to be a stepping-stone rather than a stumbling-block is a good desire, and nothing in it needs to be refused. But I'd weigh one principle carefully against the way you asked the question: "We must devote ourselves to the portion of the path immediately before us rather than desiring the last step before accomplishing the first." That changes the shape of the answer. You don't need a grand plan for becoming a stepping-stone; you need the next small, concrete thing—the apology you owe, the conversation you've been avoiding, the habit you know is tripping someone up. What stays is the goal itself: humility, integrity, love, being quick to admit fault. What drops away is any pressure to fix your whole character at once. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care: keep it close to home, one step at a time, and don't let the ambition to be a stepping-stone turn into another way of stumbling.

prompt: I'm so busy serving that my prayer life has shrunk to almost nothing—how do I recover a life of prayer?
completion: What I'd say first is that you're not being asked to choose between serving and praying, and nothing here says your service is wrong. The principle I'd weigh is this one: prayer is no petty duty put into a corner or made of fragments of time; the best of our time and the heart of our time and strength must be given. That's a real claim, and it does push back on the idea that prayer can just be squeezed in whenever. But you've told me your prayer life has shrunk to almost nothing because you're so busy serving, and that changes how the principle lands. It doesn't tell you to abandon your duties or to feel guilty for the season you're in. It tells you to give prayer the best you can actually give, not the leftovers, and to start where you are. So a short, protected time each day, the best of what you have rather than an impossible ideal, is fine, and fine with care. What stays is the call to give God your real attention, not scraps. What changes is the scale: your best right now may be small, and that's allowed.

prompt: I want to grasp the love of Christ but it feels too vast—how do I even begin?
completion: What I'd say first is: you don't have to take it all in at once, and the fact that it feels too vast isn't a failure on your part. One principle here says knowing the love of Christ that passes knowledge is the climax of spiritual experience—a knowing by personal experience that surpasses knowledge, with infinite stretches of love beyond our highest experiences. That changes how I'd answer you: the goal isn't to get your arms around it, because you never will, and you're not supposed to. What stays is your starting point—small, concrete, today. Read one Gospel scene where Christ shows compassion, slowly. Pray simply, 'Show me your love,' and watch for it in Scripture, in the sacraments, in other people's kindness, in your own conscience. Touch one wave; the ocean teaches you from there.

prompt: How do I know God's will for my life in a specific decision?
completion: I'd say first: this is a fine thing to want, and fine to pursue with care. Take the principle that says the believer should be slow to take new steps, seek to have no will of his own, and ascertain God's will by prayer, the Word, and the Spirit, then seek His help earnestly and expectantly. What that changes is the pace and the posture: you don't have to force a fast answer, and you don't have to pretend you have no preferences. What stays is your actual decision, made with the information and freedom you have. So pray, read Scripture, get honest counsel, and then choose, trusting God to guide and redirect.

prompt: I feel discouraged comparing myself to the heights of the Christian life—should I be?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: no, you shouldn't be discouraged, and comparing yourself to the heights of the Christian life isn't wrong in itself—it's fine, with care. One principle I'd weigh is this: while we're in this life it's full speedful to see both at once—the higher beholding of God that keeps us in spiritual solace and true enjoying, and the lower beholding of self that keeps us in dread and makes us ashamed—but we should hold us much more in the higher. That changes the shape of your comparison: it's not you against the saints, it's you before God, and the higher beholding should outweigh the lower. What stays is your honest sense of your own limits—your temperament, your season of life, the small steps you can actually take. Those limits are real, and the lower beholding shouldn't crush you into despair; it should keep you humble. So keep looking up more than you look down, and don't let the heights of others become a scoreboard.

prompt: Can I be holy if I still have obvious flaws and blemishes in my life?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, and I'd want to be careful about what that yes means. You're asking whether obvious flaws and blemishes rule out holiness, and I don't think they do. Take the first principle seriously: one does not become holy all at once, and we help one another by advice and yet more by good examples. That fits your situation exactly. Holiness grows; it isn't a finished state you either have or don't. So your flaws don't disqualify you, and you don't need to hide them or pretend they're gone. What stays is the honesty part: bring the blemishes into the light, let people who care about you speak into them, and keep moving. What changes is the despair. You don't have to wait until you're spotless to begin. It's fine, and it's fine with care.

prompt: I feel my prayers are too bold or too high to be answered—should I scale them down?
completion: I'd say first: no, don't shrink your prayers to fit your fear. The principle I'd weigh is that a little lifting up of the heart suffices—a brief inward remembrance, one act of worship, is a prayer very acceptable to God. That changes the scale question: boldness isn't measured in length or volume, so you don't need big words to ask big things. What stays is your honesty about feeling out of your depth—that's fine, and it's fine to pray briefly and simply. Keep the request as large as it truly is, and let it be short if that's what you can manage.

prompt:

completion: Yes, that changes things. I would change my answer because the new fact is that he has explicitly asked you not to pray for him, and that request matters. prompt:

prompt:

prompt:

prompt:

prompt:
